articles.title: 1,000 Patriot missiles arrive too late for this winter, so Ukraine asked the Ramstein arms coalition to open its warehouses
articles.body:
Ukraine is contracting about 1,000 missiles for its American-made Patriot air defense systems, but most arrive only in later years, so at the Ramstein meeting of its allies it asked for interceptors out of their existing stocks before winter, the Defense Ministry said. Nine governments announced new contributions there, and Germany was the only one to commit interceptors from its own stocks. The Ramstein format meeting is the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, a coalition of roughly 50 countries that coordinates weapons for Ukraine, named after the US air base in Germany where it first met in 2022.
Ukraine contracts for later, asks for stock now
Ukraine's Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara told partners the country is signing for roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles, whose PAC-3 version is the only round in its arsenal that reliably stops Russian ballistic missiles, paid for with partner support and the European Union's credit line. Those deliveries take time. So Ukraine asked allies to release missiles from their warehouses now and take the improved contracted rounds later. It made the same case for air-to-air missiles and shoulder-fired launchers, which crews use against cruise missiles and, as a stopgap, against the jet-powered Shahed attack drones, the Iranian-designed weapons Russia now flies at Ukrainian cities by day.
The European Commission cleared the loan money for interceptors days earlier. How many rounds it buys depends on the price Washington sets.
What partners pledged
The ministry listed the results by country.
- 
Germany promised interceptors for Patriot systems and for F-16 fighter jets, plus drone purchases.
- 
The United Kingdom put up £100 million ($135 million) through PURL, short for the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List, the NATO mechanism that lets allied and partner governments buy US-made arms for Ukraine. London added another 95,000 drones by the end of the year and tens of thousands of extended-range artillery shells financed by other countries.
- 
The Netherlands pledged $300 million for the Drone Line, Ukraine's program that holds a drone-strike zone over the front, and 300 counter-drone missiles.
- 
Estonia committed to keep its support at at least 0.25% of its economic output in 2027.
- 
Norway confirmed a previously announced $200 million for Patriot missiles.
- 
Spain gave €2 million ($2.3 million) for fuel through NATO's procurement agency, plus air-defense missiles and artillery ammunition.
- 
Lithuania put $10 million into PURL.
- 
Poland prepared a €50 million ($58 million) package including air-defense equipment.
- 
Sweden pledged $28 million, half of it to PURL.
It was the coalition's 36th session, co-chaired online by Germany and the United Kingdom according to the German Defense Ministry's invitation, and the first for Khmara and for Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi, the general who took over Ukraine's army in July.
Brussels cleared Ukraine to spend EU loan money on American Patriot missiles for the coming winter of Russian attacks
Germany opens its own warehouse
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said he decided, alongside the NATO summit, to give Ukraine urgently needed PAC-2 interceptors, an older Patriot round, from the stocks of the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, before winter. Russia has announced it will attack Ukraine's energy system. He told the others to check their reserves and do the same.
Germany will also step up deliveries of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from the same stocks, the US-made rounds fighter jets fire at incoming drones and missiles, and keep delivering IRIS-T air defense systems, including serially produced guided missiles for them. Ukraine intends to order several thousand more IRIS-T rounds using the EU loan.
The money and the deadline
Allies allocated more than $10 billion over the past year for American weapons through PURL and the US foreign military sales program, $3.5 billion of it under the EU loan, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said. Khmara said partners promised €70 billion ($81 billion) this year, while Ukraine sees €62 billion, and the missing €8 billion is needed to meet that pledge, with the total defense deficit at €23 billion ($27 billion), according to the ministry's readout. He asked for those decisions by November. A day earlier, Ukraine handed the alliance a list of priority air- and missile-defense needs, the Defense Ministry reported.
Two timelines at the table
Elbridge Colby, the US under secretary of war for policy and the Pentagon's top policy official, told the group his department cannot predict when the war ends, that Russia is rebuilding its forces and defense industry, and that Ukraine's needs will persist for months and years. Europeans already lead on conventional defense and provide most of the support, he said.
Russia is expanding its manpower too, and by Ukraine's estimate plans to mobilize about 300,000 more soldiers this year and the same in 2027, Khmara said, Radio Svoboda reported. He presented the war plan Ukrainian forces now operate under, and said their drone kill zone stops Russian advances and kills more than 30,000 Russian soldiers a month, by the military's own count.

articles.title: Kiev wants advance Patriot shipments against unbought missiles
articles.body:
Kiev wants advance Patriot shipments against unbought missiles
Ukraine wants its Western donors to supply highly sought-after Patriot interceptors from their own stockpiles, which would be replenished later with 1,000 missiles that Kiev plans to purchase with EU money.
The unorthodox proposal was outlined on Tuesday by Ukrainian Defense Minister Evgeny Khmara during a video call with Western arms donors. It comes amid a global shortage of US-made weapons, with Ukraine competing for supplies against numerous other countries while arguing that its need to intercept Russian ballistic missiles should take priority.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky previously sought to secure 300 Patriot interceptors for the upcoming winter. His reported effort to impress US President Donald Trump with long-range strikes on Russian refineries and e-commerce warehouses has produced no clear results.
The attacks were allegedly intended to persuade Trump to approve additional Patriot supplies. Kiev also overspent Western donor funds while pursuing the strategy and has a $27 billion military budget deficit.
Speaking to members of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, Khmara said his country is contracting 1,000 Patriot missiles “through the EU loan,” but acknowledged that the purchase does not resolve the immediate shortage.
“The majority of these missiles will only start to be shipped in the coming years, which is why we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today in exchange for future improved missiles from our contracts,” he said.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said at the same meeting that Berlin is working to provide additional Patriot interceptors of the older PAC-2 model from its own stocks, along with air-to-air missiles that Ukraine uses against Russian drones and cruise missiles, including from Western-donated F-16 fighter jets.
Western Europe’s purse remains open for Kiev
The meeting, co-chaired by Pistorius and British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting, coincided with announcements from both the EU and the UK regarding their respective aid programs.
Together with @SecGenNATO Rutte, I welcome the agreement by Member States on the derogation for Ukraine to purchase crucial products for Patriot air defence systems.
The next disbursement of €3.2 billion will enable Ukraine to better protect its skies from Russia’s…
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced the disbursement of €3.2 billion ($3.7 billion) under the Ukraine Support Loan mechanism, saying the funds “will enable Ukraine to better protect its skies.”
The British government pledged a £100 million ($136 million) “winter air defense package,” with the money slated to be spent on US-made weapons through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) program.
Trump’s mediation efforts renewed
Trump has sought to distance the US from the Ukraine conflict, arguing that European NATO members should bear more of the burden of the prolonged hostilities with Russia. Last week, his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Moscow and Kiev as part of an effort to revive US-mediated peace talks.
The latest US proposal contains “worse” terms for Ukraine than those previously on the table, according to Ukrainian MP Anna Skorokhod. Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Alaska in August 2025 to discuss a possible off-ramp in the conflict, but Zelensky rejected key terms sought by Moscow.
In June, Zelensky announced a 40-day “pressure campaign” involving an escalation of long-range attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure and trade. Moscow retaliated with strikes that left Ukrainian ports effectively cut off from maritime routes.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1658: Ukraine’s new top commander is pushing to give combat-tested sergeants real authority
articles.body:
Exclusives
Team news
Vacancy: deputy editor-in-chief.
Military
Ukraine is sending its winning brigades to where the fighting is worst. The 46th just turned up outside Kramatorsk. Sloviansk and Kramatorsk are the last two big cities in the Donbas that Russia does not hold. The 46th Airmobile Brigade left the southeast in early July and reached them before anyone outside the army knew.
Trump’s peace envoys left, and Russia hit Kyiv with ballistics—the one thing Ukraine still struggles to stop. Only two ballistic missiles came down overnight, and the shortfall is now the centerpiece of what Kyiv is asking its allies to deliver.
Ukraine’s new top commander is pushing to unwind a Soviet-inherited command model mid-war. He wants combat-tested sergeants to have real authority. Ukraine inherited a system where officers decided everything and sergeants were senior soldiers with no ladder of their own.
Russia deploys missile brigade to Belarus as fears grow over new threat to Kyiv. The move comes as Russia steps up aerial attacks on Kyiv from the north and Belarus allows Moscow to use its territory to help guide strikes against Ukrainian targets.
Some ten robot boats. Five hundred Russian air sorties. One very lopsided hunt. Missions that once took a night now stretch to five days, and Russia keeps its fleet hidden, a naval drone unit commander says.
Intelligence and technology
Ukrainian engine for “Bars” missile-drone passes final tests. This is the last major imported component of the jet-powered drone used for deep strikes against Russia.
A Ukrainian strike drone that quietly hit 450-plus Russian targets steps out of the shadows. The drone pairs with a scout to punch through Russian jamming.
Ukraine’s new Hryfon Zakhid runs the whole drone chain on one screen. One operator assigns targets to drone crews from a tablet, in real time and without radio.
Ukrainian Armor unveils two new troop carriers at Polish arms exhibition: fast light scout and mine-resistant MRAP. Both meet NATO’s STANAG 4569 protection standards. Both cover opposite ends of the same job.
Ukraine shows a home-built missile designed to hit ballistic targets for the first time, the Koral, at Poland’s MSPO. Its guidance combines inertial navigation, radio correction, and an active radar homing head.
European NATO members may be the second target of Russia’s winter missile buildup—Ukraine’s foreign intelligence. The warning went to the national security advisors of Europe's leaders, with a call for urgent sanctions on 55 more firms keeping Russia's missile lines running.
Ukrainian AI targeting module placed third among 60-plus entries in NATO contest. NATO and Ukraine ran the challenge through their first jointly staffed body.
Ukrainian university and the Flamingo missile-maker opened an engineering course. On the first try, zero of 150 passed. Even students who scored well on the university entrance exam flunked the physics round.
Ukraine’s Brave1 says it can down Russia’s Banderol missiles with cruising speed 650 km/h for less than what they cost, and has destroyed at least four. In July, Ukrainian troops downed Banderols with Swedish Bofors L70 anti-aircraft guns designed in the late 1940s.
Ukraine has 67 companies working to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones en masse, Zelenskyy says. Only three to five have real results. He called the whole air-defense push "Plan B" to diplomacy's "Plan A".
China calls itself neutral—but its fiber ends up in the drones that hit Ukraine. The papers, reviewed by Western governments, trace drone-grade material straight from a Chinese state firm to a sanctioned Russian plant.
International
Brussels cleared Ukraine to spend EU loan money on American Patriot missiles for the coming winter of Russian attacks. The request went in four days earlier, and the funds come from the bloc's existing credit line rather than any new pledge.
Ukrainian journalist asks Trump’s envoy to his face whether he was disgusted to sit across from “international criminal” Putin. Witkoff wouldn’t answer directly. Earlier, Russia's FSB put a $400,000 bounty on Ukrainian journalist Dmytro Gordon.
Humanitarian and social impact
A Russian drone hit a Kyiv television newsroom in broad daylight while the channel was live on air. At least 5 people were injured, the building is partly destroyed, and firefighters put out the blaze at the site.
Russian-occupied nuclear plant ran on diesel for almost three weeks. Ukraine ended that, and the UN’s nuclear watchdog calls it a crucial step against an accident. The IAEA calls it a crucial step to prevent a nuclear accident at a site that had been facing a possible station blackout.
Russia burns occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant’s last-resort generators as everyday power, Ukraine says. Off-site power has been gone since 20 August, and the plant has cut its running generators to two to stretch the fuel that is left.
“Now on the 1,657th day”: Ukraine’s crews restored power to over 900,000 homes last week as Russia keeps striking grid before winter. Crews brought it back to 596 settlements, most of them in Odesa and Donetsk.
Kyiv stockpiles food and water as Russia’s new aerial tactics threaten a brutal winter. Russia has already targeted food storage around Kyiv, while Ukraine’s limited air defenses struggle to stop ballistic missiles and faster drones.
Political and legal developments
Russia’s FM says war must end so there is “no more Nazism” in Europe. Russian occupation official already said what that means: erasing Ukraine and stopping its aid. The collaborator put it plainly: "denazification is re-Russification".
Read our earlier daily review here.

articles.title: Everyone knows the F-35 has problems. So why is everyone buying it?
articles.body:
The F-35 was supposed to rule the skies. It can barely outrun its problems
The F-35 multi-role fifth-generation fighter has made headlines for various reasons: its deployment in the conflict with Iran, deliveries to nations participating in the F-35 program, new missiles designed for the aircraft, and staggering operational costs. Even though production of the F-35 has surpassed 1,000 units, doubts persist regarding the program’s overall effectiveness and the aircraft’s compliance with all the standards of a fifth-generation fighter. Let’s take a closer look.
In June 2015, a report by an American test pilot appeared online under the title “F-35A High Angle of Attack Operational Maneuvers.” It revealed that the latest F-35 was outperformed in a mock dogfight by the fourth-generation F-16D aircraft. Despite the F-35’s advertised advantages, it struggled to get behind the F-16D and lagged in energy maneuverability and pitch rate. What the media overlooked was that the test involved an experimental prototype of the F-35 that lacked operational combat software. Additionally, this prototype was restricted to a 5.5 G overload limit compared to the F-16’s ability to withstand up to 9 G. Once the F-35 received a full software update (starting with Block 3F), the upgraded versions decisively outperformed F-16s and other fourth-generation aircraft during Red Flag exercises – not through maneuverability, but by leveraging their stealth capabilities at long ranges without entering close combat.
Therefore, the main advantage of the F-35 fifth-generation fighter is its stealth capabilities. For the US, stealth is the defining characteristic of fifth-generation aircraft. This refers to the low radar cross-section achieved through the aircraft’s design and specialized coatings that disrupt radar wave reflection. The American strategy hinges on the belief that stealth aircraft can employ long-range missile systems while remaining undetected by enemy aircraft, effectively avoiding dogfights by striking the enemy from a distance.
The second major advantage of fifth-generation fighters is their capability for network-centric warfare, utilizing information systems that enable not only data sharing but also directing other aircraft and managing drones. An ‘invisible’ aircraft can detect adversaries either directly or through its wingmen and is capable of orchestrating attacks independently or by coordinating strikes with other planes and drones. Technically, the F-35 is already equipped for such operations.
Other characteristics of the F-35 are more problematic. For example, fifth-generation fighters have a powerful engine capable of sustained supersonic flight without using an afterburner. While the F-35 formally meets these criteria, the F-35B and F-35C variants are restricted from flying above Mach 1.2 for extended periods due to risks of thermal damage to their stealth coatings and tail surfaces. How can a supersonic jet not fly at supersonic speeds? Moreover, the F-35A appears to struggle with sustained supersonic cruising. Compounding these concerns are reports in the media regarding the P&W F135 engine. Reportedly, it faces issues like turbine blade wear, overheating, and a shortage of components for timely repairs.
On top of that, the operational cost of the F-35 is historically high. The total cost of the development and lifecycle of the F-35 has soared to nearly $2 trillion and continues to rise, making it the most expensive weapons system in history. For end users, however, the hourly flight cost is what truly matters. Operating an F-35 runs between $35,000 and $42,000 per hour, while standard F-16s operate at around $22,000 per hour. Overall, this is extremely expensive for a mass-produced fighter.
Another area where the F-35 falls short compared to its competitors, including Russia’s Su-57 and likely others, is maneuverability. Of course, if the ‘invisible’ fighter manages to hit its target undetected, it may never have to engage in a dogfight. But should close combat occur, the F-35 will face significant disadvantages against highly agile fifth- and even fourth-generation aircraft.
Those are some of the most obvious issues in the “generation conflict” between different aircraft iterations. However, there are deeper implications tied to the reliance on software and the high costs associated with the aircraft. The software for the F-35 is arguably the most complex in modern weaponry, encompassing over 24 million lines of code. Media outlets frequently report on coding errors and recall the 800+ “unresolved bugs” identified by Pentagon auditors. Yet, a sophisticated aircraft cannot function without powerful software, and this raises the question: How can one make such a complex software system secure?
Given that the F-35 clearly has its share of issues, it leads to another important question, namely: Why is it being produced in such massive quantities? Today, it stands as the only fifth-generation fighter jet in the Western world, with over 1,300 units already built and plans for another 2,000 on the way. In the next decade, more than 20 countries will incorporate these jets into their arsenals. So what’s behind this global trend?
The answer seems to lie not in the aircraft’s capabilities or technological advancements, but strictly in the political arena. The F-35 isn’t just a fighter; it is a symbol of close alignment with the US. Countries that purchase the F-35 gain certain privileges from Washington. For example, Israel possesses carte blanche for combat operations and unrestricted access to US weapons arsenals. As for Germany, it may be acquiring the F-35 because it’s currently the only aircraft on the market certified to carry US nuclear weapons within NATO’s nuclear sharing program. This factor may have played a decisive role in Germany’s decision.
Some countries – potentially South Korea, Japan, and Türkiye – are counting on the F-35’s network-centric warfare and a broad range of munitions while they develop their own viable alternatives to the ‘golden’ F-35. These nations are actively developing their own fifth-generation fighters and are even looking ahead to sixth-generation designs. However, they need a modern aircraft today, and therefore may be willing to overlook certain flaws of the “Battle Penguin” (the unofficial nickname for the F-35 due to its stout appearance). Maintaining strong ties with Washington is crucial for these countries as well. So political commitments and the urgency of having a contemporary fighter jet go hand in hand. After all, they aren’t going to buy Russian Su-57s, are they? Washington and Brussels wouldn’t like that. Though perhaps it wouldn’t be such a bad idea.

articles.title: Middle East live: US destroys five Iranian oil tankers as Iran threatens Kuwait and Bahrain
articles.body:
Middle East live: Tehran targets US base in Jordan after Washington destroys five Iranian tankers
Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Wednesday said it fired ballistic missiles at a base in Jordan used by the US military, attacked 10 ships, and threatened to strike tankers located off Kuwait and Bahrain in retaliation for US forces’ destruction of five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday. Follow our liveblog for the latest updates.
Iran Guards say war can end if US halts threats, meets demands
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday that the war with the US could end if Washington stopped threatening the Islamic republic and met Tehran's conditions, including regarding its nuclear programme.
"If the enemy wants an end to this situation, it must, while completely stopping the war, refrain from renewed threats, withdraw the Israeli regime's army from Lebanon, end the blockade of Yemen, release $24 billion in Iran's frozen assets and refrain from any interference in the country's nuclear and missile capabilities," IRGC Spokesman Hossein Mohebi said, according to the Fars news agency.
Iran says 'prohibited zone' near Hormuz to cover parts of Gulf of Oman and beyond
Iran's Guards said on Wednesday that a new "prohibited zone" outside the Strait of Hormuz would cover parts of the Gulf of Oman and beyond, adding they would announce the exact coordinates later.
"It approximately starts from the direction of Chabahar, covering part of the Sea of Oman and another part of the Arabian Sea... If a vessel enters that area without coordination, it will be subject to our sanctions," Guards spokesman Hossein Mohebi told state television.
Oil rises past $100 a barrel
The price of oil surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time since July after attacks on oil facilities and ships in the Middle East threatened to debilitate an already weakened supply chain.
Brent crude, the international standard, jumped nearly 3 percent to $100.72 early Wednesday. US benchmark crude gained 2.4 percent to $95.25 a barrel, and US gasoline prices rose sharply overnight. The average price for a gallon of regular gasoline ticked up 7 cents overnight to hit $4.22, now more than a dollar above what it cost at this point last year, according to AAA.
Diesel prices, which can have an outsized impact on consumers because it is used in shipping and production, hit an all-time high Friday and has continued to climb since. The average price for a gallon reached $5.94 overnight and is now 9 cents higher than it was Friday.
UK PM Burnham says Israel sanctions show Britain leading on 'world stage'
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said that sanctions on imports from Israeli settlements in the Israeli-occupied West Bank demonstrated Britain's "leadership on the world stage", arguing that support for a two-state solution must be backed by action.
"Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice. Where people are being bullied out of their homes, intimidated, we will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them," Burnham told British lawmakers.
Diplomatic row escalates as UK, France and Canada move to sanction Israeli settlements
Britain, France and Canada said Tuesday they will ban imports from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, with a UK minister accusing Israel of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians there.
The announcement prompted a furious Israel to unveil immediate counter-measures targeting Britain, as Jerusalem-based journalist Jordana Miller reports.
Iran condemns US attacks on tankers as threat to regional security
Iran's foreign ministry strongly condemned US strikes on its oil tankers, describing the attacks the previous day as a threat to regional security.
"The aggressive actions by the United States against Iranian commercial vessels not only increase the dangers of tensions in the region but are also considered an overt threat to regional and international peace and security," the ministry said in a statement, adding that Iranian forces had targeted US military facilities in the region in "self-defence".
IRGC says maritime restricted zone to extend into Gulf of Oman, Arabian Sea
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a maritime restricted area would extend from Chabahar in Iran into parts of the Gulf of Oman and the Arabian Sea, with its precise coordinates to be announced.
The announcement follows comments on Sunday by Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, who was quoted by state media as saying Iran would establish a restricted zone outside the Strait of Hormuz in the coming days.
'An intense night': What we know about the latest exchange of fire between Washington and Tehran
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said Wednesday they pummelled a US military base in Jordan, vowing retaliation for American strikes on Iranian oil tankers that dragged the foes deeper into war.
Tehran's bombs came after US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday in response to Iran targeting an American warship, the second such attack in less than a week.
FRANCE 24's Reza Sayah reports from Tehran, Iran.
US military denies reports of Iranian strikes on its warships
The US Central Command denied reports Iranian forces had hit its warships operating in the Middle East and said all attempted attacks had failed, in a post on X.
"Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces have claimed they struck two US Navy destroyers operating in the Middle East. This is completely FALSE," US CENTCOM said.
UK rejects Israel's 'damaging' retaliation over sanctions against West Bank settlers
British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband condemned as "regrettable and damaging" Israel's decision to order the closure of the UK's consulate in Jerusalem as retaliation for London-led Western sanctions over Israeli settler violence.
"We anticipated this might happen because we saw other countries, the Dutch, for example, who had announced sanctions, who had seen these reprisals from Israel. I think they're regrettable and damaging," Miliband told BBC Radio.
Israel on Tuesday ordered the closure after 12 countries including Britain, Canada and France announced they would sanction trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, following a surge in settler attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
Israel said it would also expel British representatives at a centre monitoring the US-brokered ceasefire plan in Gaza, bar British training for Palestinian Authority forces and ban 12 Britons, mostly members of parliament, from visiting the country.
But Miliband rejected suggestions that the sanctions would impact intelligence cooperation with Israel.
"We have important intelligence and security relationships with Israel, and I'm confident they will continue," he said, declining to go into details.
UK maritime monitor says it received report involving several merchant ships in the northern Gulf and Gulf of Oman
Several vessels in the Gulf region were on fire, a British maritime agency reported, after Iran said it had attacked 20 ships trying to pass through the Strait of Hormuz.
"Reports indicate the vessels were subject to disabling fire as part of ongoing military activity in the region," the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) said.
In Pictures: Families gather at remains of Iranian school destroyed in deadly US air strike
Families gather at the shattered remains of the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, Iran, on September 7, 2026, to grieve and remember more than 120 children killed by a US air strike on the first day of the US-Israeli war against Iran. Photos: Vahid Salemi, AP
Houthis report more than 30 Saudi strikes on several regions, the group's media says
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis reported more than 30 Saudi strikes on several regions, a day after the rebels launched major attacks on their neighbour, injuring dozens.
"Saudi aircraft launched 32 airstrikes on various areas across the governorates of Marib, Al-Jawf, Taiz and Hodeida over the past few hours," the rebels group's Almasirah television said.
Deadly fighting reignited in Yemen last week, when the Houthis launched a major campaign to seize territory near the Bab al-Mandab strait.
The strait has become an increasingly important route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, choking Gulf exports.
The latest fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, mostly combatants from both sides, according to an AFP tally based on sources from each camp.
Israel tells British consulate in East Jerusalem to close, sources say
Israel has informed the British consulate in East Jerusalem that it must close and that diplomats assigned there will lose their accreditation within 30 days, an Israeli official and a source familiar with the matter told Reuters.
British representatives assigned to a US-led Gaza coordination mission in Israel, as well as British diplomats based in Ramallah, must leave within seven days, the source familiar with the matter said.
Iran says it captured US submarine drone in Strait of Hormuz
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday it had captured a US uncrewed submarine at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz.
Iranian state media said the vessel was a Dive-LD, a large autonomous underwater vehicle built by California defense firm Anduril. The 5.8-metre submersible can carry out missions including mine countermeasures, seabed mapping, intelligence gathering and the inspection of underwater infrastructure such as cables and pipelines, the company has said.
"We trapped one of the most modern, intelligent and unmanned submarines of the terrorist American army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. This submersible is equipped with the latest technologies," the Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by Iranian state media.
In response, a Pentagon spokesperson said an underwater drone had "malfunctioned more than a day ago."
"It was surveying regional waters in support of ongoing operations. The defective drone was an older model that neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment," the spokesperson said.
Iran Guards say they attacked US vessels and oil tankers in Gulf
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said on Wednesday they attacked two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Gulf in response to what they called a US attack on five Iranian tankers, Iranian state media reported, citing a statement from the group.
The group said it attacked 10 ships attempting to cross what it described as a "prohibited and unsafe" area of the Strait of Hormuz.
Six commodity vessels transit Strait of Hormuz, below 10-day average
Six commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from nine a day earlier and below the 10-day average of about 12, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday.
The figures could change as some ships typically switch off their transponders during the voyage.
Of the six vessels, five were entering and one was exiting, initial data from shiptracker Kpler showed at 0200 GMT. They included one Panamax and one intermediate tanker.
Oil prices jump as Iran launches fresh attacks on US military assets
Oil prices jumped for the fourth straight session, gaining more than $1 in early trade on Wednesday after Iran launched fresh attacks on US military assets in the Gulf as the war between Washington and Tehran continued to spill out across the region.
Brent crude futures rose $1.57, or 1.6%, to $99.49 a barrel by 0001 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude was at $94.63 a barrel, up $1.60, or 1.72%.
Brent crude prices have jumped by a quarter since early August as hopes for a permanent resolution to the six-month-old war faded and as fighting flared again.
Jordan says air defences destroyed 18 Iranian ballistic missiles
Jordan's air-defence systems have destroyed 18 of 20 ballistic missiles originating from Iranian territory, the state news agency reported on Wednesday, citing the armed forces.
Two missiles fell in unpopulated areas and there were no casualties, the news agency reported the military as saying.
Monitoring and assessment operations were continuing, the agency reported.
Yesterday's key developments:
- Israel said it would close the UK's consulate in east Jerusalem and bar entry to 12 British nationals, including ex-prime minister Jeremy Corbyn, in response to sanctions on Israeli settlements.
- France and 10 other countries said they would join the UK in banning goods from illegal Israeli settlements.
- Iran's navy warned of retaliatory strikes on ships after the US attacked Iranian oil tankers.
(FRANCE 24 with Reuters, AP and AFP)

articles.title: Russia’s New Jet Drones With Chinese Engines Challenge Ukraine’s Defenses
articles.body:
Flying at heights of several kilometers and close to the speed of a commercial aircraft, Moscow’s new long-range jet-powered drones are causing havoc among Kyiv’s overt-stretched air defenses.
In recent weeks Moscow has been launching waves of the attack drones at the Ukrainian capital, paralyzing the city with near constant air alerts.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Sunday slammed the “horror that’s been happening in the sky these past few days” in response to Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s new , and vowed a response.
The new drones pose a challenge to Ukraine’s previously effective and low-cost anti-drone defense shield, that was hastily developed following Russia’s 2022 invasion.
Ukraine has quickly become a world leader in drone defense and has struck deals with several Western and Middle Eastern countries to share its technology.
However, its network of drone interceptors – which had been shooting down the vast majority of Russia’s more conventional drones, powered by internal combustion engines and propellers – faces a more challenging task against the new jet-powered devices.
Experts say they are fitted with Chinese-made aircraft-style mini jet engines and can fly five kilometers in the air at speeds of 400-600 kilometers (250-370 miles) per hour – up to three times the speed of previous versions based on Iran’s Shahed drones.
Rutte: Civilian Deaths in Ukraine Highest Since May 2022 as Aid Delays Cost Lives
The latest model is larger, six meters (20 feet) long with a 5.5 meter (18 feet) wingspan , and a warhead containing up to 90 kilograms (200 pounds) of explosives, nearly double the payload of earlier versions.
Such an altitude and speed puts them out of range for Ukraine’s current fleet of interceptors and “wipes out the progress we had made in the fight,” Ukrainian military expert Sergii Zgurets told AFP.
In terms of air defense, analysts say the new drones more closely resemble cruise missiles than conventional drones.
Russia is estimated to have launched around 2,800 of the jet-powered drones in August, up from 1,500 in July and just a few hundred in June.
A Ukrainian Air Force spokesman said around 60% are destroyed, compared with more than 90% of slower, lower-flying drones.
Kyiv brought to a standstill
The new attacks come with Kyiv already under strain following a sharp increase in Russian ballistic missile strikes, which have killed dozens since the start of the summer.
On Friday, a jet-powered drone struck the headquarters of Ukraine’s security services in the historic center of Kyiv, a highly symbolic hit carried out in broad daylight.
Ukraine accused Russia of using the strike to disrupt the weekend visit of US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv as they sought to revive stalled peace talks.
The wave of attacks has, at times, brought Kyiv to a near-standstill, with up to a dozen air alerts ringing out every day.
During alerts, many businesses and institutions close and the metro service is restricted, causing road gridlock and forcing people onto the streets.
Many schools, which returned from summer break last week, have announced a switch to remote learning.
The disruption to social and economic life has become so severe that authorities announced a rare relaxation of security protocols to allow the city of around three million people to keep functioning.
Ukraine races to develop a response
Kyiv officials have faced criticism for failing to anticipate the threat.
Analysts say Russia began producing jet-powered drones 18 months ago and can now manufacture around 3,000 a month.
Moscow “has a window of opportunity with these jet drones,” Ukrainian blogger Nikolaevsky Vaniok, who is close to the country’s air defense community and followed by more than 2.6 million people on Telegram, told AFP.
In response to the increased threat, Zelensky convened his military cabinet last week to accelerate production of faster interceptor drones.
Prototypes already exist and work is underway “to bring this new weapon up to the required level of efficiency,” he said.
One major Ukrainian arms company producing interceptors for conventional drones said it was “actively working on a solution.”
Zgurets, head of the Defense Express analysis center, argued that Ukraine needs a broader response combining aviation, surface-to-air systems, electronic warfare and more strikes against launch and production sites inside Russia.
“The Russians have gained an edge in this technological cycle,” he said, warning it could take “up to six months” for Ukraine to develop effective countermeasures.

Germany's Merz cancels phone call with Trump after social media post celebrating AfD win to 'make Germany great again'
German chancellor Friedrich Merz cancelled a planned phone call with US President Donald Trump on Wednesday, hours after Trump publicly celebrated a regional election win by Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland party.
A spokesperson for Merz declined to give a reason for the cancellation, but noted in response to questions from journalists that it was not due to scheduling conflicts, AFP said.
Trump, in a post on his Truth Social platform, hailed the “really big night” for the AfD, and used an abbreviation MGGA, apparent reference to an adapted version of Trump’s trademark slogan, “make Germany great again.”
“Wow! The Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night. They finally got tired of the absolutely horrible Immigration rules and regulations which have hurt Germany so badly. THEY ARE ON THE RISE, and not going to take it anymore!MGGA!!! President DJT”
AFP said Merz’s spokesman did not directly respond to Trump’s comments and declined to comment if there is a link between the two developments, but noted that the chancellor had frequently objected “in general terms” to “interfering in or commenting on the domestic political situation, particularly regarding elections”.
Coffin of King Harald being moved to the royal mausoleum at Akershus Fortress
Back in Oslo, the funeral procession with the coffin of Norway’s King Harald V is now again on the move.
After a funeral service at the Oslo Cathedral, the coffin is now being moved towards Akershus Fortress, where the late monarch will be buried in the royal mausoleum, next to his parents and grandparents.
After the ceremony at the cathedral, four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral in a “missing man” formation, their tribute to the king.
A senior politician in the Social Democratic party, Merz’s coalition partners, Dirk Wiese, condemned Trump’s social media comments as “interference” with German politics, and calling them “unacceptable.”

EU unveils ‘buy European’ public procurement rules to counter China
Jennifer Rankin
in Brussels
European authorities will be encouraged to buy more domestic goods and services when they spend public money under the EU latest effort to counter China’s economic might.
In a further “Buy European” plan, the European Commission published proposals on Wednesday for a sweeping overhaul of EU public procurement rules.
National authorities and public bodies, such as schools and hospitals, will be encouraged to buy goods and services made in Europe but, unlike earlier plans to promote domestically manufactured clean tech, there will be no binding “made in Europe” quotas.
Brussels officials are concerned that many public agencies think existing EU rules oblige them to choose the cheapest bid when spending public money, which can lead to the contract going to a non-European firm.
The European Commission’s lead official on industrial policy, Stéphane Séjourné, told reporters the regulation would give public sector buyers greater legal certainty and clarity about purchasing goods and services made in Europe.
“Purchasers can have a more preferential approach to European bids [and] restrict or reject bids from countries which do not have a public procurement agreement or do not play by binding rules in terms of public procurement internationally,” he said.
Séjourné hopes the proposals will encourage more democratic scrutiny over the spending of public money by local authorities.
“It won’t be the European Commission’s fault if purchasers were to prefer Chinese buses to European buses because … in the [draft regulation] there is every possibility to give preference to European buses.”
Meanwhile in Serbia, the country’s president Aleksandar Vucić dissolved parliament and announced snap elections for next month as he seeks to extend his hold on power by running for prime minister.
Reuters reported that Vucić, a populist who has been in power as president or prime minister for 12 years, has faced nearly two years of anti-corruption demonstrations triggered by the collapse of a railway station awning in the city of Novi Sad in November 2024 that killed 16 people.
At least 20 injured after passenger train crashes with truck in Poland
At least 20 people have been injured, four of them seriously, after an InterCity passenger train struck a truck at a level crossing in Poland and derailed.
Poland’s railway operator, PKP Intercity, said 120 people were on board at the time of the crash.
Russia hopes to see restarted peace talks with Ukraine, says Europe 'harming itself' by cutting off Russian gas
Russia hopes that peace talks between Ukraine and Russia, mediated by the United States, will resume in the near future, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said in comments reported by Reuters.
No such direct talks have taken place since February.
But the Kremlin will not publicly discuss potential elements of a possible peace settlement, Peskov added.
He was speaking after Russian president Vladimir Putin and US president Donald Trump had a telephone call on Tuesday to discuss prospects for ending the war.
Peskov also said that European countries have found themselves in a difficult position amid rising gas prices, and that they could buy gas at cheaper prices from Russia.
European natural gas prices have soared amid the war in Iran, hitting their highest level last week since late 2022, when the start of the Ukraine conflict prompted Europe to cut off Russian pipeline gas.
Peskov said Europe was harming itself by buying expensive gas at spot prices as opposed to the more affordable Russian option, and suggested that the controversial Nord Stream pipeline could be restarted soon.
Kremlin’s spokesperson also confirmed that Russia would respond to Hungary’s decision to expel 10 Russian diplomats from Budapest.
Funeral procession for Norway's King Harald begins
Back to Oslo, the funeral procession for King Harald is about the begin, and the 1.2km route to the Oslo Cathedral is lined up with 1,900 soldiers from all branches of the Norwegian defence forces.
The procession is expected to walk very slowly – at around 60 steps per minute – and will include the royal family, including King Haakon, followed by a royal car with the widow, Queen Sonja.
Other distinguished guests – including foreign royals, heads of state, prime ministers – will follow.
Thousands of members of the public are also along the route, with more screens set up to help them follow the events.
Irish police investigate suspected drone sighting ahead of Trump's visit this weekend
Meanwhile, Irish police are investigated a suspected – and as of yet unconfirmed – sighting of a large drone over the Irish Sea on Tuesday night – just days before US president Donald Trump is expected to visit the country.
The drone was first reported by a pilot of an Aer Lingus plane just after 5pm local time. He said the “large black” drone was operating at 6,000ft.
In a statement reported by the Irish Times, the Garda said: “Gardaí in the Dublin Region are aware of an alleged sighting of an unconfirmed object over the Irish Sea, off the east coast, earlier this evening, Tuesday, 8 September 2026.”
The incident comes just days before US president Donald Trump is expected to visit Ireland for the Irish Open golf tournament this weekend.
Ireland also currently holds the rotating presidency in the European Council, and regularly hosts senior EU ministerial meetings in the country.
Swiss emergency services responding to a reported explosion at hydroelectric powerplant in Ticino canton
Swiss media are reporting an explosion at a hydroelectric power plant in the Swiss canton of Ticino, and part of the building reportedly collapsed.
A major emergency response operation is under way.
Local media carried conflicting reports about potential injuries. They also said that it’s not clear if the explosion happened within the old plant, or a new facility being built next door, which is meant to open in 2027.
Norway to bid farewell to King Harald at ceremonial funeral in Oslo
Meanwhile, large crowds are gathering in Oslo for the funeral of late King Harald V, which is expected to attract some of other leading royals from Europe and beyond, including Britain’s Prince William, Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino, Spain’s King Felipe, and Denmark’s King Frederik. Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy is also in Oslo.
A procession on foot from the royal palace to Oslo Cathedral is expected to start in about half an hour, with a church ceremony at midday UK time (1pm local time).
Despite its recent troubles, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, a Norstat poll for broadcaster NRK published on 1 September found, the first poll taken since Harald’s death, as reported by Reuters.
French far-right leader Bardella faces domestic criticism over migrant deal with Reform UK
Rowena MasonandAngelique Chrisafis in Paris
Reform UK has insisted its deal with France’s far-right National Rally to return migrants back across the channel was fully approved by the party and signed off by its president, Jordan Bardella, amid a furious backlash in France.
The agreement unveiled on Friday between Nigel Farage and Bardella, who is the 30-year-old protege of presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, appeared to directly contradict Le Pen’s long-held policy of refusing to accept the return of those who arrive in the UK in small boats from France.
Le Pen was pressed for her position by journalists from France TV, the state broadcaster, on Monday. Le Pen declined to comment, saying she would talk about the issue soon, but at a time of her choosing.
In 2021, Le Pen said she wanted a rewriting of border agreements for the UK to specifically send people arriving on boats back to their countries of origin, instead of returning them to France.
Since the agreement, Bardella has come under fire from political parties in France for signing the deal, with Benjamin Haddad, the Europe minister, criticising Bardella for “submission” that was “against our interests and sovereignty”.
Some French media have questioned whether Bardella was duped by Reform, querying whether the French translation accurately conveyed the meaning by Farage that the National Rally (RN) was prepared to accept any migrants back who travel by small boat.
'Russia's frontline is moving west,' Moldova's president warns
Moldovan president Maia Sandu warned that “Russia’s frontline is moving further west” after a Russian strike on the Moldovan-Ukrainian border overnight, a day after a drone incursion into Moldovan airspace.
“We condemn these attacks and this brutal war. Our thoughts are with the victims and with Ukraine. Moldova will keep strengthening its air surveillance and defences with our European partners – and I urge more air defence support for Ukraine,” she said.
The overnight attack forced the closure of the border checkpoint, around 500 kilometres (310 miles) south of Kyiv, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service said.
Europeans want a united Europe but question whether it can get there, study finds
Jon Henley
Europeans overwhelmingly want a strong, united and independent Europe but question whether it can get there, according to a study that suggests a continent-wide crisis of confidence is creating fertile ground for far-right narratives of decline.
The report, based on 5,800 interviews in France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Poland and the UK and analysis of the way Europe is discussed in the politics and media of 15 countries, paints a picture of an ambitious but disillusioned public.
It found that 68% of respondents spoke about Europe in terms of a “general deterioration or loss of normality”, compared with just 12% who said they viewed the present moment as a time of “European awakening and renewal”.
Many recognised the major challenges facing Europe, including war (43%), economic pressures (33%) and the need for greater international autonomy (29%). But 74% said Europe was not dealing well with them, and 56% believed its future was “in danger”.
The problem is not lack of ambition: an overwhelming 73% of respondents harbour a strong European vision of unity and political integration (35%), peace and security (28%) or prosperity (19%), while only 13% hope for “less Europe” or EU dissolution.
For many, said the study’s author, Paweł Zerka, a senior fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations (ECFR) thinktank, the problem was “not that they’ve stopped wanting a stronger Europe, but that they no longer believe it’s achievable”.
The result, Zerka added, was an “imagination gap. People can picture the kind of Europe they want, but struggle to imagine a credible path from where it is today to where they want it to be. These are matters of policy, not just communication.”
Major material damage from Leipzig drone attack prevented 'only by pure chance,' Merz says
In his comments, Merz also responded to the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport last month, saying it had been prepared in Russia over an extended period and that a disaster was only narrowly averted.
“This attack was planned in Russia for months and was specifically targeted at Germany, and only by pure chance was major material damage and harm to people prevented,” Merz told the parliament.
Russia has rejected any involvement in the drone incident at Leipzig airport.
Chancellor Merz, AfD's Weidel clash over German policy on Ukraine, migration, economy
Over in Germany, AfD’s Alice Weidel said in the Bundestag the result of the Saxony-Anhalt election over the weekend showed “the people finally want a change in policy,” saying the ruling coalition should be “over.”
She also harshly criticised the government’s track record on migration, “war propaganda” against Russia, and on energy, calling for resumption of deliveries through the Nord Stream pipeline.
“You failed to understand the message the voters in Saxony-Anhalt sent you last Sunday. But that hardly matters, because your time is up anyway,” she told chancellor Merz.
Responding to her comments, Merz said Weidel “is and will remain a destructive force,”as he pledged Germany “will continue to support” Ukraine, “because it is defending our freedom too.
“You are openly demonstrating the downright grotesque reversal of who is the victim and who is the perpetrator,” he said in a speech, which was repeatedly interrupted by AfD.
Merz also strongly criticised Weidel’s “remigration” proposals, saying they amounted to an attempted “ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” which would leave Germany “no longer able to function” as one in six skilled workers are of immigrant background.
“Not a single nursing home will remain open, and not a single hospital in Germany will remain open, not a single restaurant will be able to operate in Germany. That would be the result of your immigration policy,” he said, while stressing that his government will push to tighten its policy against irregular migration.
Morning opening: 'Too little response' to Russian strikes on Ukraine, Zelenskyy says
Jakub Krupa
At least two people died were injured in Russian attacks on Ukraine overnight, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying “there has been too little response from the international community to these strikes.”
Two people were killed, three injured and 16 evacuated after a strike on the Starokozache border crossing with Moldova. Four people were injured after a Russian drone struck an apartment building in Kyiv. More strikes were reported in Dnipro, Mykolaiv, Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia and Zhytomyr.
“A response is needed – Moscow must not go into the winter believing that it can get away with missile and drone terror without consequences. The aggression must be stopped here and now, before it spreads any further,” Zelenskyy said.
He called for “effective” sanctions against Russia and support for Ukraine, saying “the partners who can help know exactly what is needed every day.”
The Russian defence ministry said that its forces had struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel carrying military equipment in the Black Sea en route to the port of Odesa, as well as a warehouse in Kyiv, belonging to a company manufacturing drones, Russian news agencies reported.
I will keep an eye on this.
Elsewhere, Germany’s embattled chancellor Friedrich Merz is facing AfD’s leader Alice Weidel in a general debate in the Bundestag this morning after a bruising result in the Saxony-Anhalt state election on the weekend. I will monitor it for key lines.
Over in Oslo, Norway will bid farewell to King Harald V with a funeral paying tribute to the 35-year reign of the monarch, with many international guests expected to attend.
Lots to cover.
It’s Wednesday, 9 September 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: How Russia Is Trying to Paralyze Kyiv Without Occupying It
articles.body:
Russia failed to capture Kyiv in 2022. It is now trying to dictate how the city sleeps, travels, and works.
The latest attack began early on Tuesday, Sept. 8, just hours after the expiration of a three-day pause in strikes on Kyiv and Moscow, which was observed during the visit of US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff. Russian missiles and drones killed three people and wounded 16, according to Ukrainian officials. The strike damaged at least 14 high-rise buildings, a dormitory, a school, a clinic, and multiple warehouses.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Attacks are spread across the entire day
For much of the war, Kyiv’s air-raid routine followed a grim but predictable rhythm: Russian drones arrived at night, missiles struck before dawn, and the city dusted itself off to restart in the morning.
Russia is now deploying smaller groups of drones throughout the day and night. Many are jet-powered models that travel faster and are significantly harder to intercept than the propeller-driven Shahed drones used earlier in the war.
Kyiv Post documented more than 100 jet-powered drones approaching Kyiv during one 12-hour period.
Russia launched more than 2,800 jet-powered drones against Ukraine in August, averaging roughly 90 a day, according to Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat. Their use increased fivefold in July compared with June.
Rutte: Civilian Deaths in Ukraine Highest Since May 2022 as Aid Delays Cost Lives
During one four-day stretch in late August, Russia launched nearly 1,500 drones, more than half of them jet-powered. Kyiv and the surrounding region faced attacks for five consecutive days, disrupting commutes and preventing metro trains from crossing the Dnipro River during alerts.
Between Aug. 27 and Sept. 1, Kyiv endured more than 60 air-raid alerts totaling 52 hours. The city spent more than two full days under alert within a six-day period.
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed that Russia had not necessarily increased the total number of drones used in each campaign. Instead, Moscow was distributing a comparable number across more hours to maximize fatigue and economic disruption.
A single drone approaching Kyiv can trigger citywide sirens, interrupt transit, and send workers into shelters. Once the all-clear sounds, another group can repeat the cycle.
The economic target is time
Every alert carries an economic cost. Beyond physical destruction, the sirens mean delayed workers, interrupted production, closed stores, suspended deliveries, and disrupted public transport. Schools move children into shelters, while medical and emergency crews must continue operating under the threat of additional strikes.
Russia is also targeting the logistics that keep Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities supplied.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi estimated in late August that Russian strikes had destroyed roughly 90% of the food-logistics capacity operated by major retail chains, contributing to temporary shortages of milk, sugar, fruit, and vegetables in Kyiv supermarkets.
The attacks have hit Nova Poshta sorting centers, supermarket distribution facilities, and warehouses storing books and consumer goods. Russian strikes have also hit food-storage facilities in Odesa and destroyed Epicentr hypermarkets.
“They are hitting civilian businesses, food warehouses, hypermarkets, postal terminals, warehouses where books are stored,” Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said.
In August, air alerts consumed 21.8% of scheduled operating hours for Ukrainian shopping centers. In practical terms, malls lost more than one out of every five hours in which they were supposed to operate.
The government’s response shows the scale of the problem. Ukraine is introducing a two-level alert system:
- Yellow alerts will indicate drone threats. Businesses may remain open if employees and customers have access to shelters. Authorities have recommended keeping Kyiv’s metro fully operational.
- Red alerts will indicate missile threats, including ballistic missiles and large combined attacks. Businesses must stop operating and people must move to shelters.
“The economy must continue to function, taxes must flow into the budget and people must receive their salaries,” Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said.
Kyiv is also reducing its curfew and adjusting transport rules to limit the economic damage caused by prolonged alerts.
A modern siege logic
Kyiv is not facing a physical siege comparable to the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Sarajevo. During the Bosnian War, Sarajevo was encircled and subjected to 1,425 days of shelling and sniper fire in a campaign that international courts found was intended to terrorize civilians.
Kyiv remains connected to the rest of Ukraine. Goods, weapons and people continue to move. Russian artillery does not surround the capital.
The similarity lies in the use of sustained danger to control civilian life. Russia cannot erect checkpoints around Kyiv, but it can use air-raid alerts to interrupt movement. It cannot physically close every factory, but it can force repeated work stoppages. It cannot occupy the capital, but it can make normal life dependent on when the next drone is launched.
The three-day pause for Witkoff and Kushner demonstrated how selectively that pressure can be applied. Russia and Ukraine agreed not to attack each other’s capitals during the envoys’ visit, but Putin continued to reject a broader ceasefire and insisted on Russia’s existing territorial demands.
The diplomatic pause protected the capitals during the talks but did not protect civilians elsewhere or stop fighting along the front.
Beyond psychological warfare
Civilian exhaustion is only one effect of the campaign. Continuous drone waves also force Ukrainian air-defense crews to work extended shifts, leaving less time to rest, relocate, and repair equipment.
By combining comparatively inexpensive drones with ballistic and cruise missiles, Russia forces Ukraine to decide when to use its most capable and limited interceptors. Patriot systems are essential for stopping ballistic missiles but cannot be used economically against every drone probing Kyiv’s airspace.
Defending the capital also creates a strategic trade-off. Radars, launchers, and interceptors assigned to Kyiv cannot simultaneously defend power stations, airfields, weapons factories, and other Ukrainian cities.
Russia therefore imposes costs even when most of its drones are intercepted. Ukraine must expend ammunition, keep crews constantly active, and defend a growing number of potential targets. The strikes also demonstrate that Kyiv’s political and security institutions remain targets.
For example, on Sept. 4, a Russian drone struck the Security Service of Ukraine headquarters in central Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the drone had been directed towards the office of acting Security Service (SBU) chief Oleksandr Poklad.
Preparing for a winter war
Witkoff and Kushner arrived in Kyiv after more than three hours of talks with Putin in Moscow. They described their discussions with Zelensky as substantive and said there had been “significant progress” toward restarting trilateral negotiations, although no dates or venues were announced.
The central dispute remains unchanged. Russia demands that Ukraine surrender territory it still controls in Donbas. Kyiv refuses, while battlefield analysis indicates that Russia could require years to capture the rest of the Donetsk Oblast at its current rate of advance.
Zelensky is preparing for the possibility that the war will continue into winter. During the Kyiv talks, he requested a winter package covering air defense, energy support, and access to US liquefied natural gas.
“If the war continues in the winter, we strongly count on the winter package,” Zelensky said. However, the US delegation announced no new Patriot batteries. Ukraine recently received a small number of Patriot interceptors, while Britain has pledged additional air-defense assistance.
Neither measure eliminates the shortage.
Ukraine needs separate production tracks for drones and ballistic missiles. Zelensky said 67 Ukrainian companies were working on systems capable of intercepting jet-powered drones, although only three to five had demonstrated results.
Ukraine has also sought US permission to manufacture anti-ballistic systems and interceptors. In July, President Donald Trump said that Washington would license Ukrainian production of Patriot interceptors, but he later appeared to reverse that position.
However, on Sept. 2, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that licensing negotiations remained underway.
Even if an agreement is reached, experts estimate that establishing production would take at least a year.
The goal is friction, not collapse
The campaign does not have to force Kyiv to capitulate to impose strategic costs. Its immediate effect is to make daily life slower, less reliable, and more expensive.
When trains stop, warehouses burn, stores close, and workers spend hours in shelters, Russia inflicts damage without advancing on the ground. By forcing Ukraine to expend interceptors and concentrate air defenses around the capital, Moscow reduces the resources available to protect other cities, infrastructure and the front.
The aerial campaign has already killed civilians, disrupted transport, damaged commercial logistics, and forced Ukraine to redesign its warning system.
Countering it will require more than Patriot missiles. Ukraine needs cheaper anti-drone interceptors, dispersed warehouses, alternative transit routes, more shelters, and geographically precise alerts that prevent one drone from shutting down a city of millions.

articles.title: Russia is raining death on Ukraine’s women and children. Our hands shake but we keep going for love | Alina Sarnatska
articles.body:
My grandma was as hard as nails. She had just turned 17 when the Nazis entered her village in the Kyiv region, near what is now the city of Bucha. She hid in the attic to avoid being taken for forced labour. They didn’t find her that time, but a few weeks later she was caught working in the fields. They put her in a cattle wagon and took her to Germany. She escaped and walked a couple of hundred kilometres back to her village. Grandma said that life was hard for everybody during the war, but she was lucky.
In the past month, two of my friends here in Kyiv happened to tell me that their hands have started shaking during Russian airstrikes. Everybody who knows that my hands shake during airstrikes tells me their stories. One day, during an airstrike in the Donetsk region, I had a meltdown and have never recovered. Today you could say I am an ambassador for people whose hands shake during airstrikes.
Those two friends said the same exact thing: their hands never used to shake before and now they do. Each one wrote: “I don’t understand what’s just happened to me.”
For nearly five years, the Russians have been targeting these women and their children with drones, rockets, jet-powered drones and missiles. They have threatened us with nuclear weapons. They have used an Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile in combat; carried out a siege; again threatened a nuclear strike; tried to freeze us by destroying Ukraine’s heat and power systems in the middle of winter; blown up a dam, flooding two city districts; used more drones and fired yet other types of long-range missiles at Ukrainian cities; organised terror attacks; and, once again, threatened to wipe us out with nuclear weapons.
In the early hours of 19 July, the general staff of the armed forces of Ukraine reported a massive combined Russian attack: 41 missiles and 125 drones, with Kyiv as the main target. Next morning, I got a message from my friend Valya. “Everything was fine, and then all of a sudden something happened,” she wrote. “Everyone but me is at home asleep. I’m the only one who’s so anxious.”
After every airstrike, the women I know “pull themselves together”, take their children to preschool, and go to work. Because children need to be fed – and if the state-run preschool doesn’t have a bomb shelter, the private one that does costs money. The women I know sleep beside their children in the corridors of their apartment buildings, in underground parking garages, in the metro or in pedestrian tunnels. “Everything’s fine,” say these women. After Russia fires dozens of missiles at Kyiv overnight, they say: “It was loud, but everything’s fine.” And they wonder why their hands shake and they even blame themselves for being weak.
My grandma’s name was Dina and she was as hard as nails. She would get very angry when I snuggled up to our relatives. Once, my grandma’s sister was over and I climbed on to her lap and wrapped my arms around her. Grandma Dina yelled at me: “Get down, what a disgrace, you’re a big girl now!” I was seven. My grandma was afraid I would be spoiled. Whenever I cried, she would say to my mother: “Look how you’ve spoiled her, how will she cope with life?”
Grandma Dina liked to feed stray cats. Grandpa protested, but she did it anyway. When she went out to feed them, for a few minutes she became a completely different person. First, she scolded them for being a nuisance, wearing her usual face. Then, as they ate, she would start to smile a bit and stroke their thin, fluffy backs. With one hand on her thigh, she would lean over and pet each cat once or twice, smiling. Then she would pick up the bowl, straighten up, and her expression would return to normal.
One morning, I found a large grey cat dead under a bush; a cat that my grandma had been feeding for 10 years, as long as I had been alive. He had probably died of old age or sickness. I burst into tears and ran to my grandma. She rolled up a towel and gave me a whack on the ribs. “Now stop that crying, you’re a big girl now!” When my mother came home from work in the evening, I said: “I think Grandma’s a robot.” To which mum replied: “Nonsense, now go finish your soup.”
There was nothing soft about Grandma Dina. If she were still alive today, she would be well prepared. She didn’t know much about getting along with people, but she did know how to pull herself together.
Now I understand that she could not cut herself any slack or allow herself any feelings of self-kindness and that’s why she also felt no compassion for others. Compassion was too risky for her.
And it’s true, we cannot let ourselves be as emotional or compassionate as we were before the war. We cannot live, let alone work, as we did before. On top of that, war reveals the sharp contrast between our reality and the cult of the self displayed on social media. Viral posts about “success, energy and choosing yourself” are irrelevant to anyone caring for a sick child when it is 5C inside your apartment.
Enduring daily death and the violence of Russia’s attacks has changed us irreversibly. The skin of Ukrainian women has thickened into armour. These women take part in combat, live under constant airstrikes, and keep working and caring for their families through it all.
But if it were up to me, I would keep my belly soft. I still want to hug people, hold them close, and feel the warmth of their hands. So what if Grandma Dina would say I’m not ready for life? I think that love is worth the risk.
We stay calm because our children are watching us, because they need to be taken to preschool in the morning, because there is still work to do. But when resilience becomes an obligation, every trembling hand starts to feel like a personal failure. I do not want survival to take away my tenderness towards other people, or towards myself.
Translated from Ukrainian by Larissa Babij
- 
  Alina Sarnatska is a Ukrainian writer, playwright and war veteran. She is the author of two books and nine plays, and her work has been staged and presented internationally
