articles.title: Iran-backed fighters in Yemen, Iraq unite to threaten the Gulf
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran-backed fighters in Yemen and Iraq are joining forces to threaten the Gulf, officials say
In July, Saudi Arabia and the United States bombed Iran-backed militias in Iraq after blaming them for drone attacks on Saudi oil facilities that had been claimed by Yemen's Houthi rebels, another Iranian ally.
Now, regional officials tell The Associated Press that the Houthis helped the Iraqi militias plan and execute the two-day swarm attack, showing a new level of coordination.
Iran spent decades building up armed groups on Israel's frontiers that suffered major losses in the wars following Israel's genocidal war on Gaza.
Regional officials and experts say Iran is now using the Iraqi militias and the Houthis to threaten Saudi Arabia and other American allies in the Gulf in order to drive up the costs of the war launched by the US and Israel in February.
It is a risky strategy. A wave of Houthi attacks on Saudi oil facilities on Tuesday threatened to reignite full-scale war with the kingdom. Iraq has ordered militias to disarm by the end of this month, though powerful Iran-backed groups have refused to do so. A new American effort to economically isolate Iran could spark further escalation.
A pincer movement 
The Houthi involvement in the Iraqi drone attack was confirmed by two Saudi officials, citing intelligence, and a senior Iraqi security official. They said Houthi emissaries worked in an operations room run by Iraqi militias.
Saudi Arabia and the US responded with joint airstrikes that killed at least 20 Iraqi fighters, six Iranian advisers and at least one Houthi official. The death of the Houthi, not previously reported, was confirmed by a Houthi official and an Iraqi militia member.
A US military official said Houthis had been killed in previous strikes in Iraq. The US is concerned about the Houthi presence there and their ability to launch attacks on other countries, including Saudi Arabia, the official said.
Two officials with the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), an umbrella group of militias that is officially part of Iraq's security forces, denied involvement in the attack on Saudi Arabia and denied that the Houthis were operating under its auspices. The PMF includes powerful militias backed by Iran that sometimes act independently.
All the officials and the militia member spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to media. The Houthis did not respond to a request for comment.
Cooperation grew during the war on Gaza 
Cooperation between the Iraqi militias and the better organised Houthis had grown throughout the war in Gaza, when they coordinated attacks on Israel, according to the Houthi and regional officials. At the height of the war, Houthi leader Abdel-Malek al-Houthi spoke of a joint operations room.
After the US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February, Iran and its allies began firing on Gulf nations to broaden the conflict and inflict pain on major oil producers hosting US forces.
"Iran has a hybrid strategy in the current war. We are not fighting on one front and we are not using one tool," Mahdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran's parliament speaker, wrote on social media in June.
"The Houthis' growing prominence during the Gaza war opened up a new horizon in Iraq. Many groups there became eager to support the Houthis, and in return, the Houthis started sharing their military expertise with Iraqi militias," said Ahmed Nagi, senior Yemen analyst at the Crisis Group, an international think tank.
Now they are "squeezing Saudi like with pliers," Nagi said.
A week before the drone swarm attack, the Houthis declared a blockade against Saudi shipping in the Red Sea, threatening another critical trade route as the wartime disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has jolted the world economy.
Since late July, the Houthis have carried out over a dozen attacks against Saudi oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea, according to the war monitor group ACLED.
On Tuesday, they launched a wave of attacks on oil and other facilities in southern Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people, including women and children, Saudi authorities said.
The Houthi blockade has forced Saudi Arabia to adopt a “dark” transit policy that includes turning off tracking signals on oil tankers in the Red Sea, according to ACLED.
Saudi oil exports in the crosshairs 
Saudi Arabia had diverted much of its oil to the Red Sea after Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. When the Houthis began attacking, the kingdom started shipping more oil north to the Suez Canal and Egypt's SUMED pipeline, whose flows have risen from 650,000 barrels a day in June to over 1.9 million in August, according to global shipping monitor Kpler.
Last month, the Houthis showed they can target that route as well, striking a Saudi tanker in the northern Red Sea with a missile. The tanker had reportedly traveled from the Saudi port of Yanbu to the Suez Canal, some 1,000 kilometers (700 miles) from Houthi territory.
The Houthis "are willing to weather some shorter term pain for what they feel will be longer term gains," such as extending their reach along the Red Sea coast, said Adam Baron, a Yemen expert at the New America think tank in Washington.
"The train to a return to full scale war has left the station, and it's unclear if anyone is going to jump in to stop it," he said, citing the US focus on Iran and the Saudis' reluctance to intervene in Yemen again.
The rebels seized Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, in 2014. The following year, the Saudis joined with Yemen’s internationally recognized government in a counteroffensive, likely fearing that the kingdom could end up with a Hezbollah-like group on its doorstep.
The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and at times pushed Yemen to the brink of famine. A ceasefire that had mostly held since 2022 is now in tatters.
For years, a Saudi-led blockade has raised pressure on the Houthis while exacting a heavy toll on ordinary people in rebel-held parts of Yemen.
The Houthis have often responded by escalating hostilities, and renewed fighting could allow them to gain control of energy-rich areas of eastern Yemen, said Elisabeth Kendall, a Yemen expert at Cambridge University's Girton College.
The Houthis, who control northern and central Yemen, have been smuggling in advanced weapons for years, circumventing the blockade and a UN arms embargo. Iran denies arming the rebels, but Iranian-made weaponry has been found on the battlefield and in intercepted shipments.
The rebels have an array of cruise and ballistic missiles, drones and unmanned submarines.
Saudi-backed forces in Yemen are fighting back on a number of fronts, including the crucial port city of Hodeida and the province of Taiz along Yemen's west coast. The Houthis have attacked Mokha, the main Red Sea port still held by the government.
Saudi Arabia appears reluctant to directly target the Houthis again, but if the rebels continue to escalate, "it will have to act decisively once and for all," Kendall said.

articles.title: Russian sources warn Ukraine’s drone war has entered a new sea
articles.body:
- Russian sources describe a pattern of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian-linked assets expanding from the Black Sea into the Caspian and Baltic seas and now the Mediterranean.
- Ukraine's SBU has publicly claimed only one of three cited Mediterranean strikes, the December 2025 attack on the tanker Qendil.
A Russian military-affiliated Telegram channel has raised alarm that Ukraine’s reach at sea now extends beyond the Black Sea into the Mediterranean, framing a string of drone strikes on Russian-linked vessels there as part of a wider pattern that has already put Russian military and commercial assets at risk across three separate seas.
Ukraine’s drone campaign against Russian naval and shipping targets started in the Black Sea, where a senior U.S. defense official said last year that Ukrainian forces had destroyed or damaged at least 32 medium to large Russian naval vessels, forcing much of Russia’s fleet to relocate away from Crimea. Kyiv has since extended that campaign into the Caspian Sea, over 1,000 km from Ukrainian territory. Ukraine’s military intelligence claimed its first Caspian strike in November 2024, damaging the missile ships Tatarstan and Dagestan at the port of Kaspiysk in Russia’s Dagestan region. Ukrainian forces have hit Caspian targets repeatedly since, including three Lukoil offshore drilling platforms in January 2026 and an FSB border patrol boat in May 2026, with Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces publicly claiming responsibility for each strike.
Ukraine has also struck Russian assets in the Baltic Sea. In May 2026, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian drones hit the Baltic port of Primorsk, setting it on fire, and struck an oil tanker, a Karakurt-class missile ship and a patrol boat. Kyiv also blew up the Russian Baltic Fleet corvette Boyky at Kronstadt Naval Base. Ukrainian or suspected Ukrainian drones later crossed into NATO airspace over the Baltic states and Finland that same spring, according to open-source tracking, during the wider campaign against Russian oil export infrastructure at ports including Primorsk and Ust-Luga.
Against that backdrop, the Mediterranean now appears to be the newest theater. Ukraine’s SBU security service publicly claimed responsibility for a December 2025 drone strike on the Qendil, an Oman-flagged crude oil tanker tied to Russia’s sanctioned shadow fleet, more than 2,000 km from Ukraine. The SBU said its Alpha special unit used aerial drones to critically damage the empty tanker, and Reuters confirmed the vessel shown in strike footage matched the Qendil using file imagery.
Two more Mediterranean incidents remain unconfirmed by Ukraine. In March 2026, the Russian-flagged LNG tanker Arctic Metagaz caught fire and sank between Libya and Malta while carrying gas from the Russian port of Murmansk. Russia’s Transport Ministry blamed Ukrainian naval drones and called the strike an act of terrorism; Libyan port authorities confirmed the vessel suffered explosions and a fire before sinking, and all 30 crew members were rescued.
Ukraine did not respond to the allegation. In the most recent incident, on September 6, 2026, Russian opposition journalist Alexander Nevzorov published footage he said showed the sanctioned, Russian-flagged cargo ship Lady Mariia struck 12 times by drones while carrying Iranian weapons and armored vehicles toward Russia. Neither the strike’s origin nor the cargo claim has been independently verified.

articles.title: Battle-tested drone interceptors show up at U.S. training exercise in Germany
articles.body:
- U.S. soldiers trained on a counter-drone defense system at the Combined Arms Training Center in Grafenwoehr, Germany, which offers nearly 60 courses.
- Images from the post also showed Merops AS-3 Surveyor interceptor drones, built by Perennial Autonomy and already used against Shahed-style drones in Ukraine and the Middle East.
U.S. soldiers trained on a counter-drone defense system during a course at the Combined Arms Training Center in Grafenwoehr, Germany, the U.S. Mission to NATO said in a social media post.
The training center, known as CATC, is run by the 7th Army Training Command and offers close to 60 courses for U.S. troops, ranging from transporting hazardous materials on European public roads to combat skills practiced in simulated environments. The post did not specify which counter-drone course the soldiers attended or name the specific system they used.
Grafenwoehr has become a regular training site for U.S. and allied forces working on countering small drones, a threat that has grown more urgent as cheap attack drones have played a larger role in combat in Ukraine and the Middle East. The U.S. Air Force runs a separate Joint Multidomain Counter-Unmanned Aerial Systems Course at the same training area, which brings together Air Force, Army and Marine Corps personnel for a program that ends with a 48-hour field exercise.
Images accompanying the post also showed Merops AS-3 Surveyor interceptor drones built by California-based Perennial Autonomy, a company whose systems have been used against Russian Shahed-style drones in Ukraine. The Merops interceptor costs roughly $15,000 per unit, according to Army Secretary Daniel Driscoll, compared with an estimated $30,000 to $50,000 for a Shahed-type drone. The U.S. Army has since bought large numbers of the interceptors and has used them against Iranian-designed drones in the Middle East, alongside Patriot air defense batteries.
In May, the Pentagon’s Joint Interagency Task Force 401 awarded Perennial Autonomy a three-year contract worth up to $500 million to supply the Merops interceptor along with two other drone systems, the Bumblebee ISR quadcopter and the Hornet strike drone, across the U.S. military. All three systems were already in use by American forces before the contract was signed.

articles.title: Ukraine reported hitting warships and an oil terminal in a Russian port city whose mayor claimed only falling debris
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones set a fuel-oil terminal on fire in the port of Novorossiysk again overnight on 9 September, monitoring channels reported. Novorossiysk's mayor claimed drone debris came down on enterprise grounds in the Russian city. Ukraine's military later reported strikes on the naval base there, including on warships that carry cruise missiles.
Analysts placed the fire on a fuel-oil terminal
Ukrainian defense news outlet Militarnyi located the strike through geospatial intelligence (GEOINT) analysis, which matches published photos and video against satellite imagery and maps. That work showed drones hitting the mazut (fuel-oil) terminal inside the port in Krasnodar Krai. Fire broke out on the terminal grounds, and at least one storage tank took damage. Around midnight, residents began reporting the sound of drones overhead, Russian air defense fire, and explosions.
The Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ started posting videos of the attack on the port around midnight, further into the morning sharing more footage of the fire at the fuel-oil terminal. Russian news Telegram channel Astra wrote of fires on the grounds of several enterprises and near a residential building, with a column of dark smoke in eyewitness video. Its analyst then established from that footage that the burning object was the Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal. Astra called the work open-source intelligence (OSINT) analysis, meaning conclusions drawn from publicly available imagery and records.
Satellites feeding NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which flags heat sources from orbit, recorded several seats of fire in Novorossiysk after the night raid. An OSINT reading of eyewitness video also placed a fire at an apartment building in the city.
Novorossiysk mayor Andrei Kravchenko claimed overnight that air defenses were still fighting off the drone attack. He stated that drone debris had come down at several enterprises and near a residential building, and claimed that preliminary information showed no casualties. Kravchenko later acknowledged hits on enterprises while describing the cause as "falling debris."
Ukrainian drones and missiles hit the same naval base overnight on 12 August, damaging Kalibr-carrying frigates and stopping all three of the port's grain terminals.
Ukraine's account named ships, the harbor, and the terminal

articles.title: Kyiv Warns Russia Will “Test” New Long-Range Missile Against Western Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new, currently unnamed ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers (500 miles) by the end of 2026 and could attack western Ukraine as trials of the system.
Maj. Gen. Vadym Skibitsky, deputy head of Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR) delivered the assessment during a recent meeting of the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“According to our estimates, Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers by the end of this year,” Skibitsky said.
Ukrainian intelligence believes Russia could attempt to strike targets in western Ukraine during as part of its testing regime.
Skibitsky said Russia was increasing the intensity of missile and drone attacks against Ukraine in an effort to trigger a social and economic crisis. Moscow is also seeking to increase its production of ballistic missiles and extend their range, he said.
Skibitsky urged Ukraine’s partners to strengthen sanctions against Russia and restrict its access to foreign components used in the production of long-range weapons.
Intelligence says Russian losses exceeded recruitment
Skibitsky also said Russia lost about 43,000 military personnel in August while recruiting around 39,000 people into its armed forces.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, the Russian General Staff believes intensified mobilization is the only way Moscow can achieve its main military objectives.
Abramovich Loses Third Bid to Escape EU Sanctions
“Russia has not abandoned its strategic goal of destroying Ukrainian statehood and is waging a war of attrition despite heavy losses,” Skibitsky said.
He said those objectives included the complete occupation of Ukraine’s Donbas region and attempts to secure the strategic initiative on the battlefield.
Russia intends to mobilize about 600,000 people during 2026 and 2027, with half of that number expected to be recruited by the end of this year, according to HUR’s assessment.
Belarus could support hybrid operations
Skibitsky said Russia’s broader plans also included attempts to blockade the Black Sea and draw Belarus into the war against Ukraine alongside hybrid operations targeting NATO.
However, Ukrainian intelligence has not detected signs that Belarus is currently preparing offensive military formations on its territory, he said.
“At present, we do not see real indicators of preparations for strike groups on Belarusian territory, but we remember January and February 2022,” Skibitsky said.
He identified domestic political risks, limited military capabilities and possible economic problems as the primary factors discouraging Belarus from directly entering the war.
However, HUR considers it likely that Belarus will continue supporting Russian hybrid activities, including allowing its territory to be used to increase pressure along NATO’s borders and to intensify information and psychological operations.
Skibitsky said Russia remained a threat to both Ukraine and Europe. He thanked partner countries for their support and again called for stronger sanctions to deprive Moscow of foreign components used in weapons targeting Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian air defenses down 12 smart bombs, 713 Ukrainian drones over past day
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 8. /TASS/. Russian air defense systems have shot down 12 guided aerial bombs, a rocket from a US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, and 713 fixed-wing drones of the Ukrainian armed forces over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense systems shot down 12 enemy guided aerial bombs, a US-made HIMARS rocket, and 713 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the statement reads.
Ukraine loses nearly 1,285 troops in special op zone over past 24 hours
Ukraine has lost approximately 1,285 troops in the special military operation zone over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
According to its statement, Russia’s battlegroup North wiped out up to 180 Ukrainian servicemen, the battlegroup West eliminated up over 190 enemy troops, the battlegroup South wiped out over 190 military, the battlegroup Center eliminated up to 380, the battlegroup East destroyed up to 300 troops, and the battlegroup Dnepr wiped out over 45.
Russian forces strike Ukraine’s UAV production facility in Belaya Tserkov
Russian forces have struck the Warbirds of Ukraine facility in Belaya Tserkov, manufacturing TRX drones with a range of 450 km, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result, the following targets in the Kiev Region were struck: an industrial facility (Warbirds of Ukraine LLC) in Belaya Tserkov, which manufactured unmanned aerial vehicles for various purposes. At this facility, the company [Warbirds of Ukraine] was developing and testing TRX UAVs with a striking range of 450 km," the statement reads.
Russian forces strike encircled Ukrainian troops in Kharkov Region
The Russian Armed Forces have struck encircled Ukrainian troops in the Kharkov Region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Inside the ‘cauldron, ’ enemy units were defeated in the area of the settlements of Malaya Volchya, Varvarovka, Buzovo, and Nefedovka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Battlegroup North continues to encircle Ukrainian troops in Kharkov Region
Russia’s battlegroup North is expanding the outer ring of encirclement around Ukrainian troops, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The battlegroup North continues to expand the outer ring of encirclement around enemy formations in the Kharkov Region," the statement said.
Russian forces take control of Dolgenkoye, Berezniki in the Kharkov region
Units of Russia’s Battlegroup North have established control over the settlements of Dolgenkoye and Berezniki in the Kharkov region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Control has been established over the settlement of Dolgenkoye in the Kharkov region. The inner ring [in the Kharkov region] continues to narrow, and the settlement of Berezniki in the Kharkov region has come under the control of Russian troops," the ministry stated.
Russian Armed Forces strike Khimtransagro logistics center in Kiev Region
The Russian Armed Forces have struck the Khimtransagro logistics center in the Kiev Region overnight, which was being used for military logistics, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result, the following targets were hit: the Khimtransagro logistics center in the Shkarovka settlement, Kiev Region, which was used for the delivery and distribution of military cargo, including components for unmanned aerial vehicles of various types," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike missile plant in Kiev that produced UAV components
Russian forces struck a Kiev-based missile assembly and component plant overnight that was manufacturing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) components, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"In the city of Kiev, a missile assembly and component plant (Kiev Radio Plant JSC, Trimen-Ukraine LLC), which manufactured components for reconnaissance and strike UAVs, including long-range ones, used to strike civilian targets on Russian territory, was hit," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike Shark, Hornet drone assembly sites in Kiev
Russian forces have struck assembly sites of the Ukrainian armed forces’ Shark and Hornet reconnaissance and strike drones in Kiev, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"An industrial enterprise (Element UA LLC), manufacturing and storing components for Hornet-type medium-range strike unmanned aerial vehicle (UAVs), a retail and warehouse complex belonging to the Ukrspetsystems company, on the premises of which Shark fixed-wing reconnaissance UAVs and medium-range strike UAVs were assembled and stored, were hit," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian Vasilkov airbase, fuel, lubricants depot in Borispol
Russian forces have struck Ukraine’s Vasilkov airbase, a fuel and lubricants depot in Borispol, and the electronic intelligence center of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in Markhalevka, the Russian Defense Ministry reported. According to the ministry, the strikes were carried out overnight.
"In addition, in the Kiev region, the Ukrainian armed forces’ Vasilkov airbase, a fuel and lubricants depot in Borispol, and the SBU’s electronic intelligence center in the Markhalevka settlement were hit," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike Smart Ammunition logistics center
The Russian military has struck a major logistics center of the Smart Ammunition company in Belaya Tserkov, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result, <…> the R-Plast logistics center in Belaya Tserkov, which manufactured and stored ammunition for medium-and long-range unmanned aerial vehicles, was hit. It was a major logistics center of the Smart Ammunition company," the ministry stated.
At least 384 Ukrainian UAVs downed over Russian regions overnight
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 384 Ukrainian UAVs over Russian regions and the Black Sea over the past night, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"During the past night, from 8:00 p.m. Moscow time [5 p.m. GMT] on September 7 to 8:00 a.m. [5 a.m. GMT] Moscow time on September 8, air defense forces on duty intercepted and destroyed 384 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over the territories of the Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Volgograd, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Tambov, Oryol, Rostov, Saratov, Smolensk, Moscow and Krasnodar regions, the Republic of Crimea, and over the Black Sea," the ministry said.

articles.title: Germany sending ‘urgently needed’ Patriot air-defence missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
Germany sending ‘urgently needed’ Patriot air-defence missiles to Ukraine
- Germany is sending urgently needed Patriot interceptor missiles from its military stockpiles to Ukraine amid increased Russian missile attacks.
- The UK announced £100 million to supply interceptors, ammunition, and drones to support Ukraine's air defence.
- Ukraine seeks about 1,000 Patriot missiles but most deliveries will only start in coming years, urging allies to provide current stockpile missiles now.
AI generated
BERLIN – Germany is sending Ukraine further “urgently needed” interceptor missiles for Patriot air-defence systems from its own military stockpiles, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said on Sept 8.
“I have decided... to deliver urgently needed PAK-2 interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine,” Pistorius said, during an online meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group.
He also appealed to other supporters of Ukraine “to look into their own stocks and make similar deliveries”.
However, Pistorius did not specify the number of interceptors or mention a timeline.
Faced with Moscow’s intensified ballistic missile strikes on the capital, Ukraine has warned of its urgent need for US-made Patriots amid dwindling supplies.
Patriot interceptors are among the few air-defence weapons in Kyiv’s arsenal that are capable of shooting down ballistic missiles, which fly at high speeds on steep trajectories.
However, the United States is conserving its stocks after having used a large number of Patriot interceptors during the war with Iran.
US deliveries of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine have been drastically reduced, and other countries are also clamouring for the weapons.
“I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
“But please, if in doubt, decide in favour for Ukraine.”
The United Kingdom announced earlier on Sept 8 that it was releasing £100 million (S$170 million) for interceptors, large-calibre ammunition, and drones for Kyiv.
Ukraine’s new acting defence minister, Yevgeniy Khmara, underscored the importance of air-defence weaponry as the country tries to fend off increased Russian drone and missile strikes.
“Just last night, the enemy has resorted to another mass air attack,” Khmara said at the meeting.
Ukraine is currently placing orders for roughly 1,000 Patriot interceptors with help from supporters and a loan from the European Union, Khmara said.
“However, the majority of these missiles will only start to be shipped in the coming years, which is why we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today,” Khmara told Pistorius and other officials from countries supporting Ukraine. AFP

articles.title: US turning Australia into military base – Guardian
articles.body:
US turning Australia into military base – Guardian
The US is turning Australia into a forward base for potential military operations in the Pacific, with American forces and defense contractors controlling or having access to roughly two-thirds of the country’s military facilities, The Guardian reported on Sunday.
Citing data compiled by the Nautilus Institute for Security and Sustainability, the newspaper identified 110 facilities across Australia with some form of US military or corporate presence out of 168 surveyed.
The US military directly controls 17 facilities, including the Pine Gap intelligence complex in central Australia, which plays a major role in US surveillance and military operations. The facility tracks missile launches, intercepts communications and provides targeting information for American forces around the world.
Other installations include a naval communications station in Western Australia used to communicate with submerged US submarines and RAAF Base Tindal in the north, which is being expanded to accommodate nuclear-capable B-52 Stratofortress bombers.
“These aircraft are able to land on Australian soil carrying nuclear weapons. The US government won’t tell Australia if and when they are. The Australian government won’t ask,” The Guardian wrote.
Beyond the facilities it directly controls, the US military has access to dozens of Australian installations, while American defense contractors, including Lockheed Martin and Northrop Grumman, operate at others. According to the Nautilus data, 41 of the 168 facilities surveyed have no significant US presence, while the status of another 17 remains unresolved.
The American footprint is also expanding. In June, AFP reported that the US was preparing to establish a permanent stockpile of battle-ready weapons, ammunition, and equipment for the Marine Corps in Australia, with the facility expected to reach full capacity by 2028.
“Over more than a decade, the United States has been preparing the capacity for high-tempo warfighting operations with China, springboarding from Australia,” Richard Tanter, the author of the Nautilus database, told The Guardian.
“From a Chinese perspective, Australia is not so much hosting US bases on its territory, it’s a US base in its own right… Australia is a serious piece of real estate in the US warfighting machine,” added Tanter, an honorary professorial fellow at the University of Melbourne.
Canberra maintains that the growing American presence strengthens Australia’s security. Defense Minister Richard Marles said in June that the expanding US footprint was important both for building the country’s military capabilities and for its national security.
Marles also argued that the US presence helped counter what he described as China’s “very significant military buildup” in the region.
Former Australian Defense Minister Christopher Pyne has similarly said the 2021 AUKUS pact between Australia, the US, and UK goes beyond Canberra’s acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines. He described the arrangement as establishing “a new United States submarine base in the Indian Ocean” that would provide Washington with a “massive strategic advantage.”
Tanter criticized Canberra’s approach, calling it “a massive institutional failure in Australia, a kind of learned incapacity at a political, parliamentary and bureaucratic level.”

Kyiv’s long-range drones and US President Donald Trump’s surprise announcement that the Washington would allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles on in the country. However, Trump's deal has yet to materialize. Moreover, Russia has ramped up cruise missile launches and Ukraine has run out of air defenses to stop them. Moscow is also failing to stop incoming missiles. In today’s edition we ask: What happens in war when offense proves better than defense for both sides?
Could this lose-lose situation make mediation efforts like the one undertaken in the past days by Donald Trump’s emissaries more relevant? When Russia is still calling the war a ‘special military operation’, what will it take for Moscow and Kyiv to get serious about a lasting settlement? The Kremlin is looking beyond the battlefield to the momentum enjoyed by Putin-friendly populists in France and Germany, as well as the US midterm elections and NATO. In that context, we look at Berlin’s calibrated response to a drone attack at Leipzig Airport. Is war in Ukraine about to wind down or escalate a whole further?
Produced by François Picard, Andrew Hilliar, Juliette Laffont, Ilayda Habip, Charles Wente.

articles.body:

NATO-Ukraine Council Holds Extraordinary Meeting on Urgent Air Defense Needs
An extraordinary meeting of the NATO-Ukraine Council at the level of Permanent Representatives convened at NATO Headquarters in Brussels to address the urgent need to strengthen Ukraine’s air and missile defense capabilities.
Chaired by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, the session was initiated by Ukraine ahead of the upcoming Ramstein-format meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group on September 8, according to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The NATO meeting comes against the backdrop of revelations that Moscow spent years digitally rehearsing a war with the Alliance. Russia’s General Staff had conducted extensive computer simulations modeling full-scale wars against NATO, the U.S., and Ukraine.
This includes scenarios like seizing Sweden’s Gotland island—and has since updated these virtual war games with real-world battlefield data from Ukraine.
During the meeting, Deputy Minister of Defence of Ukraine for European Integration Sergiy Boyev and Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Brigadier General Serhii Sobko presented allied representatives with a detailed assessment of current air threats and submitted a priority list of urgent requirements for air and missile defense systems.
“It is important to focus on helping Ukraine here and now. Right now, timeliness is more important than volume. Drones and air defense systems will determine the course of this winter and whether Ukraine emerges from it weaker or stronger,” Boyev stated in comments published by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
Following the presentation, Ukrainian officials called on NATO allies to transition from what is politically possible to what is operationally necessary by rapidly providing defense capabilities directly linked to protecting Ukrainian lives.
The delegation also urged partners to mobilize the resources required to meet NATO’s stated level of €70 billion ($81.2 billion) in military support for Ukraine by the end of the year.
The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense noted that the delegation emphasized how reinforcing the country’s air defenses serves security interests of the Alliance.
“A russian drone or missile destroyed over Ukraine will never reach a NATO country. Likewise, a russian service member killed in Ukraine will never reach Alliance territory,” said Alyona Getmanchuk, Head of the Mission of Ukraine to NATO.
Strengthening Ukraine’s air and missile defense remains the central focus for allies heading into the September 8 Ramstein-format meeting, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine reported.
The British government had also recently announced a £100 million ($135.1 million) military aid package to supply Patriot missiles, air defense interceptors, artillery rounds, and drones. Funded through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) , the equipment is designated to protect critical infrastructure ahead of expected Russian winter strikes against Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure targets.

articles.title: Call of corruption: What you should know about Ukraine’s billion-dollar scam industry milked by Zelensky’s government
articles.body:
Call of corruption: What you should know about Ukraine’s billion-dollar scam industry milked by Zelensky’s government
Ukraine’s enormous and toxic scam-call industry has suddenly been put under unprecedented pressure from forces Vladimir Zelensky cannot control.
Zelensky’s prosecutor general, Ruslan Kravchenko, tendered his resignation after Western-backed investigators accused his own chief cybercrime prosecutor of extorting protection money from scamsters, allegedly on behalf of his chief. Kravchenko has nevertheless insisted he stepped down for political reasons.
Ukraine’s industrial-scale scam-call network preys on the weak, robbing vulnerable people of their life savings and in some cases pushing them into violent crime. But the competition is literally cut-throat and explosive, and is believed to be behind a recent bomb attack linked to Ukrainian agents in Monaco.
How big is Ukraine’s scam-call industry?
Scam-calling rapidly developed between 2014 and 2016 in Ukraine. The keys to its swift growth were corruption in law enforcement, global technological advances in transborder communications and e-banking, and the abundant labor force.
The Geneva-based NGO Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC) estimated in April that the industry generates $1 billion a month and employs 60,000 people.
Who do Ukraine’s scam-call centers target?
One of Ukraine’s specifics is that young men defrauding Russian pensioners can rationalize their actions as fulfilling their patriotic duty without going to the front line.
Moscow perceives the crime business as a national security threat, claiming it works hand in glove with intelligence agencies. Russian authorities have reported dozens of cases in which a fraud victim was enticed to carry out criminal activity, from firebombing rail equipment to bringing a disguised explosive device to the office of a law enforcement agency.
However, true criminals go where the money is. Last year, GI-TOC estimated that half of victims of Ukrainian offices were Russian, but now reportedly 80% of them focus on Western nations.
How are Ukraine’s scam centers run?
Basically, they are the modern incarnation of telemarketing fraud, known as “boiler rooms” in English criminal slang. Ukrainian “offices” have their own “cold callers” – criminals who search for potential victims, “closers” – more skilled manipulators who actually defraud their marks, “floor managers” to oversee each individual operation, and “drops” who exfiltrate stolen money. In fact, most Ukrainian terms are borrowed.
Who owns and protects Ukraine’s scam-call industry?
The criminal networks normally run in regular office spaces, each with its own IT support to spoof phone numbers and grease the digital cogs and wheels. Larger offices have dedicated HR, accountants, security, and marketing.
Many of the centers pay bribes to officials, though there is a dispute over how compromised the government is. Western media tend to say paying off local police gives you a tip of an impending raid ordered from Kiev.
But Ukrainian media – and last week’s allegations – suggest a top-to-bottom network rife with infighting, hostile takeovers, and selective enforcement of the law.
Who works at Ukraine’s scam centers?
The workers are overwhelmingly young people in their late teens and early twenties, most of them male, aimless in life and with a taste for making quick cash, according to industry insiders.
“They are convinced that scamming people is better than enduring mockery working as a cashier,” a scam office tech guy told Ukrainskaya Pravda for an exposé it published. “For them it’s a small-time alluring crime.”
Why does the West allow its citizens to be targeted by Ukrainian scammers?
European law enforcement agencies are limited by the fact that their governments are determined to support the government in Kiev to keep the war with Russia rolling.
However, earlier this year, Ukrainian media reported that Western pressure reached a point where a major crackdown was imminent. Zelensky’s messaging aligned with the narrative.
Why has Ukraine’s profitable and connected scam-call center industry been targeted?
Zelensky sent a law to the Ukrainian parliament in early September, seeking tougher punishments for fraudsters.
Some Ukrainian media argued that Zelensky ordered the clampdown to pre-empt the latest scandal, initiated by Western-backed anti-corruption agencies. Last year he tried and failed to place the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) under the Prosecutor General’s Office.
The same agencies are chasing down multiple, multimillion corruption schemes linked to Zelensky’s inner circle that you can read about in RT’s ‘State of Corruption’ series.
In short, officials close to Ukraine’s leader have been accused of taking over $100 million in kickbacks from Ukraine’s energy industry, laundering millions to secure bail for a former energy minister, creaming millions from a missile and drone maker that was originally a TV production company run by Zelensky’s business partners, and running a system of vote-buying in parliament.
What impact has the sudden clampdown on Ukraine’s scam-call centers had?
Between January and mid-July, law enforcement reportedly took out over 2,000 jobs in the scam industry. But in just a single week in August, officials reportedly raided 95 scam offices where some 1,794 scammers were employed.
While the now-departed Kravchenko boasted of the results, NABU surveillance of his cybercrime underling, Sergey Kropiva, who the agency has accused of running a nationwide protection racket, reveals it was a PR exercise.
“We are not bending over backwards,” he allegedly told an accomplice. “We are dragging our heels, hitting ten of them [fraud offices] a week… The important thing is good media coverage of all this s**t.”
Ukrainian media say as of early August there were roughly 2,000 offices in Ukraine, each employing dozens or even hundreds of people and half of them paying protection money to corrupt officials.
According to Zerkalo Nedeli, the bribes amounted to roughly $240 million per year, 15% of which found its way to the Prosecutor General’s Office in Kiev.
Kravchenko is widely seen as having upped the ante following his appointment by Zelensky in 2025, triggering an industry-wide turf war. His downfall was described in the press with a crime-slang saying: “The cat got ruined by his own greed.”
If prosecutors creamed 15%, who has been taking the other 85%?
Corrupt officials are reportedly scattered throughout the Ukrainian government, from the border guard service, to Ukraine’s financial regulator, to national police, to secret services.
People at the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and the military intelligence agency HUR are allegedly on the take. The firefights in Kiev in which the two services engaged last week were described by some outlets as a conflict for scam proceeds.
There were claims in the Ukrainian press that scam money not only lines the pockets of security officials, but also generates off-the-books funding for their operation, not unlike the CIA did under President Ronald Reagan, when it sold weapons to Iran to fuel right-wing Contras insurgents in South America. The CIA reportedly overhauled both the SBU and HUR after the 2014 coup in Kiev.
What kind of risks are the Ukrainian heads of scam-schemes prepared to take?
One of Kropiva’s recorded conversations linked the ongoing semi-crackdown with “that guy in Bali.”
The reference was apparently to the kidnaping of two Ukrainian citizens in the Indonesian island province that took place in February. One of them escaped, while the other was held for ransom and later dismembered.
The victims were identified by the media as Igor Komarov and Yermak Petrovsky, the sons of suspected career crime bosses who were allegedly working together in the fraud business. The horrific torture video of Komarov was national news in Ukraine.
The bombing of exiled businessman Vadim Ermolaev and members of his family in Monaco in June was organized by a duo of HUR and SBU agents, according to Ukrainian investigators.
Ermolaev’s son Artur was previously sentenced to a suspended term in Estonia for running scam-call centers that victimized Estonian citizens to the tune of $114 million. There was speculation that the bombing attack was a warning for the father to stay away from the industry.
Meanwhile, Kropiva himself was quite brazen in his managerial role, bragging that he can “screw everyone in the law enforcement” and do what he wants, the recordings show. His alleged accomplice and girlfriend complained when he told her to remove Instagram photos proving her lavish lifestyle.
She came to her bail hearings wearing what journalists recognized as a $3,400 Saint Laurent jacket, which probably didn’t help her case.

articles.title: Ukraine reveals ‘game changer’ RAM-2X strike drone
articles.body:
Ukrainian defence manufacturer UKRSPECSYSTEMS has publicly identified itself as the maker of the RAM-2X precision-strike uncrewed aerial system, revealing a weapon the firm says has already been used extensively in combat and produced at scale rather than a new developmental design.
The company unveiled RAM-2X under its own name at the MSPO defence exhibition in Kielce, Poland, on 8 September, after previously withholding its involvement for Ukrainian security reasons. UKRSPECSYSTEMS says the system has been manufactured and employed operationally at large scale by Ukraine’s Defence Forces.
Speaking to the UK Defence Journal ahead of the announcement, Rory Chamberlain, Managing Director of UKRSPECSYSTEMS UK, said the company had wanted to discuss the system publicly for some time but had been prevented from doing so by Ukrainian security considerations.
He said those restrictions had now reduced sufficiently to allow UKRSPECSYSTEMS to identify itself as the manufacturer and begin discussing a capability that had previously remained largely hidden behind operational footage and battlefield reports.
Chamberlain told us RAM-2X became fully operational in 2024. Asked what the company meant when it described the system as being used at large scale, he would not provide an exact figure but said the scale was already in the “tens of thousands”, adding that this was a low estimate. On the company’s account, RAM-2X has already been developed, adapted and employed through several years of high-intensity war before the company has been able to put its name publicly alongside the system.
In its formal announcement, Chamberlain said: “RAM-2X isn’t new to the battlefield; what is new today is that we can finally talk about it publicly. It has been developed through combat and continuously improved using feedback from the Ukrainian units operating it.
“What matters is not simply the range or performance of an individual aircraft. RAM-2X demonstrates a different approach to precision strike: matching the effector to the target and generating military effect at a price and scale that can be sustained in war. And when RAM-2X is connected with SHARK-M, the result is much more than two drones. Persistent reconnaissance and precision strike become part of the same operational system – finding, tracking and engaging demanding targets at depth.”
Combat footage opened to public scrutiny
Alongside the reveal, UKRSPECSYSTEMS has opened what it calls the X-Archive, a collection of combat footage the company says was supplied by Ukrainian military units operating RAM systems and cleared for public release. The initial material concentrates on Russian air-defence equipment, with the company saying RAM systems have been credited with strikes against more than 450 air-defence-class targets.
That figure is the company’s own and refers to RAM systems collectively, so it should not be read as confirmation that RAM-2X alone conducted all 450 engagements. UKRSPECSYSTEMS is progressively releasing footage that it says can now be publicly associated with the RAM family after previously circulating without attribution.
Chamberlain also gave the UK Defence Journal additional detail on how the desired effect against such targets has changed during the war. He said RAM-2X had moved from an approach in which attacks could seek a mission kill, disabling a system sufficiently to take it out of the fight, towards one where Ukrainian forces increasingly sought complete destruction. The reason, he explained, was that equipment left damaged on the battlefield could subsequently be used as a decoy, changing the Ukrainian concept of operations.
Chamberlain said: “So now we aim for total kill on all the systems.”
He said SHARK reconnaissance aircraft remain over the area to provide rapid battle damage assessment after an engagement, allowing the unit to establish the effect of the strike.
Dmytro Khasapov, General Director of UKRSPECSYSTEMS, said: “This is not the beginning of RAM-2X’s story. It is simply the first time we are able to tell that story publicly. RAM-2X was developed in Ukraine, through combat, against real targets and in one of the most demanding electronic-warfare environments in the world. When we say combat-proven, we mean evidence, not a marketing claim. That is why, alongside RAM-2X, we are opening the X-Archive so people can see declassified evidence of the system at work.”
Up to 180km range with a 3.5kg warhead
RAM-2X is intended for precision strikes against high-value targets at operational-tactical depth. UKRSPECSYSTEMS gives the aircraft a range of up to 180 kilometres, endurance exceeding two hours and a 3.5kg warhead. According to the company, the system incorporates automatic target lock and tracking, while available options include optical navigation for operations where satellite navigation is denied and AI-based object recognition.
That electronic-warfare resilience is particularly important in Ukraine, where satellite navigation, control links and communications are routinely subjected to jamming and other forms of interference.
Rather than presenting RAM-2X as an isolated aircraft, UKRSPECSYSTEMS is positioning it as part of a broader reconnaissance-strike architecture connecting sensors, communications, ground control, software and effectors.
SHARK-M links reconnaissance directly to strike
A central element of that architecture is the relationship between RAM-2X and the company’s SHARK-M reconnaissance UAS, a pairing UKRSPECSYSTEMS calls the “Killer Duo”. SHARK-M is used for persistent reconnaissance and targeting, while RAM-2X provides the strike component. The company says the reconnaissance aircraft can also act as a communications relay in heavily contested electronic-warfare conditions.
Asked how closely the two aircraft are integrated, Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that information is shared automatically between the systems. That matters particularly for attacks at depth because targets may move between initial detection and the arrival of the strike aircraft. Persistent surveillance, he said, allows the target to remain under observation throughout that process.
Chamberlain said: “They’re all automatically shared. So it’s that full integration, and you have to understand that in Ukraine, your targets are often moving, and when we are looking at the deep strike as well, and the time onto target, it’s important that you have ISR with persistence there.”
The company’s wider argument is that shortening the connection between finding a target and attacking it can be as important as the performance of the strike aircraft itself.
Battlefield imagery used to train target recognition
Chamberlain also explained how UKRSPECSYSTEMS is using years of reconnaissance imagery to develop the AI-based object recognition offered with RAM-2X. He said the company’s ISR systems have been observing Russian targets since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, building up imagery as equipment, camouflage and operating practices have changed.
That includes seeing targets in low light, partly hidden by vegetation or otherwise presented differently from a clean reference image. Chamberlain said this material is used to train recognition systems across RAM-2X, SHARK and the company’s wider portfolio.
The approach, he said, allows the recognition tools to be updated as Russian forces adapt their own methods, rather than relying on a static library of target imagery.
More than 1,500 drones produced each month
The scale of UKRSPECSYSTEMS’ wider operation has also increased considerably during the war. Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that the company now employs well over 4,000 people and is approaching 5,000, while producing more than 1,500 drones per month across its portfolio.
He declined to disclose the exact mix of aircraft making up that monthly output or how far production exceeded the 1,500 figure, citing operational security. The company says it is also working to much shorter development cycles than those normally associated with conventional defence programmes.
Chamberlain said hardware changes could be introduced approximately every three weeks, while software could be updated around every six weeks, with broader system updates occurring on roughly three-month cycles or faster. He said that pace was necessary because equipment that works effectively on the Ukrainian battlefield cannot be assumed to remain effective indefinitely as enemy tactics, electronic warfare and countermeasures evolve.
UK interest as exports begin to open
The public disclosure of RAM-2X also comes as UKRSPECSYSTEMS begins looking beyond Ukraine, with the gradual easing of Ukrainian defence export restrictions opening opportunities with NATO customers.
Chamberlain told the UK Defence Journal that the company is already seeing British interest and hopes ultimately to offer the capability to the British Army. He said: “So you know the Ukrainian export rules are starting to relax, and with the start of the drone deal, that means the export is open for those NATO customers, and obviously we have the UK showing interest, which is great, and we hope to bring this for the British Army.”
He added that there was also considerable interest elsewhere within NATO.
Commander calls RAM-2X a ‘game changer’
The commander of Ukraine’s 15th “Black Forest” Brigade, using the callsign Sarmat, whose formation has operational experience with the system, told us: “RAM-2X has been a game changer for the Ukrainian battlefield. For destroying HVT targets over 150km RAM-2X is the best.”
The unit price of RAM-2X has not been publicly disclosed, but the UK Defence Journal understands it is priced as a genuine consumable, allowing it to be employed in substantial numbers rather than treated like a scarce, high-end missile. We understand that a successful RAM-2X strike can in some circumstances destroy equipment valued at two to three orders of magnitude more than the cost of the UAV itself, and potentially four orders of magnitude at the upper end.
For context, the UK Defence Journal understands a P-18 Terek radar to be valued at around $3.6 million, an S-400 launcher at approximately $15 million and a Buk-M3 launcher at around $30 million. Those figures do not mean every RAM-2X sortie attacks equipment of that value, but illustrate the economics behind matching comparatively inexpensive precision-strike UAVs against high-value battlefield systems.
The comparison with conventional precision weapons is not exact, though. Different weapons have different ranges, payloads, survivability and target sets, but the underlying concept is to make precision strike affordable enough to be used repeatedly and replenished at wartime scale.
Chamberlain said this ability to change quickly was fundamental to the company’s approach, arguing that equipment has to remain relevant to battlefield conditions rather than simply meeting a fixed specification. He told the UK Defence Journal that UKRSPECSYSTEMS continually adapts its systems as operating conditions change, adding that the evidence of their performance was already visible in combat.
Why this all matters
Asked finally why he was personally so enthusiastic about RAM-2X and the wider UKRSPECSYSTEMS approach, Chamberlain pointed less to any single specification than to the speed at which the system changes with the battlefield. He said: “You know, this is not, dare I say, a snake oil kind of scenario. The images are there. The reality is there.”
Larger changes, he said, come every few months or faster as Ukrainian units encounter new threats, tactics and countermeasures. Chamberlain said: “You have to be relevant on a battlefield to win a war.”
That, perhaps more than the 180km range or the numbers produced, is the point UKRSPECSYSTEMS is trying to make with RAM-2X. The aircraft being shown at MSPO is not a frozen design emerging from a development programme, but a weapon the company describes as shaped by combat, changed by combat and still changing with it.
RAM-2X is being displayed alongside the wider UKRSPECSYSTEMS portfolio at MSPO in Poland from 8 to 11 September, marking the first time the company has been able to publicly connect its name to a strike system that it says has already spent years operating in the war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia plans to test new ballistic missiles with a range of up to 800 km
articles.body:
Russia plans to test new ballistic missiles with a range of up to 800 km
Russia is planning to test a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 km by the end of 2026.
Source: Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Head of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU), at a meeting of the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council
Quote: "According to our estimates, Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 km by the end of this year."
Details: DIU believes that Russian forces may attempt to strike targets in Ukraine's west during tests of the new ballistic weapon.
"Russia, the aggressor state, is also increasing the intensity of missile and drone strikes on Ukraine in an effort to provoke a social and economic crisis. To this end, Moscow seeks to ramp up the production of ballistic missiles and increase the range of these weapons," DIU quoted Skibitskyi as saying.
Skibitskyi called on Ukraine's partner countries to tighten sanctions against Moscow to prevent the Russians from obtaining foreign components, particularly those used in long-range weapons.
The Russian military uses various types of ballistic missiles to attack Ukraine. Russian forces deploy 9M723 missiles from the Iskander-M system, KN-23/24 missiles supplied to Russia by North Korea, Zircon missiles and other types of weapons.
Background: Ukrainska Pravda previously reported, citing DIU, that as of August 2026, Russia was meeting its monthly missile production targets at 110-120%, while production of some types of missiles was exceeding planned levels.

articles.title: Foreign-made components, technologies again found in Russian weapons – Sybiha
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha emphasized the need to systematically close sanctions loopholes following yet another massive strike by Russia, in which foreign-made components and technologies were once again found in the weapons used.
"And once again, inside the weapons Russia uses to attack us, we find foreign-made components and technologies," Sybiha said in a post shared on X social media on Tuesday.
According to him, during the massive combined strike, Russia used ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones, and foreign-made components and technologies were once again found inside Russian weapons.
"There is something fundamentally wrong when technology developed in countries that stand for peace and security ultimately ends up inside Russian missiles launched at Ukrainian homes," the minister said.
Sybiha said the flow of such components into Russia cannot be viewed as a side effect of global trade. According to him, Russia is deliberately seeking loopholes in sanctions, creating procurement networks, using intermediaries and third countries, and obtaining critically important components to keep its military machine running.
"Every such component that reaches Russia is another opportunity for Moscow to produce more missiles. Every loophole left open gives the Russian military-industrial complex more room to operate. Closing them is therefore not a technical matter of sanctions compliance. It is a matter of saving lives," the foreign minister said.
He called for significantly stricter export controls, stronger law enforcement, and real consequences for those who help Russia circumvent restrictions. According to him, critically important technologies must be made inaccessible to Russia at every stage of the supply chain.
In addition, Sybiha emphasized the need to target sanctions against the entire ecosystem that supports Russian weapons production and procurement.
"It is not enough to sanction the missile after it has been built or the factory after it has expanded production. We must disrupt the networks that make this production possible in the first place," the minister said.
"We know how these chains work. We know Russia is exploiting the gaps. Now we need to close them – systematically and decisively," he added.

articles.title: Zelensky Arrives in Norway for Royal Funeral, Talks on Winter Air Defense Package
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre in Oslo on Tuesday, Sept. 8, for talks focused on strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, securing interceptor missiles, advancing the FREYJA anti-ballistic program, and preparing Ukraine for winter.
“I had a good meeting with the Prime Minister of Norway, Jonas Gahr Støre,” Zelensky wrote on X after the talks.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He said the two discussed Ukraine’s air-defense needs, interceptor missiles, and further work on FREYJA as Russia intensifies missile and drone attacks against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
Zelensky also expressed condolences over the death of King Harald V and thanked Norway’s royal family and people for their support for Ukraine.
Zelensky and First Lady Olena Zelenska arrived in Norway earlier on Tuesday ahead of Wednesday’s farewell ceremony for the late monarch.
Hours before Zelensky’s arrival, Russia launched a major missile and drone attack on Kyiv, killing five people and injuring 35. Residential buildings, a school, clinic, dormitory, and warehouses were among the sites damaged.
“Our priority right now is the winter package,” Zelensky said. “The main issue is strengthening air defense and assistance in other areas important for getting through the winter.”
The Norwegian prime minister warned that intensified Russian missile and drone attacks on homes and critical infrastructure were making the coming winter especially difficult for Ukraine.
What Ramstein Revealed: 300 Patriots, a $27 Billion Gap and Russia’s Longer War
“Ukraine faces a harsh winter,” he said, adding that Norway would continue standing with Ukrainians.
Air defense and winter resilience
Protecting Ukraine’s skies and critical infrastructure is increasingly urgent as Kyiv prepares for its fifth winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Moscow has repeatedly attacked Ukraine’s power generation, transmission, and heating infrastructure during the colder months, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heat.
Norway has emerged as one of Ukraine’s most significant European supporters. Oslo allocated NOK 85 billion ($9.2 billion) to Ukraine under the Nansen Support Program for 2026, including NOK 70 billion ($7.6 billion) in military assistance and NOK 15 billion ($1.6 billion) in civilian and humanitarian aid.
Norway has also proposed maintaining the same NOK 85 billion ($9.2 billion) level of assistance in 2027, with most expected to go toward military support.
Building on the Drone Deal and Ellisiv Accord
The Oslo talks build on an expansion of Ukrainian-Norwegian defense cooperation agreed less than three weeks ago.
During Støre’s visit to Kyiv on Aug. 23, the two leaders signed an Agreement on Defense and Security Cooperation under the Drone Deal format and a declaration establishing the Ellisiv Accord strategic partnership.
The Drone Deal aims to combine Ukraine’s battlefield experience and defense technologies with Norwegian investment and industrial capacity, expanding joint production and technology sharing.
Norway has also committed NOK 1.2 billion ($130 million) to the development and procurement of maritime drones produced by Norwegian and Ukrainian companies.
FREYJA anti-ballistic defense
During their meeting in Oslo, Zelensky and Støre also joined European defense industry representatives for talks on accelerating anti-ballistic missile defense capabilities.
The discussions centered on closer European industrial cooperation to strengthen Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
The push comes as Ukraine presses allies for more Patriot interceptors. Contracts are already in place for roughly 1,000 Patriot missiles backed by allied funding, but most are expected to arrive only in future years, leaving an urgent capability gap ahead of winter.
Germany announced additional Patriot interceptors for Ukraine on Tuesday, while the UK unveiled a £100 million ($135 million) winter air-defense package through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL).
On Wednesday, Sept. 9, Zelensky and Zelenska are expected to attend the funeral of King Harald V, who died on Aug. 28 at age 89.
