articles.title: Tehran Targets U.S. Base in Jordan In Retaliation for U.S. Destroying Iranian Oil Tankers
articles.body:
Iran said it targeted a U.S. base in Jordan with a series of missiles overnight after the U.S. military struck five Iranian oil tankers amid renewed hostilities in the region.
“The defeated and aggressor U.S. terrorist military, out of desperation, attacked several Iranian commercial and oil vessels,” said the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), according to Iranian state media.”This powerful battle will continue.”
A spokesperson for the Jordanian Armed Forces said a barrage of “20 ballistic missiles” had been launched towards its territory. The country’s air defense system successfully intercepted and destroyed 18 of the missiles, while the remaining two” fell in areas devoid of population centers.”
The IRGC on Wednesday claimed to have targeted two U.S. vessels and eight oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz as part of its wider retaliatory operations, as reported by Iranian state media.
U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said it had received reports involving several merchant vessels in the region that were subject to "disabling fire,” but it was unable to confirm the nature or impact of the disturbances.
U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM), in response, denied the IRGC’s claims, saying that “no U.S. Navy warship has been struck” as “all IRGC attempted attacks failed.”
The escalation comes after CENTCOM on Tuesday said it destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers in response to Iran targeting U.S. Navy ships with ballistic missiles over the previous two days.
“The U.S. warship successfully evaded the attempted Iranian attacks and continued to patrol regional waters. No American personnel were harmed,” said the U.S. defense force.
The active hostilities and attacks on shipping mark a serious escalation in the reignited war, which experienced a brief respite before flaring up again last week.
The U.S. and Iran are trading retaliatory attacks as President Donald Trump pursues a campaign of military and economic pressure on Iran, with Tehran threatening it could escalate the conflict further by targeting U.S. oil and gas interests in the Gulf.
Iran has specifically denounced the U.S. attacks on its oil shipments, with the Iranian Foreign Ministry on Wednesday insisting the strikes are “not only a dangerous escalation of tensions in the region, but also a clear threat to regional and international peace and security.”
Iran-backed Houthis escalate regional instability with attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure
Meanwhile, the Iran-backed Houthi militia in Yemen contributed to the regional instability by launching attacks on four cities in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday, with the aim of targeting oil infrastructure.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said 73 people had been injured in the strikes.
The attacks came after weeks of escalation between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen, shattering a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war.
“The U.S. has a very strong defensive military relationship with Saudi Arabia, and we’re watching those events very closely. It’s been going on for some time,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Tuesday.
The renewed fighting threatens to further disrupt shipping through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a critical trade route off the Arabian Peninsula for oil and global commerce.

articles.title: Germany 'ready to provide missiles for Patriots,' Zelensky says
articles.body:
Germany is 'ready to provide' additional supplies of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 8.
"These are exactly the kinds of decisions that bring peace closer: when you reduce the aggressor’s ability to destroy lives," Zelensky said in a post on social media. No timescale was given for the arrival of the additional interceptors.
"Preparing Ukraine for winter is of the highest priority and it requires us to act resolutely and immediately," German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said in comments at the Sept. 8 meeting of the Ramstein Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"In addition to PAC-2 interceptor missiles, Germany will further step up its continuous provision of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to provide greater quantities to Ukraine," Pistorius said, also committing to deliver additional IRIS-T air defense systems to Ukraine.
Ukraine relies on the American-made Patriot air defense system for its defense against Russian ballistic missiles, which Moscow has been increasingly using to pound Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine's stocks have dwindled as supplies have been diverted to the Persian Gulf due to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Ukraine's new Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara urged Ukraine's foreign partners to secure funding for additional Patriot interceptors before winter at the meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"To ensure Ukraine's resilience, we need solutions in the field of air defense," Khmara said. "We are concluding contracts for the supply of about 1,000 missiles for Patriot systems with our partners and through an EU loan," he said.
Khmara noted that long lead times for the manufacture of Patriot interceptors meant such missiles "will be supplied only in the coming years, so Ukraine is asking partners to provide missiles from their stocks today."
The announcement of the additional German support came after Kyiv suffered another overnight Russian drone and missile assault. Five people were killed in the Ukrainian capital and 25 were injured.
An additional £100 million package of British support was also announced on Sept. 8, with the funding also being directed toward additional Patriot interceptors.

articles.title: Russia prepared first Avangard hypersonic missile test in nearly eight years but canceled the launch, says expert Pavel Podvig
articles.body:
Russia appears to have been preparing to conduct its first test of the Avangard hypersonic system since 2018, but the launch was canceled for unknown reasons, writes Pavel Podvig, an expert on Russia’s strategic nuclear forces. Podvig, who has spent years observing Russia’s protocols for conducting such tests, reached that conclusion after analyzing aviation warnings issued ahead of the apparent launch and notices distributed by local authorities.
According to Podvig, the test was planned for Sept. 3-5. A UR-100N UTTKh intercontinental ballistic missile carrying an Avangard hypersonic glide vehicle was expected to launch from the Dombarovsky/Yasny area in Russia’s Orenburg region and to fly toward the Kura missile test range on the Kamchatka Peninsula.
Ahead of the expected test, Russia issued NOTAMs, or Notices to Air Missions, temporarily closing sections of airspace. The restricted areas covered Dombarovsky along with expected rocket-stage impact zones in the Tyumen Region and the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Region and the area around the Kura test range.
Residents of the Vikulovsky, Vagaysky and Sorokinsky districts of the Tyumen Region were also warned about an upcoming launch. Sept. 3 was listed as the primary date and Sept. 4 as a backup date.
Podvig said the locations of the restricted areas indicate that the planned test involved Avangard rather than Russia’s Sarmat intercontinental ballistic missile. In particular, the NOTAM around Dombarovsky covered the missile silo used for previous Avangard tests but did not include the silo from which Sarmat had previously been launched.
Another indication that an Avangard test was planned, Podvig said, was the fact that an area near the village of Vikulovo in the Tyumen Region was designated in the September notices as an expected rocket-stage impact zone. The same area was used during previous Avangard tests in 2013, 2015, 2016, and 2018.
Avangard is a Russian strategic missile system equipped with a hypersonic glide vehicle capable of carrying a nuclear warhead. Unlike a conventional intercontinental ballistic missile warhead, the glide vehicle travels toward its target through the atmosphere at hypersonic speed and can maneuver both laterally and vertically. The capability is intended to make its trajectory harder to predict and more difficult for missile defense systems to intercept.
Vladimir Putin first publicly unveiled Avangard in 2018 and the system’s last known test took place in December 2018.If a fresh test had been successful, Russian authorities almost certainly would have publicly reported it due to Avangard’s symbolic importance to the country’s missile program, Podvig explained.
Notably, there were also no signs that an accident occurred during a Russian launch attempt. If a launch failure had occurred, Podvig said, the NOTAMs could have been expected to be canceled early. Instead, they remained in effect and simply expired after Sept. 5.
“The bottom line is that Russia apparently planned to launch Avangard from Dombarovskiy to Kura, but had to scrub the test for some reason. We should expect another attempt at some point,” Podvig concluded.
The Russian authorities have not publicly commented on preparations for such a test, nor about its cancellation.

articles.title: UK brings forward maritime role for Protector drones
articles.body:
Britain is bringing forward plans to give the RAF’s Protector drone a maritime capability, with a review of the programme now under way and revised milestones expected by December 2026.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard disclosed the move in response to a written parliamentary question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked what progress had been made towards integrating Protector with P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft and Type 26 frigates.
Pollard said: “The Defence Investment Plan directed Maritime capabilities for the PROTECTOR RG Mk1 be brought forward, and a review of PROTECTOR is therefore currently underway. Rebaselined milestones are expected by December 2026, with a Review Note to follow.”
He added: “In the interim the Capability Sponsor, Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, is progressing capability development activity.”
The 2025 Strategic Defence Review recommended exploring a maritime surveillance capability for Protector, integrated with the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon fleet and the Royal Navy’s new Type 26 anti-submarine warfare frigates.
The review said Protector should be enhanced with maritime surveillance equipment and improved connectivity to give the long-endurance remotely piloted aircraft wider utility. It also placed Protector within the planned evolution of Britain’s anti-submarine warfare force under Atlantic Bastion, envisaging underwater, surface and airborne drones operating alongside Type 26 frigates, P-8 maritime patrol aircraft and nuclear-powered attack submarines.
The concept would use Protector’s endurance to provide persistent surveillance over large maritime areas while connecting its sensor picture with crewed aircraft and warships. The aircraft can remain airborne for more than 30 hours, providing a potentially useful means of maintaining coverage without continuously committing a P-8 to the same task.
The concept is not entirely new to British forces, of course. In 2021, a maritime-configured MQ-9B SeaGuardian, the maritime variant of the aircraft family on which Protector is based, took part in a series of demonstrations in the UK.
During Exercise Joint Warrior, SeaGuardian operated with an RAF P-8 in a manned-unmanned teaming demonstration supporting anti-submarine warfare activity, including the tracking, monitoring and reporting of sonobuoys.
The maritime MQ-9B configuration demonstrated at the time included a maritime surface-search radar, Automatic Identification System receiver and electro-optical and infrared sensors. General Atomics has also developed an anti-submarine warfare mission kit capable of working with sonobuoys.
Those capabilities should not be taken as confirmation of the final equipment fit for British Protector aircraft, which has yet to be disclosed or properly evaluated.
Defence had already begun examining a wider maritime role before publication of the Strategic Defence Review. In January 2025, ministers said Britain was working with the NATO Intelligence, Surveillance and Reconnaissance Force to scope options for using Protector in the North Atlantic and Arctic.
After the Strategic Defence Review, however, the Government stopped short of giving a timetable. Asked in October 2025 when Protector would be integrated with P-8 Poseidon and Type 26, Pollard said the maritime capability was being considered through the forthcoming Defence Investment Plan.
The published Investment Plan subsequently allocated £590 million to Protector over the four years to 2029-30, but did not explicitly describe the maritime surveillance programme. It separately committed £260 million to upgrade the RAF’s P-8 Poseidon aircraft and equip them with the UK-built Sting Ray torpedo.
The latest answer now confirms that the Investment Plan actually resulted in a direction to bring Protector’s maritime capabilities forward, with detailed programme milestones being reconsidered as part of the wider Protector review.
That review comes as the overall aircraft programme works through a number of outstanding issues. The latest government major-projects assessment rated Protector Red, citing its pending programme rebaseline alongside trained crew numbers, Full Motion Video metadata dissemination and delays to weapons testing.
Some of those issues have since moved forward. Protector is already being employed operationally, Paveway IV has been operationally available since March 2026 and Brimstone 3 testing has progressed to analysis ahead of operational clearance.
By December, Defence now expects to have rebaselined the milestones governing the programme, including the work intended to turn Protector from a predominantly land-focused persistent surveillance and strike aircraft into another sensor within Britain’s increasingly integrated North Atlantic maritime force.

articles.title: Battlefield sees 263 clashes over past day – Ukraine's General Staff
articles.body:
Battlefield sees 263 clashes over past day – Ukraine's General Staff
A total of 263 combat clashes have occurred on the battlefield over the past day. Ukrainian defence forces have hit seven clusters of Russian military personnel, eight UAV ground control stations and an artillery piece belonging to the Russians.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook, information as of 08:00 on 9 September
Quote: "In total, 263 combat clashes were recorded over the past day. Yesterday, the enemy launched two missile strikes and conducted 79 airstrikes, dropping 302 guided aerial bombs. In addition, the invaders deployed 9,233 kamikaze drones and conducted 2,601 strikes on Ukrainian settlements and positions, including 42 from multiple-launch rocket systems."
Details: Ukrainian defence forces hit seven areas where Russian military personnel were concentrated, eight UAV ground control stations and an artillery piece belonging to the Russians over the past 24 hours.
On the North Slobozhanshchyna front and in the operational zone in Russia's Kursk Oblast, two Russian assaults were recorded. The Russians conducted 79 strikes on Ukrainian positions and settlements; they also carried out one airstrike, dropping one guided bomb.
On the South Slobozhanshchyna front, Ukrainian forces repelled 10 Russian attacks. The Russians attempted to advance towards the settlements of Lyman, Starytsia, Vovchansk, Chaikivka Mala Vovcha, Rubizhne and Ustynivka.
On the Kupiansk front, the Russians attempted to improve their positions six times, conducting assaults towards the settlements of Kupiansk, Kurylivka, Hlushkivka and Novoosynove.
On the Lyman front, Russian forces launched 11 attacks towards the settlements of Shyikivka, Druzheliubivka, Novoselivka, Lyman and Dibrova. All attacks were repelled.
On the Sloviansk front, the Russians conducted seven offensive actions near the settlements of Yampil, Kryva Luka, Kalenyky, Mykolaivka and Rai-Oleksandrivka.
On the Kramatorsk front, Russian troops conducted one attack towards the village of Yurkivka.
On the Kostiantynivka front, 17 Russian attacks were recorded. The Russians conducted assaults near the town of Kostiantynivka and towards the settlements of Novoselivka, Mykolaipillia, Sofiivka, Rusyn Yar, Illinivka and Kucheriv Yar.
On the Pokrovsk front, the Russians conducted 49 attacks. They attempted to advance towards the settlements of Dorozhnia, Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Vodianske, Shevchenko, Nadiia, Myrne, Serhiivka, Udachne, Novomykolaivka, Novopidhorodnie, Dobropillia, Hannivka, Krasnopodillia and Novopavlivka.

articles.title: Iran retaliates after US strikes on oil tankers (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Iran retaliates after US strikes on oil tankers (VIDEOS)
Iranian forces have struck eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf and targeted two US Navy vessels in retaliation for attacks on Iranian shipping, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said on Wednesday. It claimed the strikes inflicted “significant damage” on the ships.
US Central Command later rejected the claim that American warships were hit, saying, “no US Navy warship has been struck” and all IRGC attacks failed. CENTCOM added that US forces destroyed ten Iranian tankers over the past week, describing the vessels as part of a multi-billion-dollar network funding the IRGC.
The IRGC said it also targeted ten other ships that allegedly attempted, with US military support, to pass through an area of the Strait of Hormuz that Tehran declared prohibited and unsafe. The IRGC said it remains in control of shipping through the strategic waterway. The claims have not been independently verified, and there has been no immediate US confirmation of damage to the vessels.
The attacks came after the IRGC Navy issued an “urgent warning” late Tuesday, telling tanker crews around the docks and anchorages of Bahrain and Kuwait to immediately abandon their ships.
“We warn all crew members of the tankers in the vicinity of the docks of Kuwait and Bahrain... to immediately leave their vessels, whether at anchor or at the docks, as they will be targeted,” the IRGC Navy Command said.
The statement accused Bahrain and Kuwait of hosting US forces and being “partners” in Washington’s attacks on Iranian shipping.
Additional footage of a PATRIOT battery conducting a massive ballistic missile engagement over Jordan tonight. 
Well over a dozen interceptors can be seen engaging incoming Iranian ballistic missiles. pic.twitter.com/u69lJKtFJ7
Iranian retaliation began shortly afterward, with numerous videos circulating online showing ballistic missiles being launched from locations across Iran toward US military facilities in the region.
Videos from Jordan appear to show intense air-defense activity, with Patriot interceptors engaging incoming projectiles, including what some OSINT accounts identified as medium-range ballistic missiles equipped with cluster warheads.
Multiple OSINT accounts identified Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, a major facility used by US forces east of Amman, as one of the principal targets. Some reported missile impacts near the base, but neither the impacts nor the type of warheads used have been officially confirmed.
US Central Command said it destroyed five Iranian crude oil carriers after the IRGC allegedly targeted a US Navy warship with ballistic missiles twice over the previous two days. The command said four tankers were struck in the Gulf of Oman and a fifth near Kharg Island, adding that US forces ordered their crews to abandon ship before the vessels were rendered inoperable.
The latest attacks follow another round on Saturday in which US Central Command said it struck three Iranian crude carriers after ballistic missiles were fired toward a US aircraft carrier and guided-missile destroyer. Two tankers were disabled and a third, which was carrying no oil, was destroyed after the crew was ordered to abandon ship.
Iran subsequently claimed that it struck three tankers traveling along what it described as an unauthorized route through the Strait of Hormuz, as well as three US-linked vessels elsewhere.
The maritime confrontation has become an increasingly prominent front in the six-month conflict. The US maintains a naval blockade restricting traffic to and from Iranian ports, while Iran has imposed its own controls over passage through Hormuz and recently announced plans for an additional restricted maritime zone in the Persian Gulf.
Around one-fifth of global oil supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the war, making threats to commercial shipping particularly sensitive for energy markets. Oil prices continue to climb, with Brent breaking above $100 a barrel on Wednesday for the first time in nearly two months as markets price in growing risks to global energy supplies.

articles.title: Russian drone strike near Ukraine-Moldova border kills at least two as Ukraine targets oil terminal
articles.body:
Russian drone strike near Ukraine-Moldova border kills at least two as Ukraine targets oil terminal
An overnight Russian drone strike at a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova killed at least two people, Odesa's regional governor said Wednesday. Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said that 17 drones had hit Moldovan territory in August alone as both Kyiv and Moscow ramp up long-range strikes on military and energy infrastructure.
Two civilians were killed in a Russian drone strike at a checkpoint on Ukraine's border with Moldova, the regional governor said Wednesday.
"Tonight, enemy drones attacked the Starokozache international road checkpoint on the border with Moldova," Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper wrote on social media.
"Sadly, there are casualties among the civilians who were near the checkpoint: according to preliminary information, two people were killed and three wounded."
An image attached to Kiper's message showed a deserted border post littered with debris.
The attack forced the closure of the checkpoint located around 500 kilometres south of Kyiv, Ukraine's State Border Guard Service said.
A Moldovan driver was also injured in the attack, according to the country's foreign ministry.

Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan on Wednesday said Russia's war against Ukraine was "increasingly endangering the lives of our citizens as well".
Tofan said 17 drones had hit Moldovan territory in August alone, more than during the whole of last year.
"The attacks have intensified so much," he said in a video of a cabinet meeting posted on Facebook. "It's becoming the norm, yet at the same time it's clearly an extremely worrying development."
Ukraine hits Russian oil terminal, naval base
Both Ukraine and Russia continued to exchange air strikes on each other's infrastructure.
Ukrainian forces struck targets in Russia's Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk and in the Krasnodar region, including a naval base and a terminal for loading oil, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday.
Zelensky said military port facilities and warships allegedly carrying missiles had also been struck.
For its part, the Russian defence ministry said that its forces had struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel carrying what it alleged was military equipment in the Black Sea en route to the port of Odesa, as well as a warehouse in Kyiv belonging to a company manufacturing drones, Russian news agencies reported.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

articles.title: Defense Forces down 165 Russian UAVs – Air Force

On the night of September 9, Russians attacked the territory of Ukraine with Iskander-M ballistic missiles, S8000 "Banderol" missiles, as well as 196 strike UAVs of the Shahed and Gerbera types, and "Parodiya"-type decoy drones, reported the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

articles.title: Despite Russian strikes, Ukraine’s BTR-4 maker built 600 vehicles
articles.body:
- Ukraine's KhKBM has built more than 600 BTR-4 armored personnel carriers since the 2022 invasion, with capacity for about 200 a year.
- The state currently has no active contract for new BTR-4Es, though the company has parts in stock for 100 to 200 more vehicles.
A Ukrainian armored vehicle maker has built more than 600 BTR-4 troop carriers since Russia’s full-scale invasion began, working through repeated missile strikes on the country’s defense industry.
The Kharkiv Morozov Machine Building Design Bureau, known as KhKBM, disclosed the production figure to a Militarnyi correspondent at the MSPO defense exhibition in Kielce, Poland.
The company relocated its operations after the 2022 invasion put its home city of Kharkiv within range of Russian strikes, and it has kept building the eight-wheeled BTR-4 armored personnel carrier throughout the war.
KhKBM says it can build about 200 BTR-4s a year at current capacity. The vehicle’s BTR-4E variant is roughly 80% Ukrainian-made by component count, according to the company representative, a level of domestic content that has let the plant keep working even as some imported parts became harder to source during the war.
Despite that output, the state currently has no active contract to buy more BTR-4Es, the KhKBM representative said. Militarnyi first reported the funding gap in June, when plant workers said they were finishing the last government order on their production lines.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry has not placed new armored vehicle orders since the start of 2026, according to earlier Militarnyi reporting, with procurement officials saying deliveries are continuing under contracts signed in prior years while the General Staff works out this year’s requirements. KhKBM says it has enough parts in stock to build another 100 to 200 vehicles even without a new order.
The company used MSPO to show an updated BTR-4E fitted with a rear ramp built to a specification the military requested, which KhKBM plans to make standard on future production vehicles. The armor meets NATO’s STANAG 4569 standard, with frontal protection rated to stop 12.7 mm armor-piercing incendiary rounds and side and rear armor rated against 7.62 mm rounds. Mine protection comes from layered armored plates rated to STANAG levels 3a and 3b, backed by an aramid anti-spall liner inside the hull.
The updated vehicle also carries slat armor around its perimeter and upper hull to defeat shaped-charge weapons, along with chain and rod curtains meant to counter loitering drones that wait above a target before striking. KhKBM has fitted the vehicle with a Ukrainian-made electronic warfare system and says it plans to eventually add an active protection system and additional anti-drone netting to both the hull and its gun turret.
The exhibited BTR-4 also carries a new turret called Topaz, which KhKBM said is still undergoing testing.

articles.title: Iran seizes ‘most modern’ US submarine drone (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Iran seizes ‘most modern’ US submarine drone (VIDEO)
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has announced the seizure of “one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines” in the possession of the US military. The Pentagon downplayed the incident, saying it was an old drone without any sensitive equipment.
On Tuesday, the IRGC published a video of what it claimed was the advanced US undersea drone, which could perform a wide range of tasks, from seabed mapping to intelligence and surveillance operations, pipeline inspection, and anti-submarine warfare support.
The footage shows a grey, metallic, torpedo-like cylindrical vessel around 5.8 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, weighing around 2.7 tons. The undersea vessel can spend up to 10 days underwater and reach a maximum depth of 6,000 meters, according to the IRGC statement.
The Iranian military identified it as a Dive-LD drone developed by US defense contractor Anduril Industries that entered service in April 2025.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) sought to downplay the incident, claiming Iran obtained a malfunctioning older-model drone that did not carry any sensitive equipment.
The undersea vessel was surveilling regional waters and “neither collected sensitive data nor carried any classified sonar or radar equipment,” US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins, a CENTCOM spokesman, said in a statement.
The incident comes amid yet another escalation between the US and Iran. Late Tuesday, Iran launched ballistic missiles toward US military bases in the Middle East in what it called retaliation for an earlier US attack on Iranian oil tankers near Kharg Island. The IRGC also issued an “urgent warning” late Tuesday, telling tanker crews around the docks and anchorages of Bahrain and Kuwait to leave their vessels immediately ahead of potential attacks.

articles.title: Can Ukraine’s newly shown Koral become home-built answer to Patriot? Expert evaluates system displayed at Poland’s MSPO expo
articles.body:
Ukraine's newly shown Koral missile could become a home-built answer to the Patriot in addition to the "Freya" project. However, the system has yet to prove it can stop Russian ballistic missiles, Ivan Kyrychevsky, an arms expert at Defense Express and a soldier in the 413th REID regiment of the Unmanned Systems Forces, said on a YouTube broadcast.
Currently, the PAC-3 version of the Patriot is the only weapon in Ukraine's arsenal that reliably stops Russia's maneuvering Iskander ballistic missiles, and its interceptors are scarce, costly, and rationed for Ukraine by the US.
But in the podcast, Kyrychevsky places Koral, on the data available so far, at roughly the older PAC-2 level. A PAC-2-class interceptor can handle aircraft and simpler ballistic targets, yet it is not the ideal tool against the fast, maneuvering Iskander and Kinzhal that do the most damage. That leaves Koral a hedge against dependence, not a replacement.
The missile sits a tier below Patriot
Kyrychevsky based the judgment on photos released at the expo. The Koral missile lacks the gas-dynamic surfaces that would let it maneuver in flight, he said, and it carries a different warhead from the "hit-to-kill" round on the PAC-3. He did not treat that as disqualifying.
"We are in a situation where we do not just need means against ballistics, but means of at least some technological level," he said.
Cost tilts Ukraine toward its own missile
The economics push in the same direction. A PAC-3 interceptor runs about $10 million for export, and Kyrychevsky noted that even the US Army finds the missiles expensive to spend at the rate the fighting around Iran has demanded.
"We are better off building our own analog of the Patriot, even a mediocre one, than staying dependent on the regularity of external deliveries," he believes.
Winter still hinges on the Patriot
For all that, Kyrychevsky was blunt about the near term. Koral still needs to be tested against Russian ballistic missiles, even experimentally, to confirm its claimed performance, and power cuts at the plants that build it could slow production.
“My assessment for now is roughly this: hopefully, we’ll be able to put the ‘Koral’ to the test against Russian ballistic missiles on an experimental basis," he said.
This winter, he said, Ukraine will need Patriot interceptors regardless of whether it develops its own. Work on Koral began in 2016, and the system was first shown in 2021, a fast pace for a weapon of its kind, and a separate European project, Freya, is advancing on a parallel track.
In July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Ukraine, in cooperation with other European countries, was working on an anti-ballistic missile defense system called “Freya". It is intended to serve as a cheaper and more widely deployable alternative to Patriot air defense systems.
Zelenskyy noted that, in theory, Ukraine could develop “Freya” on its own, but doing so would take significantly more time — potentially years. The system would require not only a missile and launcher, but also radars, command-and-control systems, and many other components. Even with European partners, the process will not be quick.

articles.title: Ukrainian Drones Strike Fuel Oil Terminal, Military Assets in Krasnodar

articles.title: Transferring Patriot missiles from European stocks to Ukraine not a systemic solution – Czech expert
articles.body:
Transferring Patriot missiles from European stocks to Ukraine not a systemic solution – Czech expert
Michal Smetana, Director at the Peace Research Center Prague and Associate Professor of International Studies at Charles University, said this in remarks to Ukrinform, commenting on a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"The United States is a key player when it comes to interceptors for Patriot systems. Without American supplies, it is practically clear that Ukraine will face a significant shortage of them this winter," the expert said.
Michal Smetana / Photo: Michal Smetana/Facebook
According to the expert, the transfer of some of their Patriot interceptor stocks by European countries to Ukraine could provide partial relief, "but it is not a systemic solution."
In the long term, Smetana believes, new and cheaper systems for defending against ballistic missiles need to be developed. In this regard, he mentioned the pan-European Freyja project.
"However, deploying it against Russian attacks is a medium-term prospect, and even under the most optimistic estimates, unfortunately, this will not be a solution for this winter in Ukraine," Smetana said.
He added Russia can be expected to try to exploit the situation and concentrate its ballistic attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure during the fall and winter.
As reported, a virtual meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group was held on September 8. During the meeting, Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said Ukraine needs 300 Patriot interceptor missiles from partners' existing stocks, 500 air-to-air missiles capable of countering cruise missiles, man-portable air defense systems and $2 billion for drones.

articles.title: US destroys five Iranian tankers as Tehran launches retaliatory strikes on Jordan
articles.body:
US CENTCOM said crews were warned to abandon ship before its strikes after the IRGC fired missiles at a US Navy warship twice in two days. Tehran launched missile strikes on US targets in Jordan and warned tankers near Kuwait and Bahrain to evacuate.
US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday after the Revolutionary Guards fired ballistic missiles at a US Navy warship twice in two days, as Iran launched missile strikes on US targets in Jordan.
US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the crews of all five vessels — the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco and Derya — were warned to abandon ship before the strikes.
The targeted warship evaded both Iranian attacks without casualties, CENTCOM said.
Iranian state-affiliated news agency confirmed one oil tanker was struck near Jask and another tanker four miles off Kharg Island. Iran's state broadcaster has reported that a commercial vessel was also attacked in the coastal waters of Jask county.
According to Tasnim, citing local sources, the attack on the tanker near Kharg caused no casualties.
Iran launched missiles at US targets in Jordan following the tanker strikes, according to Iranian state-run television.
"Given the malign actions of the terrorist US military in targeting several oil tankers of the Islamic Republic of Iran, we warn all tanker crews in the area of the ports of Kuwait and Bahrain, which host these terrorists and are partners in their aggression, to leave their vessels immediately, whether at anchorage or at the quays, as they will be targeted," IRGC said.
The Khatam al-Anbiya central command followed with a threat to US bases in the region.
"The US military has ordered Iranian oil tankers to evacuate so that it can strike them; therefore I declare that any attack on Iranian oil tankers will result in US bases in the region being targeted by the armed forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran," Major General Abdollahi said in a statement.
Jordan's military said its air defence systems intercepted 18 ballistic missiles launched toward its territory and that two others landed in uninhabited areas. No casualties were reported.
Jordan hosts several US military installations and has been a repeated target of Iranian strikes since the war began on 28 February.
Iran also said it had captured a US unmanned underwater vessel at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz before dawn, broadcasting images of what it described as the captured drone on state television. Iran had claimed to have struck a US Navy sea drone on Sunday.
The Trump administration separately announced new sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian commercial and private airlines and foreign cargo providers, in a further effort to isolate Tehran from its remaining trading partners.
The exchange marks one of the sharpest escalations since the framework deal the two sides signed in June broke down the following month.
Both sides have been attempting to assert control over the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil passed before the war began.
The US has been enforcing a naval blockade of Iranian ports while Tehran has sought to impose its own transit regime on commercial shipping through the strait.

articles.title: Ukraine Unveils Koral Air Defense Missile Launcher for First Time
articles.body:
Ukraine unveiled a self-propelled launcher for its Koral surface-to-air missile for the first time Tuesday at the MSPO international defense exhibition in Poland.
An image released by Ukraine’s state-owned defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom showed a missile being launched from a mobile system mounted on the chassis of a Czech-made Tatra truck.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Ukrainian military news outlet Militarnyi, the Koral missile which is reportedly compatible with launchers used by the S-300 and Patriot missile system, is designed to intercept aerial and ballistic targets as part of an air defense system, according to information presented by the developer.
In exceptional circumstances, it could also be used against radar-visible targets on land or at sea. The missile weighs 450 kilograms (992 pounds), including a 36-kilogram (79-pound) warhead. Its guidance system combines inertial navigation, radio-command updates and an active radar-homing seeker.
The missile is 4.8 meters (15.7 feet) long and has a diameter of 230-300 millimeters (9-12 inches). Its wingspan is 835 millimeters (33 inches), while its control surfaces span 685 millimeters (27 inches).
Development work on the Koral project began in 2016. Documents from that period described the missile as part of a planned ship-based surface-to-air missile system.
The project became more widely known in 2021, when Ukraine’s Luch Design Bureau presented a full-size model of the missile at the Arms and Security defense exhibition.
Zelensky Offers Presidential Plane for Witkoff and Kushner’s Next Kyiv Visit
At the time, Koral was described as a modular missile that could potentially be used with both land- and ship-based air defense systems. Developers also considered adapting it for use as an air-to-air missile.
The initial version had more limited stated specifications. It was expected to have a range of up to 30 kilometers (19 miles), an interception altitude of up to 10 kilometers (6 miles), a total weight of about 300 kilograms (660 pounds) and a 25-kilogram (55-pound) warhead.
The earlier design was 4.33 meters (14 feet) long and had a diameter of 230-260 millimeters (9-10 inches). Developers said the specifications could change depending on customer requirements.

articles.title: Berlin slams Kiev for not spending aid cash on German guns
articles.body:
Berlin slams Kiev for not spending aid cash on German guns
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has criticized Kiev for failing to spend enough of its Western-provided procurement money on German weapons, arguing that the country’s massive support for Ukraine should at least benefit its defense industry.
Germany is one of Ukraine’s largest bilateral supporters, providing or earmarking more than €43 billion ($50 billion) in “civilian” assistance and around €58 billion in military aid since the conflict escalated in 2022.
“We are now the strongest supporter of Ukraine in terms of financial and military support. And naturally, the German defense industry must benefit from this,” Wadephul told Bild in an interview published on Tuesday.
The minister said he raised the issue with Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky during a visit to Kiev last month.
“We stand by you, we support you. But I also have to explain this to German taxpayers, and the very least you can do is to involve the German defense industry in all procurement measures,” Wadephul said he told Zelensky.
“At the moment, we are not entirely satisfied with the level of orders in Germany,” he added, saying Kiev has been asked to review its purchases and ensure that the situation “gets better.”
Germany’s demands that the money spent on Kiev flow back to its own weapons makers mirror US President Donald Trump’s approach to Ukraine aid. Since returning to the White House, Trump has largely shifted the financial burden of supplying US weapons to European NATO members and Canada. Under the PURL mechanism, the bloc’s members now pay Washington for US-made arms that are then delivered to Kiev.
Moscow has criticized the unprecedented military buildup by Germany and the wider EU on the pretext of the ‘Russian threat’. President Vladimir Putin said in June that Western governments are no longer concealing their intentions and are “openly saying that they are preparing for war with us.”
Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has warned that Germany and the rest of Europe under their current leadership are “transforming into a Fourth Reich” and seek fight Russia “to the last Ukrainian.”
Berlin has also stepped up pressure on Ukrainian men of military age living in Germany to return home “without coercion.” Wadephul backed calls by Bavarian leader Markus Soeder and suggested that the German authorities could provide Kiev with information identifying Ukrainians receiving welfare benefits or holding registered residency status so they can be contacted for mobilization. Germany has separately backed stripping newly arriving draft-age Ukrainian men of the automatic temporary-protection privileges granted to refugees.

articles.title: EU pursues closer Israel ties on air defense and space
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — The EU is looking to Israel to support its new push for high-tech air defense and space capabilities.
Israel Space Agency boss Shimrit Maman this week traveled to Brussels where she met Tuesday with Ekaterina Zaharieva, European commissioner for startups, research and innovation for talks on key areas like AI and robotics.
The visit comes before Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her first major speech on space at a summit in Paris on Thursday, where she is expected to warn of growing hostilities and the need for Europe to step up its presence in space.
Advertisement
"It's very hard to do things on your own," Maman told POLITICO, warning that the militarization of space "is already happening — we just don't realize how much" and that Israel is seeing more interest from allies in "dual-use" technology for both civilian and defense purposes.
"One of the things we are working on is early warning systems," she said. "We saw that very nicely in the last round [of missile strikes] we had with Iran, for example. How we are managing to get [warnings to] all the civilians in Israel and not have that many casualties. That's part of that system. We are working on that very wide look that you're able to warn in advance, have that system warn the citizens."
A string of recent deals have seen the EU pursue closer military and technological relations with Israel, after several years of effective disengagement as a result of political tensions that have followed the war in Gaza. However, competition from Washington and strategic rivalries with Moscow and Beijing have created a need for allies with advanced industrial capabilities.
In 2024, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen backed calls from Polish and Greek Prime Ministers Donald Tusk and Kyriakos Mitsotakis to create an EU-funded air defense shield.
However, three senior officials involved in the discussions told POLITICO the plans did not move ahead after the Commission and a handful of capitals concluded it would need to rely on Israeli air-defense technology, which they deemed too sensitive a year into the Gaza conflict.
Now though, in a major expansion of its operations in Europe, Israeli firm Rafael Advanced Defense Systems confirmed Monday that it will open a factory producing its Iron Dome air-defense system in a former Volkswagen factory in Germany. One week ago, Greece struck a €3 billion deal with Israel’s Defense Ministry to build a new multilayered air defense network designed to take down drones, hostile jets and rockets.
Advertisement
"We see that convergence of everything, of that multi-layer defense approach," said Maman, pointing to satellite imaging and AI modeling as a key focus for joint development.
"I don't treat only defense as ballistic missiles from Iran ... think about a fire or a flash flood or even a prolonged drought ... we have a proven track record and we do have very good results," she said.
Antoaneta Roussi, Jordyn Dahl, Chris Lunday and Romanus Otte contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russia is preparing to test ballistic missiles with a range of 800 km and may attack targets in western Ukraine — the HUR
articles.body:
Russia is preparing to test ballistic missiles with a range of 800 km and may attack targets in western Ukraine — the HUR
Kyiv • UNN
Russia plans to test new ballistic missiles with a range of up to 800 km by the end of the year. The HUR does not rule out strikes on western Ukraine.
Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers. This was stated by Deputy Chief of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, who added that the enemy may attempt to strike targets in western Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
Details
As Skibitskyi said at a meeting of the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council, the aggressor state of Russia is increasing the intensity of missile and drone strikes against Ukraine in order to provoke a socioeconomic crisis. To this end, Moscow seeks to increase ballistic missile production and extend the range of these weapons.
"According to our estimates, by the end of this year, Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers," Skibitskyi said.
He clarified that during these ballistic missile tests, the Russians may attempt to strike targets in western Ukraine.
Russia's aggressive plans also include blockading the Black Sea and attempting to draw Belarus into the war against Ukraine and into hybrid operations against NATO.
"As of today, we do not see any real indicators of preparations for strike groupings, specifically, on the territory of Belarus, but we remember January-February 2022. [...] The key factor restraining Belarus is internal risks, limited military capabilities, and potential economic problems. At the same time, according to our estimates, we consider it quite likely that Belarus will continue to support [Russian] hybrid measures by providing its own territory to create pressure on the border with NATO states and increase the intensity of information and psychological operations," the major general noted.
Skibitskyi emphasized that Russia poses a threat both to Ukraine and to Europe, and also thanked the partners for their support in the war for freedom. The representative of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine called for increased sanctions pressure on Moscow in order to finally deprive the aggressor of foreign components, particularly for long-range weapons with which the aggressor kills and terrorizes Ukrainians.

articles.title: Trump, Putin hold ‘frank’ phone call as US restarts Ukraine deal efforts
articles.body:
Trump, Putin hold ‘frank’ phone call as US revives Ukraine peace efforts
The phone call comes after US special envoys travelled to Russia and Ukraine to discuss ‘a proposal to end the war’.
United States President Donald Trump has spoken by phone with his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin as the White House ramps up efforts to reach a peace deal in Ukraine.
On Tuesday, Yury Ushakov, Putin’s foreign affairs adviser, described the two leaders as having a “constructive and quite frank” hour-long conversation.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Witkoff and Kushner will travel to ‘end’ Russia’s war in Ukraine: Trump
- list 2 of 3Witkoff says peace talks have been ‘very meaningful’ in Ukraine
- list 3 of 3At least five people killed in Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s Kyiv
According to Ushakov, Putin talked with Trump about the ongoing war in Ukraine and Russia’s plans to advance its military goals on the battlefield.
“An objective and thorough analysis of the ongoing special military operation and generally our view of prospective battlefield advances and the achievement of the special military operation’s goals and tasks was given,” Ushakov said.
The adviser added that Putin pushed back against rising concern that Russia could launch future attacks in Europe, including on NATO members.
“It was underlined that we don’t have any aggressive plans regarding Europe,” Ushakov said.
The White House did not return Al Jazeera’s request for comment on the reported call.
The phone call comes just days after US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff held separate meetings with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to discuss what Trump has described as “a proposal to end the war”, Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
Ushakov told reporters Putin and Trump “exchanged views on the outcome of the visits”, saying some “very good, worthwhile ideas” were presented.
After his Sunday meeting with the US envoys concluded, Zelenskyy thanked Trump for “allowing them to come” to Ukraine, despite the ongoing fighting, which was briefly paused for the negotiations.
“It is very important that the delegation has arrived to see us. We have been waiting a long time for Steve and Jared, Witkoff and Kushner,” Zelenskyy said.
“To us, it is very important to do everything so that this war ends,” he added.
The meetings, despite being lauded by all sides, appeared to produce no breakthrough on ending the fighting. After the brief weekend truce, both countries resumed strikes.
Officials in Ukraine said Russian attacks on Tuesday morning killed at least five civilians and wounded 25 others in Kyiv.
Meanwhile, Russian officials reported three people killed in the Bryansk and Kursk regions, with 13 others wounded. Ukrainian attacks on Russian-annexed Crimea also killed approximately five people, according to local authorities.
The war began in February 2022, after Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, considered the breadbasket of Europe.
Trump has made ending the war a priority of his second administration, pledging on the campaign trail that he could achieve a settlement within 24 hours.
He later backtracked on that claim, calling it an exaggeration. Faced with reports that certain US munitions stocks are dwindling, Trump has repeatedly blamed Ukraine for putting a drain on the country’s missile supplies and finances — though critics point to US actions against Iran as a major factor.
While Trump has had a rocky relationship with Ukraine and its president, he has cultivated a close relationship with Putin, saying they went through “a hell of a lot” together.
Last year, Trump invited him to Alaska for his first visit on US soil since 2015.
The Trump administration has faced criticism for seeking to end the war in Ukraine without fully involving Ukrainian and European officials. Trump and Zelenskyy are expected to meet later in the month, according to Ukrainian officials.

articles.title: The Draghi plan at 2: Competitiveness crusade runs into Europe’s old politics
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — Two years after Mario Draghi warned that Europe faced an “existential” threat from economic decline, his plan to make the continent competitive again has become the EU’s official agenda — but implementation lags behind rhetoric.
The Commission has proposed a series of Draghi-inspired measures, from an industrial policy overhaul to new funding for competitiveness and defense. Yet grand ambition has come up against the realities of the EU legislative machine, and many proposals remain stuck in negotiations as national governments continue to defend their spending priorities and policymaking turf.
A year ago, Draghi didn’t sound too happy with how quickly his plan was being implemented. Since then, his frustration with the lack of progress has become increasingly visible. The former Italian prime minister recently co-founded the Rhine Group with Stripe chief Patrick Collison, bringing together business leaders, economists and former policymakers to push Europe from diagnosis to action.
Advertisement
The group says Europe is “in a harder place” than when Draghi’s report was published in September 2024, and warns that decline is inevitable unless governments act urgently. Its creation is itself a sign that Draghi believes the institutions responsible for delivering his agenda are moving too slowly.
Europe’s leaders broadly agree that competitiveness matters. The harder question is what they are willing to give up to pay for it.
Draghi’s main recommendation was to steer EU money from agriculture and regional payouts toward competitiveness and innovation. The Commission delivered on this in its proposal for the 2028-2034 EU budget, when it floated creating a new European Competitiveness Fund worth €410 billion. But during the ensuing budget negotiations, governments have diverged from Draghi’s advice.
The draft negotiating position prepared by Cyprus last summer downsized the ECF while increasing funding for agriculture and regional funding. In a further swipe at the Draghi report, the Commission reduced the budget’s leeway by giving countries the possibility to immediately hand €45 billion from a rainy-day fund to farmers.
On a more positive note for the EU executive, member state governments broadly approved a new budget structure that prioritizes flexibility at the expense of pre-defined allocations.
Draghi’s hopes of turning the EU into an investment hub to rival Wall Street are still very much a work in progress. The Commission proposed a host of bills to realize the former European Central Bank chief’s vision, although many of them are still making their way through Brussels’ legislative machinery — with varying degrees of success.
The Commission’s marquee markets initiative aims to upgrade the EU’s securities regulator into a financial super-cop to police the sector. Vying national and business interests threaten to undermine Draghi’s hopes for a European equivalent to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission — but you can’t fault the Commission for trying.
Beyond supervision, Draghi wanted to use the trillions of euros sitting in bank accounts to turbocharge the economy by getting people to invest their retirement savings in the stock market. The Commission did its part by amending EU rules for personal and workplace pensions, which EU governments, in turn, gutted. Any efforts by MEPs to salvage the reforms are unlikely to convince EU capitals, which are highly protective of their pension systems.
Joint EU debt is a long-standing obsession of Draghi, and one of his more controversial recommendations. The EU has previously made good use of common debt to finance a post-pandemic recovery fund, cheap loans for military spending, and Ukraine’s defense against Russia. Draghi suggested using further eurobond issues to invest in strategic projects and public goods, including electricity grids, interconnectors and breakthrough research.
Advertisement
But political appetite for more eurobonds is low. Frugal nations are reluctant to keep raising EU debt, which fuels angry rhetoric from populist parties. A bold proposal from Spain for the Commission to borrow an additional €850 billion per year on behalf of EU countries landed on deaf ears among EU countries in the Council.
In its budget proposal, the Commission included several more realistic ideas to continue issuing joint debt over the coming seven years. While these proposals have faced strong opposition from frugal Northern countries, it remains unclear whether they will survive the endgame of the budget negotiations.
The automotive sector is a shining example of the Commission implementing Draghi’s recommendations — but that doesn’t seem to have mattered when it comes to maintaining automotive jobs in Europe. At the start of this month, Volkswagen’s board unanimously approved a cost-cutting plan that will ax 100,000 jobs, or nearly 16 percent of its workforce, and shutter up to four factories on German soil. Suppliers aren’t doing much better.
Draghi also recommended giving automakers flexibility on emissions targets. The Commission has done away with a ban on combustion enginesafter 2035 and put forward a “technologically neutral” proposal for the emissions targets that automakers must reach. (It allows all powertrains past 2035, but requires carmakers to offset the extra emissions with investments in alternative fuels and green steel.) The industry and conservative-leaning parties say that’s not enough, and are negotiating a further weakening of the standards.
Recognizing the competitive threat from Chinese automakers, Draghi pushed for more investments to help the sector catch up on software and autonomous driving. Robotaxis are starting to pop up in European cities — but it’s American or Chinese tech that is powering them. A group of member states is calling on the Commission to move faster to push autonomous driving from pilot projects to full-scale deployment.
Draghi identified soaring electricity costs as a major bottleneck for competitiveness, largely due to the bloc’s high reliance on imported fossil fuels. The EU is undeniably trying to lay the groundwork for a more sustainable energy future, even as the war in Iran, gas storage woes and growing attacks on European energy infrastructure send prices upwards.
Draghi prescribed boosting Europe’s transition to renewables, specifically by modernizing, expanding and digitizing its creaking grid architecture. The EU’s grids package — unveiled last year and soon to be discussed by national capitals and lawmakers — aims to address many of these challenges, though governments agreed to water down key parts of the proposal in response to a perceived push by the EU executive for excessively centralized planning and financial power.
Draghi also frowned at Europe’s fragmented approach to energy purchases, with myriad companies and countries pursuing different priorities and often competing against each other instead of making full use of the bloc’s market power to negotiate better prices for supplies. Even though EU countries are steadily increasing their share of long-term supply deals — instead of buying on the spot market, where prices are more volatile — no centralized procurement structure has yet emerged, and the bloc has failed to decisively buy enough gas to fill its reserves amid growing competition with more centralized economies in Asia.
Draghi’s aspirational vision of a single EU telecoms market is still far from reality. Several of his ideas, such as harmonizing the allocation of mobile frequencies and phasing out legacy copper networks, have made it into the European Commission’s proposal to overhaul the bloc’s telecom rulebook, the Digital Networks Act.
Advertisement
But those ideas remain a tough sell to national governments, which are bristling, as ever, at Brussels stepping on their toes. Draghi’s call for more “commercial investment sharing” between operators and data-hungry Big Tech companies — an outgrowth of the long-running and controversial “fair share” debate — has also rippled into the proposed law, where it is expected to prove divisive in the European Parliament.
It’s still too early to know what will survive the legislative process. But the proposals inspired by Draghi are already facing serious headwinds.
Draghi’s prescription for how Europe can build world-beating companies included loosening rules around mergers — a recommendation the Commission has taken to heart. Competition chief Teresa Ribera delivered her draft overhaul of the bloc’s merger guidelines at record speed after Commission President Ursula von der Leyen imposed a dramatic acceleration to their original end-2027 deadline.
The guidelines, which are now scheduled to land in final form at the end of this year, make room for innovation and investment to be included as parameters to assess corporate mega-deals — just as Draghi called for.
How far the guidelines will allow the Commission to bend its strict antitrust rulebook, however, is yet to be seen: Von der Leyen and Ribera don’t seem to be on the same page on cheering for European champions, particularly if consumers end up getting ripped off in the process.
Slowly but steadily, the EU’s trade policy is becoming more assertive — and Draghi would probably approve. New deals with India, Indonesia, Mercosur, Mexico and Australia will bring some much-needed relief and growth opportunities to European exporters.
But on the defensive side, the EU is still mostly very, very careful. The bloc did raise tariffs on steel imports but offended allies like Japan and Korea in the process. Perhaps it comes closer to Draghi’s idea of a genuine foreign economic policy, but the EU’s biggest trading partners are already worrying about new measures and laws like the Industrial Accelerator Act, which aims to protect the bloc’s industrial base.
But how far Europe can go in its quest to be both protectionist and open to trade is an open question. When Ursula von der Leyen delivers her State of the EU speech later this month, chances are she’ll present the new contours — or at least a few investigations — to show Brussels now means business on protecting its industry. With Germany finally joining the club of EU countries running a trade deficit with China, the bloc is united in realizing that something needs to give. As one EU diplomat put it earlier this year: “We agree on the symptoms, now we need to agree on the cure.”
Draghi warned that Europe remained dangerously dependent on high-risk telecom suppliers — primarily China’s Huawei and ZTE — potentially exposing critical networks and citizens’ data to foreign eyes. When he wrote his report, 14 EU countries still had no restrictions on high-risk suppliers in place. By March 2025, a report by telecom consultancy Strand Consult showed that 10 countries had implemented the EU’s 5G security toolbox, with seven showing significant implementation, six partial and four zilch.
Advertisement
But the patchwork approach remained a problem, so in January 2026 the Commission included a proposal to turn voluntary de-risking into law through its revised Cybersecurity Act. If approved, this law would give the Commission powers to require certain sectors to phase out high-risk technology.
Draghi also urged Europe to reduce its dependence on U.S. cloud providers. Here, the picture is less impressive. Despite years of talk about technological sovereignty, Europe remains heavily reliant on non-EU providers for its digital infrastructure — leaving one of Draghi’s central warnings largely unresolved.
Defense is one of the sectors where the Commission has done the most work. Since last year, it has launched a €150 billion Security Action for Europe rearmament plan to provide EU countries with low-interest loans to buy weapons.
It has also proposed allocating €131 billion to defense and space in the EU’s next long-term budget, a fivefold increase. The size of the final cash pot — and of the European Competitiveness Fund it lives within — is now up to EU countries. But Draghi may have just irked his closest allies in boosting competitiveness by only appointing one member from Eastern Europe — former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves — to his Rhine Group.
Draghi recommended the EU build a more consolidated defense industry, noting that having fewer, bigger defense companies has been fundamental to the ability of the U.S. to deliver the high capacity and scale required by American armed forces. Some diplomats and officials argue that the huge amount of EU money put on the table for defense could actually disincentivize consolidation of the European industry, as governments tend to like the idea only when it’s a way to save jobs.
Turbocharging Europe’s appeal as a place to carry out clinical research was at the heart of Draghi’s recommendations for the pharmaceutical sector. While the EU is brimming with promising drug candidates, industry is increasingly taking those molecules to the U.S. and China to test them in patients. The Commission has proposed the Biotech Act, designed to boost Europe’s appeal as a destination for clinical trials.
The juiciest offering to industry is a one-year patent extension for biotech drugs tested in Europe. But industry argues it doesn’t go far enough to speed up trials in Europe, while also lamenting the patent conditions. Eyes are now on the capitals and EU lawmakers who are preparing their amendments to the law. If they keep the patent extension, that would be a win for Draghi, who strongly backed intellectual property as “the key driver of medical innovation.”
The law also proposes making AI and data-driven tools core components of drug discovery, clinical trials and biomanufacturing. That would be music to Draghi’s ears. But when it comes to life sciences financing, Draghi’s wish for more cash, provided more quickly, may be thwarted, depending on how much of the Commission’s proposed €22 billion pot for health policy, bioeconomy and agriculture makes it into the final European Competitiveness Fund — and how much goes to the life sciences sector.
Green regulation was the first target of the Commission’s Draghi-inspired push to make it easier to do business in the EU, through an “omnibus” bill slashing European Green Deal-era environmental disclosure rules for business. Since then, things have got complicated.
Advertisement
Brussels’ simplification drive has continued, with a weakening of anti-deforestation rules, watered-down 2040 climate targets, and a decision to put the brakes on the EU’s most important climate policy, the Emissions Trading System. But a European summer of extreme heatwaves, wildfires and drought, combined with renewed anxiety over dependence on foreign fossil fuels, has injected new energy into the decarbonization and environmental push.
Overall, the push to slash green rules has found a natural limit with EU legislators, where weakening the rules is acceptable, but gutting them outright is not. Protecting the environment remains embedded in Europe’s political mainstream, even if that means upholding laws that business finds annoying or burdensome. But ongoing debates over emissions trading and environmental permitting laws promise to test these limits further.
Agriculture barely registered in Draghi’s grand plan for Europe’s economy. His 400-page report offered no real prescription for farming, and saw the EU’s vast farm subsidies as money that could instead be spent strengthening Europe’s industrial base, bolstering security and funding other priorities.
Two years on, negotiations over the EU’s next seven-year budget are exposing what Draghi’s report missed. Farmers may account for a shrinking share of Europe’s economy, but they remain a potent political force in Brussels. After waves of tractor protests, capitals are pushing to protect almost €294 billion in direct farm support, with billions more potentially available for agriculture. The pressure for cuts is falling instead on competitiveness, defense and foreign policy.
Draghi largely left farmers out of his plan. They are now helping decide how much of it Europe can afford.

articles.title: Streeting says UK ‘won’t flinch’ in support for Ukraine
articles.body:
Britain will provide £100 million towards the rapid delivery of additional air defence interceptors to Ukraine this winter, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has announced.
Speaking at his first Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting as Defence Secretary, Streeting said Kyiv had identified 300 Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability and $2 billion for drones among its immediate requirements.
He announced a £100 million British contribution through NATO’s mechanism for financing priority Ukrainian requirements, intended to support the rapid provision of additional air defence equipment before winter. Streeting also said military assistance would continue alongside diplomatic efforts towards an eventual settlement.
He said: “We know that this will only end through a negotiated peace. It’s really important that Russia understands that we won’t flinch in terms of our support for Ukraine as they continue to fight for their freedom and, for that matter, for ours.”
The Defence Secretary also provided an update on Britain’s existing commitment to provide 120,000 drones to Ukrainian forces during the year. More than 25,000 have so far been delivered, according to Streeting, with thousands more expected to arrive before winter. The systems cover several roles, including drones intended to intercept Russian unmanned aircraft, reconnaissance systems used to observe the battlefield and areas behind Russian lines, and attack drones.
Streeting said: “Those cover a whole range of capabilities that will help Ukraine to take the fight directly to Russia, defend itself by taking out Russian drones, and also to see what’s happening both on the battlefield and behind enemy lines.”
Britain is also continuing deliveries of large-calibre artillery ammunition. Streeting said the UK delivered its millionth round in July, with tens of thousands more expected to follow.
The additional ammunition is being provided with funding involving Britain, Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. Streeting said continued support was intended to demonstrate to Moscow that the countries backing Kyiv would not withdraw their assistance while fighting and diplomatic activity continued in parallel.
He described the Government’s commitment to Ukraine as unshakable and said supporting Kyiv would remain a central priority in Britain’s work with allied defence ministers.

articles.title: US Destroys Five Iranian Oil Tankers as Tehran Threatens Vessels Off Kuwait, Bahrain
articles.body:
US forces destroyed five Iranian oil tankers on Tuesday after Tehran twice attempted to strike an American warship with ballistic missiles in recent days, marking a renewed escalation in the conflict between Washington and Tehran.
US Central Command said the tanker crews were ordered to leave the vessels before American forces attacked them.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“American forces directed the crews to abandon ship before the vessels were struck and rendered inoperable,” CENTCOM said, according to AFP, describing the operation as retaliation for Iran’s latest failed attacks.
The five vessels were identified as the Kivik, Charminar, Horizon 1, Riesco, and Derya. They were struck in the Gulf of Oman and near Kharg Island, the center of much of Iran’s oil export infrastructure.
The attacks followed repeated Iranian attempts to hit US Navy vessels. None of the Iranian ballistic missiles struck their intended American targets, according to US officials.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington intended to continue hitting Iranian tankers if Tehran persisted in targeting US naval forces.
Speaking during a visit to Colombia on Tuesday, Rubio said each new Iranian attempt to attack US ships would bring further consequences for Tehran’s tanker fleet.
The latest US strikes quickly triggered a threat of retaliation from Iran.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy warned crews aboard oil tankers at or near ports in Kuwait and Bahrain to abandon their vessels immediately, saying the ships could become targets.
Russian Generals Simulate War With NATO for Years
The IRGC accused Kuwait and Bahrain of facilitating US military operations because both countries host American forces. Iranian state media said tankers at anchor or docked in the two Gulf states could be targeted.
The threats raised fresh concerns over commercial shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important oil transit routes.
Tuesday’s strikes came after the US military hit three Iranian oil tankers over the weekend following earlier Iranian ballistic missile attacks on US Navy ships. Washington had warned that it was prepared to further target Iran’s oil fleet if attacks on American forces continued.
Oil prices climbed toward $100 a barrel Tuesday as renewed US-Iran fighting and threats to Gulf shipping intensified fears of further disruption to global energy supplies.

articles.title: Germany pledges more air defense missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
Ayhan Simsek
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Tuesday pledged more Patriot interceptors, AIM-9 missiles and IRIS-T air defense systems for Ukraine.
Speaking at a video meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, Pistorius said Russian hybrid attacks would not stop Berlin or its partners from backing Kyiv, and Berlin will increase its support.
“Winter is coming. Preparing Ukraine for winter is of the highest priority,” he said. “It requires us to act resolutely and immediately. Together, we must take the right measures to increase Ukraine's resilience.”
Pistorius said he decided to provide Ukraine with the urgently needed Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles from the German military (Bundeswehr) stocks. He urged other contact-group members to check their own inventories and do the same.
“I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine, but please, if in doubt, decide in favor for Ukraine,” he said.
Germany will also step up the supply of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles to Ukraine from Bundeswehr stockpiles, Pistorius said.
“What is more, we are keeping up our continuous deliveries of IRST air defense systems, including guided missiles,” he said. ”I am pleased that Ukraine is going to order several thousand additional IRST-guided missiles that will be funded by the EU-Ukraine Defense Loan.”
Pistorius said Germany will keep up its continuous deliveries of drones and long-range ammunition to help stabilize the front. Beyond the ongoing support, he said Berlin will fund several tens of thousands of rounds of long-range artillery ammunition. The ammunition will be procured through the British Artillery and Air Defense Consortium and provided to Ukraine.

articles.title: Oil tops $100 as Middle East conflict intensifies
articles.body:
Oil tops $100 as Middle East conflict intensifies
Global oil prices have surpassed $100 per barrel as escalating fighting between the US and Iran, and Houthi attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure, raised fears of further supply disruptions. Brent crude broke the threshold for the first time in nearly two months.
Brent futures climbed 2.2% to $100.07 per barrel in Asian trading, their highest level since July 24. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) rose 1.83% to $94.73, while Brent has gained around 25% since early August as hopes of a lasting settlement to the US-Iran conflict have faded.
“Recent developments only reinforce the view that we’re still some way from a restart in talks. In the meantime, the market is likely to continue to price in a sizeable risk premium,” ING commodities strategists Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey wrote in a note early Wednesday.
The latest price surge followed a sharp escalation at sea. US forces struck five Iranian crude carriers on Tuesday, and Iran later claimed that it hit two US vessels and eight oil tankers in the Persian Gulf in retaliation, inflicting “significant damage.”
The attacks came after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) issued an “urgent warning” to tanker crews near Bahrain and Kuwait to abandon their ships, saying vessels in the area would be targeted. Ballistic missiles were subsequently launched from Iran toward US military facilities across the region, including those in Jordan, where air defenses intercepted 18 of 20 incoming missiles, according to the military.
The maritime confrontation has become an increasingly prominent front in the conflict. The US has restricted traffic to and from Iranian ports, while Tehran has imposed controls on passage through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital energy route that handled around a fifth of global oil supplies before the war.
Supply concerns have also intensified after Yemen’s Houthis launched missile and drone attacks on energy facilities in southern Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. The strikes reportedly forced temporary shutdowns and sparked a fire at the Jazan refinery, a major Saudi Aramco facility capable of processing 400,000 barrels of crude oil per day.
