articles.title: Confidence in imminent victory, Putin’s visit to India: statements by Kremlin spokesman
articles.body:
MOSCOW/NEW DELHI, September 8. /TASS/. Moscow is confident in an imminent victory, and combat operations are progressing very successfully for Russia, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov stated during a briefing for Indian media ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
He also noted that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India, which will take place in a few days, will be significant for both countries.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.
Conflict in Ukraine
Russia did not want and did not start the war in Ukraine but it is trying to stop it: "We actually never wanted this war. What we’re trying to do, we’re trying to stop the war that was launched before, and it was not launched by us. It was not started by us."
Russia remains open to the peaceful settlement of the Ukrainian conflict: "We do want the solution of the Ukrainian conflict by peaceful means, and Russia is open for this process."
India’s position regarding the Ukrainian conflict largely coincides with Russia’s: "We know the position of India on the Ukrainian conflict, and to great extent it corresponds with our own position".
Russia has to achieve its goals regarding Ukraine through a special military operation, although it would prefer to do so by peaceful means: "We have to reach our goals during the special military operation, but we would prefer to do it in a peaceful way."
Russian troops are advancing in the special military operation zone: ""The dynamics on the front is known to all the experts. We’re moving forward."
Russia is confident in an imminent victory: "We are sure that the victory is very near. We are very confident in our military potential, in our military. Our military actions are going on very successfully."
Russia welcomes any efforts by other countries to achieve a peaceful settlement of the conflict in Ukraine: "We welcome all the attempts to make any contribution in the sphere of the Ukraine settlement. We welcome the willingness of the Indian side to contribute. We welcome the efforts of American President President Trump."
Moscow expects the resumption of trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kiev to resolve the Ukrainian crisis: "We hope that there will be some movement in this respect. We hope to restart negotiations between three parties: Russian, Ukrainian, and American."
The conflict in Ukraine could have ended long ago, but Kiev, being incited by Europeans, does not want an end to it: "I wouldn’t say that Kiev is that flexible, and I wouldn’t say that Kiev is really willing to stop this war. Should they be willing to do that, the war [would have] been over for a long time, but they’re being provoked to great extent by some European countries."
Europeans are inciting Kiev to go to war and deluding themselves with the hope of achieving a "strategic defeat" of Russia: "They [the Kiev authorities] are still being provoked to a great extent by some European countries that cannot get rid of the idea of strategically defeating Russia. We will not let that happen, and we’re not letting that happen."
Indian citizens participating in the special military operation will be returned home as soon as their identities are established and a list of names is compiled: "Now the work is being done to make a list of those Indian citizens, who are now on the battlefield, and they will be sent back home as soon as they are determined. We are in very deep contact, profound contact with the Indian side on this issue."
Dangers of trying to preserve a unipolar world
Attempts to preserve a unipolar system in the world are very dangerous: "Unipolar system is actually collapsing, it is losing losing its competitiveness, and then at the same time, the unipolar system is trying to regain power, taking sometimes very harsh steps, injuring the global system, the global economy, the global environment and politics, the global system of international law. So this is a very dangerous process."
The global majority, represented by BRICS, is striving for a different world order: "Where every country is equal to another, where every country has a right to a say, where every country has the right to fair competition and trade, where every country is secured from any illegal sanctions or illegal pressure, where every country can secure its national interests without without experiencing somebody’s pressure and demands to do otherwise."
Sanctions and de-dollarization
Russia is not seeking de-dollarization: "It’s not because we are aiming for de-dollarization <…>. To the contrary, we’re open to every acceptable method of payment. But you know that certain countries are using some national currencies as a tool for political pressure."
Since some countries do not allow Russia to use their currency for trade, Russia must use rubles: "So, if they don’t let us use their money, we use our own money."
The United States itself is undermining confidence in the dollar as a reserve currency: "The more trust is ruined, the more trust goes in favor of national currencies. This is the process, and this is the nature of the process."
Russia considers Western sanctions unacceptable: "Of course, we do not accept, and we consider it to be definitely illegal in terms of international law, any attempts to introduce limitations on international trade and to threaten other countries' third parties for doing trade with others."
Russia intends to discuss this issue as part of settling the Ukrainian crisis, but the settlement itself is of paramount importance to Moscow: "[The] issue of sanctions is on the agenda. It is not in the front row because the settlement itself is the issue number one, but it’s an untakable part of the whole agenda of the peaceful settlement around Ukraine."
Putin’s visit to India and bilateral relations
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India, which will take place in a few days, will be significant for both countries: "In a couple of days he [Putin] will start his visit to India. <...> Jointly our two leaders are going to visit some forums."
Putin and Modi are also going to hold a mutually important bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 11.
Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi have a close yet pragmatic relationship: [They are] able to discuss in a very open and constructive way the most sensitive issues of the global agenda and our bilateral relations."
They will be discussing economic cooperation, although the specifics will remain confidential so that unfriendly countries cannot interfere: the conversation will proceed "discreetly, but in a very very constructive manner."
During the meeting, Putin will tell Modi about the current situation in the special military operation zone: "It will be another opportunity for President Putin to inform his Indian friend on the current situation on the fronts, on the war with Ukraine."
The leaders will also discuss the impact of US aggression against Iran on the global economy: "Negative consequences of all that are inevitable, unfortunately. And our two countries, they are also subject to those consequences."
India is Russia's strategic partner, and Moscow expects to develop relations with New Delhi across a wide range of issues: "We really consider it of extreme importance for our two countries that we continue to develop our cooperation in a very very wide scope of fields, we're quite successful in that."
Russia has excellent military equipment and is ready to continue supplying it to its Indian partners: "We have very good military equipment. Some of the equipment items are the best in the world, and we're ready to share them with our Indian partners."
Middle East
Russia believes that the situation around Iran is having a negative effect on the global economy: "The situation [surrounding Iran], unfortunately, is still very tense, and every day brings new turbulences. This is definitely not doing well for the global economy."
Russia would prefer that the United States and Iran return to the previously signed memorandum of understanding: "We prefer that countries involved return to the memorandum of understanding that was signed between Iran and the United States, or turn to something else that would bring peace to this region."
Trump's statement about the Moon
Space should be a space for interaction, not confrontation between countries, and cannot be subject to any "privatization": "I don't think that we can support the idea of privatization in space. It should be free of that. Space should be a ground for mutual cooperation and for mutual dialogue, not a ground for confrontation."
As for US President Donald Trump's publication, he hardly "declared" the Moon as belonging to the United States: "When [US] President [Donald] Trump said that 'the Moon is ours,' I think he meant that it wasn't their property, but he meant that very soon, hopefully, American astronauts will stand on the moon."

articles.title: US missile reserves hit hard by Iran war
articles.body:
Wars are not measured only by the number of attacks, the missiles fired, or the areas gained on the battlefield. One of the most important criteria is the cost that war imposes on the military power, economy, and deterrence capacity of the parties; a cost that sometimes shows its effects months and even years after the end of the conflict.
It is within this framework that the recent report by the Los Angeles Times on the state of US missile stockpiles after the war with Iran takes on particular importance. Citing published estimates about US defensive missile reserves, the report says Washington consumed a significant portion of its advanced Patriot and THAAD missiles during the war, and rebuilding these stockpiles at the current capacity of the US defense industry could take several years.
According to the report, the United States consumed about 60 percent of its advanced defensive missile stockpiles in the first five months of the war. The estimate by the Center for Strategic and International Studies also indicates that US global Patriot and THAAD reserves declined from about 2,800 missiles at the start of the war to about 1,100 by the end of July.
These numbers become even more significant when we consider that the production speed of the US defense industry falls considerably short of the rate at which these missiles are consumed in a major war. Based on the same estimates, American factories were producing about 620 Patriot missiles and 96 THAAD missiles annually before the war; a figure that is not sufficient to quickly replace what has been consumed in the war. As a result, restoring Patriot stockpiles to prewar levels will take at least several years, and rebuilding THAAD reserves will take even longer.
This issue is not just a logistical problem for the US military; it is directly tied to the question of deterrence.
Unlike many countries, the United States must simultaneously prepare for multiple security scenarios in different regions of the world. In its defense calculations, Washington considers China its most important long-term rival in the Indo-Pacific region, and in Europe, the possibility of a large-scale conflict with Russia is one of the key scenarios in military planning. Under such circumstances, every missile consumed in one war is part of a stockpile that will no longer be available for a potential crisis in East Asia or Europe.
For this reason, the issue is not simply whether the United States can produce several thousand new missiles. The issue is that the war with Iran showed that America's production and stockpiling capacity is not as flexible as was imagined for a high-intensity, prolonged war.
This is precisely the point at which the cost of the war for America moves beyond the tactical level and becomes a strategic issue.
Over the past decades, Washington has built a large part of its military power on technological superiority, weapons precision, and missile defense systems. But new wars have shown that this superiority faces a serious challenge when one side can place the other side's expensive defensive systems under sustained pressure through the extensive use of missiles and drones.
Under such conditions, an economic equation also takes shape: if a very expensive interceptor missile is consumed to counter a relatively cheap threat, the continuation of the war can quickly deplete the defending side's stockpiles. Therefore, the issue is not only the number of available missiles; the ratio of attack cost to defense cost also becomes important.
From this perspective, the war with Iran has imposed yet another cost on America: the erosion of part of the military capacity that Washington had stockpiled for its larger and longer-term rivalries.
This has occurred at a time when the United States is also facing other problems; from the financial costs of the war to pressure on the defense industry's supply chain, the need to increase weapons production, and the necessity of maintaining the readiness of American forces elsewhere in the world.
In other words, the end of a war does not necessarily mean the end of its costs. The conflict may stop, but rebuilding stockpiles, repairing equipment, replacing weapons, and restoring the military's operational capacity can continue for years.
From this very angle, it can be said that one of the most important consequences of the war with Iran for the United States is the cost that remains on the balance sheet of the country's military power. Washington must now strike a balance between rebuilding consumed stockpiles, increasing production capacity, and maintaining readiness for other potential crises.
This situation becomes more significant when placed alongside the political and military outcome of the war. If the United States, despite possessing one of the largest and most advanced militaries in the world, has not been able to achieve its expected objectives in a costly war, then the massive consumption of stockpiles and the multi-year need to rebuild them is not merely a financial or logistical cost; it could mean a reduction in part of Washington's strategic freedom of action.
In fact, the bill of war for America is not just the money spent or the missiles fired. Part of this bill is the depletion of stockpiles, the erosion of defensive capacity, the pressure on the military industry, and most importantly, the reduction of part of America's ability to enter another major crisis simultaneously.
And perhaps the most important consequence is this: a war that was supposed to showcase American military power may, in the end, confront Washington with a difficult question; if the next major crisis occurs in East Asia or Europe, how quickly can America bring its consumed capacity back to the field?
MNA

articles.title: Ukraine shows a home-built missile designed to hit ballistic targets for the first time, the Koral, at Poland’s MSPO
articles.body:
Ukraine has shown off, for the first time, a home-built missile designed to shoot down ballistic targets. The Koral surface-to-air missile appeared at the MSPO defense expo in Poland, in an Ukroboronprom image showing a launch from a self-propelled launcher on a Czech Tatra truck chassis, Militarnyi reports.
It is unclear what is meant by “ballistic targets.” Russia has a wide range of ballistic weapons, from Iskander ballistic missiles to Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles.
More broadly, the term “ballistic target” can refer to an object following a ballistic trajectory after the powered phase of its flight has ended, with its subsequent motion governed primarily by gravity and aerodynamic drag. This category can also include rockets fired by multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), such as the Grad and Smerch.
Evolution of the Koral
The missile weighs 450 kg, including a 36-kg warhead. Its guidance system combines inertial navigation, radio correction, and an active radar homing seeker. The missile is 4.8 meters long and has a diameter of 230/300 mm.
At the initial stage, the “Koral” was advertised with significantly more modest specifications: an engagement range of up to 30 km, an engagement altitude of up to 10 km, a weight of around 300 kg, and a 25-kg warhead. The missile was 4.33 meters long and had a diameter of 230/260 mm. At the same time, the designers emphasized that the specific specifications could vary depending on the customer’s requirements.
History of the developement
Development of the “Koral” began as early as 2016. Initially, the project was conceived as part of a ship-based surface-to-air missile system. In 2021, the Luch State Design Bureau unveiled a full-scale mock-up of the missile for the first time at the “Arms and Security” exhibition.
At the time, the “Koral” was presented as a unified, modular missile for both land-based and shipborne SAM systems, with potential applications as an air-to-air missile as well.

articles.title: Child among four killed by Ukrainian drone attacks – Russian governor
articles.body:
Child among four killed by Ukrainian drone attacks – Russian governor
Four people, including a child, were killed overnight in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Russian Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk, Krasnodar Region Governor Veniamin Kondratyev has said.
Another 29 people were injured across the city, the official said on Wednesday morning. Three of the victims are in a serious condition, he added.
Novorossiysk is a key hub for Russian maritime trade, which Kiev has been trying to disrupt with regular long-range attacks on ships and port infrastructure.
Kondratyev stressed that only civilian sites were targeted by Ukrainian forces. A church and a kindergarten were damaged, as well as three private homes and five apartment blocks, he reported. Ukrainian strikes also damaged homes in the resort town of Anapa, located some 40 km northwest of Novorossiysk.
Gelendzhik, another resort town in Krasnodar Region to the southeast of Novorossiysk, came under what Mayor Aleksey Bogodistov described as a “most massive and lengthy” drone raid. He did not report any casualties.
Russian air defenses intercepted 596 Ukrainian drones in 12 hours overnight into Wednesday, the Defense Ministry said.
In June, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky ordered mass attacks on Russian ships, which was part of Kiev’s bid to cause more economic damage. Moscow responded to Zelensky’s “40-day pressure campaign” by ramping up its own long-range strikes, leaving Ukraine effectively cut off from maritime trade.
On Tuesday, Zelensky reiterated his calls for a pause in hostilities in the Black Sea, claiming it would come as a relief for the entire world. Both nations are major exporters of wheat, a key food commodity.
A Türkiye-mediated agreement that ensured free shipping in the Black Sea and provided for inspections of incoming cargo ships to ensure that they were not carrying weapons existed in the early phase of the conflict. Moscow ultimately pulled out of the deal after accusing Kiev of using designated safe routes to launch naval kamikaze drones at Russian ports.

articles.title: Ukraine has developed a new RK-19 missile to shoot down Russian "Banderols"
articles.body:
Ukraine has developed a new RK-19 missile to shoot down Russian "Banderols"
Kyiv • UNN
The RK-19 has a range of up to 10 km and a 14.3 kg warhead. It was developed to intercept drones and Banderol-type cruise missiles.
Ukraine's KB Luch has unveiled the RK-19 surface-to-air missile, designed for Soviet Osa air defense systems. It is intended to replace scarce standard missiles and can be used against jet-powered drones and cruise missiles, reports Defense Express, writes UNN.
Details
The RK-19 is designed to intercept subsonic and supersonic targets. The missile uses radio-command guidance, proximity fuzing, and is equipped with a 14.3 kg high-explosive fragmentation warhead.
The declared engagement range is up to 10 km, the altitude is up to 5 km, and the maximum flight speed is 600 km/h. The missile's weight together with the transport-launch container is 163 kg.
The RK-19's specifications are close to those of the standard 9M33M3 missile for the Osa-AKM, but it has a higher maximum speed. Due to a shortage of older interceptors, Ukrainian forces had previously been forced to use less effective missiles or integrate air-to-air missiles, including the R-73.
Defense Express notes that the emergence of the RK-19 will allow the continued operation of Osa air defense systems and their use against aerodynamic targets, including jet-powered drones and Bandероль-type cruise missiles.
The cost of the RK-19 and its production volumes have not yet been disclosed.

articles.title: Ukraine asks partners for 300 Patriot missiles from existing stocks – DM Khmara
articles.body:
Ukraine asks partners for 300 Patriot missiles from existing stocks – DM Khmara
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said this during the 36th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in the Ramstein format, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
Khmara said that with the help of partners and funding from an EU loan, Ukraine is signing contracts for approximately 1,000 missiles for Patriot systems. However, most of these missiles will only begin to be delivered over the coming years.
“That is why we ask that you supply us with the missiles from your stocks today in exchange for future improved missiles from our contracts,” the minister said.
Khmara also emphasized the need to supply Ukraine with man-portable air defense systems and air-to-air missiles to counter jet-powered Shahed drones and cruise missiles.
According to him, dozens of Ukrainian companies are working on cheaper means of intercepting jet-powered attack drones, and some of the interceptors developed are already being tested in combat conditions.
The minister also urged partners to make decisions on financing Ukraine’s defense as soon as possible.
“70 billion euros for security assistance this year were promised in Ankara. So far, we see that our partners are already providing €62 billion, including bilateral assistance and the EU loan. Thank you for that. Thus, the additional €8 billion are still needed to fulfill the declaration. However, I want to stress that the overall defense deficit is €23 billion, or $27 billion,” Khmara stressed.
According to him, these funds would make it possible to finance drones and ensure their stable supply through the end of this year and into early next year.
“Up to 90% of our success on the battlefield is driven by drones,” he added.
The minister asked partners to make the necessary financial decisions by November so that their impact could be felt on the battlefield as early as winter. He also emphasized the need to maintain an adequate level of defense support for Ukraine in 2027.
“The support for Ukraine is not a subsidy. It is an investment. We are offering a mutually beneficial partnership,” the minister stressed.
As reported, the UDCG meeting is being held virtually. Opening remarks were delivered by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, UK Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting, and U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby.
Ahead of the Ramstein-format meeting, Ukraine provided NATO with a list of its urgent needs for air and missile defense systems.

articles.title: The Promise of the Kurdish Peace
articles.body:
August brought some truly transformative good news for Turkey, the Kurds, and Turkey’s immediate neighborhood in the Middle East. On Aug. 10, the Turkish Parliament passed a law establishing a legal framework for the dissolution of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), the Kurdish militant group, and creating a phased pathway for reintegration of its members into society.
For more than four decades, the Kurdish issue has run like an electrified barbed wire through conversations in Turkey. The armed conflict between the PKK and the Turkish government has killed around 40,000 militants, soldiers, and civilians, and cost Turkey losses estimated to be around $2 trillion since 1984. Following peace talks, in July 2025, the PKK held a symbolic weapon-burning ceremony, starting a process of disarmament and moving toward ending the armed conflict.
The law offers legal protections to former PKK militants who have not committed specific crimes and helps suspend prison sentences for some members of the group. Thousands of sympathizers, activists affiliated with the PKK, and Kurdish politicians have been living in exile in Europe and elsewhere to escape legal prosecution. The law opens a path for them to return to Turkey. And the passage of this law in the Turkish parliament with broad support is a transformative step toward lasting peace and the creation of a new social contract between Turkey and the Kurds, domestically and regionally.
How to make peace
In the past decade, Turkey established clear military dominance in the fight against the PKK. Changes in military technology, intelligence, and surveillance systems, especially the rise of Turkish drones, strengthened the country’s counter-insurgency efforts. Yet Turkey’s military capacity to suppress an insurgency was not the sole factor in persuading the PKK to give up arms. Turkey did suppress waves of Kurdish rebellions in the past without creating space for Kurdish aspirations, and each suppression was followed by a more formidable and more violent rebellion.
Turkey’s embrace of a political process—instead of simply pursuing a decisive military path—to end the conflict made it more acceptable to the PKK leadership and the Kurdish movement. Abdullah Ocalan, the leader of the PKK, had to persuade his comrades to dissolve their organization, abandon the armed struggle, and choose political struggle. Unfavorable broader regional trends against armed militancy may have helped convince Ocalan and his comrades to make that consequential choice.
The legitimacy of the political solution, in the eyes of the Kurds, determines its sustainability and transformative impact. The current peace process seeks to end the insurgency and transform the struggle for Kurdish rights and aspirations into a nonviolent political one. It could transform Turkey’s relations with its own Kurdish community and the Kurdish communities in Iraq, Syria, and Iran. Leaders of the Kurdish movement believe that they can achieve more through politics than through armed struggle, and that it isn’t only they who are transforming, but that the state, political, and legal systems in Turkey can also change. The promise of the future, rather than being beholden to the grievances of the past, is the way forward.
The Turks and the Kurds managed it without relying on foreign peacemakers or mediation. The disarmament and demobilization process for the PKK was designed, executed, and monitored domestically, without involving any foreign mediators. The talks were held between Turkey’s National Intelligence Organization, Ocalan, and several other leaders of his group based in the Qandil Mountains in Iraqi Kurdistan and across Europe. The process involved the Turkish parliament and political parties through a Parliamentary Committee, formed in Aug. 2025 to work on legal and political dimensions of the PKK’s dissolution, which helped garner broad support for the peace process across political divides in Turkey.
Turkey and the Kurds have entered a new phase that demands greater buy-in for the peace process from politicians, lawmakers, ordinary people, and from the institutions that will implement the new law. To ensure the peace process has broader societal support, the political class will need to make clear why it matters and what it promises. The stakes of getting that right are high for Turkey and extend beyond its borders.
Seeing like a state
The nation-state in the 20th century largely adopted a conception of nationhood based on a single identity and was intolerant, assimilationist, or exclusionary toward other identities. The effect was to politicize and mobilize the very groups it sought to submerge. This was true of Turkey as well. The Turkish Republic was based on a single identity and an overly centralized state with its own insecurities, largely stemming from the traumatic experience during the collapse of the Ottoman Empire.
Today, Turkey needs a new conception of the nation-state that is inclusive of different identity groups, and a new idea of a strong state that is premised on broader societal legitimacy. Centralization coupled with exclusion is a recipe for societal discontent, which weakens, rather than strengthens, the state. Turkey’s real challenge is building an inclusive national identity that recognizes distinct identity groups without losing the thread of what binds them together. The task of the ongoing Kurdish peace process, and the Kurdish politics that will follow it, will be to achieve exactly this: an inclusive notion of national identity capacious enough to accommodate Kurdish identity and aspirations.
The current political mood in the Middle East and elsewhere is not one of militant groups and insurgencies. The broader trend runs toward their integration into state structures or their disarmament and demobilization. How these processes of demobilization and integration are carried out will be highly consequential. If they rely solely on coercion, rather than embracing persuasion and the prospect of mutual transformation, disarmament risks being a prelude to the next cycle of violence, waged under new names and banners.
Demobilization of insurgent groups succeeds when it rests on the prospect of mutual transformation. The armed groups dissolve themselves and remake themselves as political actors, who cease to be adversaries of the state and work as agents of its transformation.
The state and the polity, in turn, must transform alongside them, arriving at a more inclusive conception of national and geopolitical identity. In Turkey, it would mean embracing Kurdishness and honoring Kurdish political, democratic, and cultural rights, and regarding the Kurds outside of Turkey’s borders not as threats but as allies.
The PKK’s demobilization will reshape Turkey’s threat perception, and with it, Turkey’s approach to Kurds in Iraq, Syria, Iran and their countries. Already, in step with the pace of the PKK disarmament, the language used by Turkish officials and Kurdish actors across the region towards each other has improved significantly.
Fruits of peace
Turkey and its neighborhood have already benefited from the peace process and the demobilization of the PKK. That process faced two formidable tests in Syria and Iran and passed both. Turkey treated the PKK’s demobilization at home and the integration of Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF)—led by a Kurdish militia with close ties to the PKK—into the Syrian state as parts of a single process.
After the fall of the Assad regime, reuniting a fractured Syria became one of the most formidable tasks for the new government. The SDF controlled almost a quarter of Syrian territory. Limited fighting and military pressure earlier in the year helped shift the balance, stripping the SDF of a large portion of the land it had held.
What helped make the SDF’s integration into the Syrian state relatively smooth was the peace process already underway in Turkey, given the SDF’s close ties to the PKK. August brought two momentous developments: Turkey’s parliament passed the landmark legislation providing for the disbanding of the PKK, the reintegration of its fighters and the dismissal of charges against thousands of its sympathizers and prisoners; and the SDF announced its own dissolution.
A parallel drama played out during the Iran War. There were fears that the Iranian Kurdish militant group known as the Party for Free Life in Kurdistan, or the PJAK, might join the American war against Iran. Given its close ties to the PKK, such a move could have weakened the PKK’s commitment to disarmament and risked a new phase of conflict among Turkey, the PKK, and the PJAK. Despite pressure from the Trump Administration and Israeli plans to draw them into the conflict, Iranian Kurdish groups stayed out of the war. The peace process in Turkey was a major factor in persuading them to remain on the sidelines.
Together, the Syrian and Iranian cases reveal the power of political imagination and legitimacy in advancing national security. In both instances, Turkey has achieved more through political engagement than through military force. Any national security doctrine devoid of political imagination or legitimacy remains incomplete. The tests posed by Syria and Iran have demonstrated the PKK’s commitment to demobilization, confirmed that its decision is strategic rather than merely tactical, and helped build trust between Turkey and the PKK.
This process will also have considerable implications for Turkey’s relations with major powers. No issue has bedeviled Turkish-American relations more than the Syrian civil war did before the collapse of the Assad regime. At its core, that crisis reflected the conflicting American and Turkish approaches to the Syrian Kurds, specifically the People’s Protection Units (YPG), a PKK affiliate that, with American military advice and support, was later rebranded as the SDF.
By enabling the SDF’s integration into the Syrian state, the PKK’s demobilization has removed the most formidable sticking point in Turkish-American relations, clearing the way for closer cooperation between the two countries in Syria and beyond. Ocalan framed the recently passed Turkish law as the first step of a 1000 kilometer journey. The Turkish model, and the peace it promises, are still a story in the making. Despite the milestones already reached, formidable challenges remain, demanding persistence and commitment.
No two conflicts or two peace processes are alike. Yet the central message is universal: peace is possible and leadership matters. Long-running conflicts around identity are not fates to be endured but political questions to be settled. In a world still defined by war and insecurity, the story of peacemaking is, inherently, a global one.

articles.title: Ukrainian engine for Bars missile-drone passes final tests
articles.body:
Ukraine has developed its own jet-powered drone, as the arms race is pushing Kyiv to produce answers to Russia's new fast Banderol and Geran-3 drones. Ukraine's “Bars” missile-drones currently consist of more than 74% Ukrainian-made components, but their turbojet engines are still imported, the developer of the “Bars” missile-drones said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine on 7 September.
The “Bars” jet-powered drone can carry out strikes at a range of up to 1,000 km, and the team plans to increase its range in the future, the developer said in the interview. To speed up and increase production of such drones for the Ukrainian army, the team is trying to make the jet-powered drone consist of as many domestically produced parts as possible. This will remove the limitation on how many such jet-powered drones Ukraine can produce and deploy in response to Russia’s use of similar drones against Ukrainian cities.
“Without exaggeration, we source them from all over the world,” the Bars developer said in the interview about the imported engines.
The UAV strikes the Russian army both in occupied territories and deep inside Russia
The developer calls Bars a missile-drone: it resembles a missile because it has a jet engine, and a drone because it can be controlled by a pilot.
The basic characteristics of Bars include a warhead weighing up to 60 kilograms, a range of up to 1,000 kilometers, and a speed of more than 700 kilometers per hour, the developer added. He also explained that the UAV’s system is a modular platform that allows the drone to be used “in different planes.”
“Our basic modularity allowed ‘Bars’ to receive three main categories of use: DeepStrike, ‘middle-strike,’ and ‘front-strike,’” the developer said in the interview.
He also said that there have been more than 40 “engineering officially” modifications and iterations of the UAV alone.
A Bars production facility is already in Europe and will begin operating in early September
The first batch of Bars drones is planned to be delivered as early as 10 October, according to the interview.
“As of today, the only limitation to scaling up the production of ‘Bars’ is the so-called ‘bottleneck,’ and it is not so much the volumes as the delivery times of turbojet engines,” the developer said.
It was previously reported that Ukraine and Germany had signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars drones. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this on 8 July 2026. He said that at the first stage of the project, Germany would finance the production, while all manufactured UAVs would be transferred to the Armed Forces of Ukraine.

articles.title: Ukraine Hopes US Will Back FREYJA as Kyiv Works With Europe on Anti-Ballistic Missile Defense
articles.body:

Ukraine Hopes US Will Back FREYJA as Kyiv Works With Europe on Anti-Ballistic Missile Defense
Ukraine hopes for US support in implementing its FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told journalists, according to UNITED24 Media on September 8.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We are preparing our own FREYJA program. We very much hope that the Americans will support this program as well. But, nevertheless, with the Europeans we will definitely achieve the desired result,” Zelenskyy said.
Until the program delivers the required capabilities, however, Ukraine will continue to need ballistic missile packages from the United States, the president said.
“I expect to meet with President Trump in the 20s of this month, to raise this issue, and, God willing, there will be a result,” Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy also said diplomatic efforts were progressing toward a trilateral format, though he did not provide further details.
“We are also moving, in my opinion, toward a trilateral format,” he said.
The comments follow Zelenskyy’s statement that the United States recognizes Ukraine’s improved position on the battlefield and its stronger negotiating leverage. Speaking about recent diplomatic efforts involving US representatives Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and others, the Ukrainian president said that assessment is shared by American military officials and analysts.

articles.title: West Braces for Ukraine War to Stretch Into 2027 as Putin Rejects Peace Push
articles.body:
US and European officials increasingly expect Russia’s war against Ukraine to continue into 2027 after the latest push to restart peace talks with the Kremlin failed to deliver a breakthrough, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, Sept. 8, citing people familiar with the matter.
US special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow before traveling to Kyiv, but the diplomatic effort failed to produce significant progress, according to the report.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Putin spent three hours with the US envoys at the Kremlin but showed no willingness to soften his position, European officials told Bloomberg. Instead, he is expected to intensify attacks on Ukraine as winter approaches.
Russia is also preparing a new campaign against Ukraine’s energy and heating infrastructure over the next six months, one source told Bloomberg. The goal would be to make life increasingly difficult for civilians while Moscow steps up hybrid attacks across Europe to weaken Western support for Kyiv.
Putin is betting that Russia will enter next spring in a stronger position, the source said, while seeking to keep the country’s increasingly strained economy afloat.
“Serious negotiations” are unlikely before then, according to the source.
Putin uses US envoys to project strength
Another Bloomberg source said Putin used the high-profile visit by Witkoff and Kushner to project strength to a domestic audience ahead of Russia’s September State Duma elections.
How Russia Is Trying to Paralyze Kyiv Without Occupying It
Three-way Russia-Ukraine talks involving the US could take place after the vote, following announcements by Witkoff and the Kremlin. But Bloomberg’s sources said the meeting is unlikely to bring the sides significantly closer to a peace deal.
The diplomatic deadlock is putting renewed pressure on Europe to bolster Ukraine’s air defenses ahead of another winter of Russian attacks.
The UK announced an additional £100 million ($135 million) in military assistance to Ukraine on Tuesday.
Germany is also preparing an urgent transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles from its own stocks, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said.
“I realize that it is not easy to balance between my own security requirements and the urgently necessary support for Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
Ukraine’s Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said on Tuesday that contracts are being signed with allies for the supply of about 1,000 Patriot missiles using the EU loan.
“I ask you to adopt the necessary financial decisions by November, so we can already see results on the battlefield this winter,” Khmara said according to Interfax-Ukraine, adding that “up to 90% of our success on the battlefield depends on drones.”
The latest warnings come as Kyiv’s allies increasingly prepare for the possibility that diplomacy will not end Russia’s war this year – and that Ukraine will once again face a winter under sustained Russian missile and drone attacks.

articles.title: Drones attack fuel oil terminal in Novorossiysk, sparking fire
articles.body:
Drones attack fuel oil terminal in Novorossiysk, sparking fire
Drones attacked the Russian city of Novorossiysk in Krasnodar Krai on the night of 8-9 September, causing a fire at a fuel oil terminal.
Source: Russian media outlet Astra; Novorossiysk Mayor Andrei Kravchenko; monitoring Telegram channels
Details: Around midnight, residents of Novorossiysk reported hearing drones flying overhead, Russian air defence systems responding and explosions. Videos of a fire near the city's port infrastructure appeared online shortly afterwards.
Kravchenko confirmed that a fire had broken out but claimed that it was caused by drone debris that had landed at the site. He did not name the facility that was attacked or provide information about the extent of the damage or any casualties.
Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) analysis by ASTRA has established that the fire broke out at the Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal.
According to Dnipro Osint, the strike had hit facilities at the port complex, damaging at least one storage tank at the fuel oil terminal.
Novorossiysk Fuel Oil Terminal is one of the main facilities in the Novorossiysk transport hub, which forms part of the Novorossiysk Commercial Sea Port, Russia's largest seaport in terms of cargo throughput. It handles the storage and transshipment of fuel oil and light petroleum products, with a throughput capacity of approximately 4 million tonnes per year.
Background:
- The Monitoring Group of the Black Sea Strategic Studies Institute previously reported that in July, systematic Ukrainian Armed Forces and Security Service of Ukraine attacks on Russian infrastructure and tankers in the Black and Azov seas reduced Russia's oil product shipments by 45.6% compared with June.
- On 12 August, Russia's two largest grain terminals in the southern port of Novorossiysk suspended operations following Ukrainian drone strikes.
- During the first 20 days of August, exports of Russian crude oil from Black Sea ports fell by a factor of 3.2 to around 1.7 million tonnes, compared with 5.5 million tonnes in July.
- According to Reuters, Russia suspended crude oil exports from the Sheskharis terminal at the port of Novorossiysk following a drone attack.
- In addition, Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC), the world's largest container shipping company, has cancelled all new bookings for cargo bound for Novorossiysk because of the risks to shipping.

articles.title: A Ukrainian strike drone that quietly hit 450-plus Russian targets steps out of the shadows
articles.body:
A Ukrainian strike drone that quietly hit hundreds of Russian targets, with air-defense systems among them, has come out of the shadows. Ukrspecsystems publicly unveiled the RAM-2X, an X-winged loitering munition long used at the front but kept classified, at the MSPO defense expo in Poland, dev.ua reports.
Its relay capability allows the strike drone to operate in tandem with reconnaissance platforms such as the SHARK-M. In this configuration, the reconnaissance aircraft provides target designation, enabling the strike drone to more effectively counter Russian electronic warfare (EW) systems.
A proven drone steps into the open
To mark the reveal, the company opened an "X-Archive" of declassified combat video, starting with strikes on Russian surface-to-air missile systems and radars — the hardest targets a strike drone faces, since they are built to shoot drones down.
RAM-series loitering munitions are now credited with more than 450 target engagements, over 400 of them against air defenses, according to the manufacturer, which cleared the footage with the units involved before releasing it.
A scout and a striker hunt together
The pairing is the point of what Ukrspecsystems calls its "system of systems."
"Those who operate our reconnaissance equipment can add a strike component that works on the same antennas and stations," the company said.
This closes the reconnaissance-strike loop with its own forces. Built on shared components, a common ground station, and a single software, the RAM-2X supports several radio bands and Starlink terminals, so a jammer that blocks one link does not blind the drone.
The specs reach deep behind the front
The RAM-2X operates at the operational-tactical level, remains airborne for more than two hours, and carries a high degree of automation, with the option to run AI assistants on board. Its warhead is an explosively formed penetrator weighing 2.7 or 3.5 kilograms.

articles.title: Ukraine is sending its winning brigades to where the fighting is worst. The 46th just turned up outside Kramatorsk
articles.body:
- Free to redeploy from the stabilized southeastern front, a key Ukrainian brigade has moved north to help defend Kramatorsk and Sloviansk
- It took two months, and almost nobody outside the Ukrainian army knew it was happening
- The 46th Airmobile Brigade's first task may be to cover a short retreat by an adjacent brigade
Kramatorsk and Sloviansk are the last two big cities in the Donbas that Russia does not hold, and taking them has been the main Russian objective in eastern Ukraine since 2022. Ukraine is now moving forces north from the southeast to defend them.
The 46th Airmobile Brigade began that move in July. The first outside confirmation came this week.
Shifting north to plug a gap between two Ukrainian corps, the brigade could protect adjacent units as they retreat a short distance from what's left of Chasiv Yar—a battleground since the spring of 2024—and straighten the Ukrainian line where the 11th and 19th Corps meet. Both corps now sit under Biletskyi's new force grouping, according to Unit Observer—a command relationship no Ukrainian outlet has reported and which open sources cannot independently confirm.
Zooming out, the reshuffle around Kostiantynivka runs alongside a wider effort to redistribute Ukrainian troops along the 1,200-km gray zone threading through southern, eastern, and northern Ukraine. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi took over as commander-in-chief on 22 July, arriving with a mandate to unwind the Soviet-inherited command model Ukraine has fought this war with, and a reputation for favoring decentralized command. The 46th began moving before he did, in early July, according to Unit Observer, so this redeployment is not his. But the 33rd Assault Regiment was partially reassigned to Biletskyi's corps after the handover.
The best-case scenario is that the redeployment helps stabilize the front 16 km south of Kramatorsk, delaying the Russian siege of that city and Sloviansk to the north. In the worst case, the 46th Airmobile Brigade and its thousands of troops are too few and too late to make much of a difference as the Center Group of Forces and its tens of thousands of troops grind through Ukrainian defenses on their slow march toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
The 46th Airmobile Brigade spent years fighting in southeastern Ukraine. But it's arguably no longer needed along the southern end of the gray zone after a Ukrainian counteroffensive that kicked off in February halted and then rolled back Russian forces, stabilizing what was once Ukraine's most vulnerable flank.
Free to fight elsewhere, the brigade began its move north toward Kostiantynivka and Chasiv Yar two months ago. The move happened almost entirely in secret. "Strict OPSEC measures have become the standard for the Ukrainian armed forces in 2026," mapper Unit Observer noted, "with units delaying posts up to several months to avoid giving away their relocation along the front line."
That discipline is now visible across the whole Ukrainian effort. The southeastern counteroffensive that freed up this brigade ran for six months with very few videos and small teams. Ukraine's Swedish radar planes flew combat sorties for half a year before the defense ministry said so. A brigade crossing the front unremarked for two months is the same practice, applied to ground forces.
Confirmed moves
Recent videos confirmed the deployment. The 46th Airmobile is now in position just north of the ruins of Kostiantynivka and just west of the ruins of Chasiv Yar, which lie 11 km northeast of Kostiantynivka. Sitting astride the juncture between two Ukrainian corps, the 11th and 19th, the brigade is set to play a crucial role in the ongoing Ukrainian defense of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
According to Unit Observer, the 46th Airmobile Brigade's move "will likely support the gradual retreat of elements of the 24th Mechanized Brigade remaining between Chasiv Yar and the village of Stinky," 6 km west of Chasiv Yar. The 24th Mechanized Brigade has fought long and hard in and around Chasiv Yar to hold back a much larger Russian force. But incremental Russian advances north and south of the 24th Mechanized Brigade's positions have put the brigade at risk of partial encirclement.
It's a dangerous position for the weary brigade. If it could fall back to the west a few kilometers, it could eliminate the risk to its flanks—and straighten and shorten the overall Ukrainian line. It's possible the 46th Airmobile Brigade's job is to safeguard the short retreat.
Desperate to save Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Ukrainian forces counterattack and reinforce
The command and control process is deceptively complex, and the confusion is exactly the kind Drapatyi is trying to engineer out. Ukraine's new corps are supposed to be its highest front-line commands, coordinating the brigades, regiments, and battalions fighting in the same sectors. But in the areas where two corps meet, it may be unclear which corps is in charge.
Ukraine's answer has been to add a layer above the corps. On 26 August, Zelenskyy announced that two reinforced groupings would take over the defense of Donetsk Oblast, commanded by Denys Prokopenko of the 1st National Guard "Azov" Corps and Andrii Biletskyi of the 3rd Army Corps, both named Heroes of Ukraine.
The 3rd Corps' zone of responsibility has grown daily since the start of the year, its deputy commander Lt. Col. Rodion Kudriashov told NV, and he framed the new groupings as Ukraine scaling up what already works.
The grouping formalizes an arrangement that had already grown up in practice. The 46th Airmobile Brigade fits the same logic. It belongs to neither the 11th nor the 19th Corps—it is an 8th Air Assault Corps unit—but it is a brigade that works, freed by an offensive that worked, arriving in the sector that matters most. It is also arriving into a corps run by its own former commander: Brig. Gen. Valeriy Skred, recently given the 19th, led the 46th through 2022 and 2023.
Only time will tell whether the reshuffling of Ukrainian forces will bolster the defense of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. And even if the redeployments do stiffen the Ukrainian line south of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, they do nothing to stiffen the line north of the twin cities.
Russian troops are closing in from that direction, too. Fortunately for the Ukrainians, there's a separate plan for that northern sector. A carefully planned series of Ukrainian counterattacks has quietly cut across a salient of Russian troops marching on Sloviansk.
The Ukrainian attacks may compel the Russians to pull back a short distance. That could give the defenders of Sloviansk more space and time to prepare for the coming siege.

articles.title: US allies lack resources to keep pace on AI, top Pentagon official says
articles.body:
The Pentagon’s top artificial intelligence official said on Tuesday that America’s closest allies lack the resources to keep pace with the US military’s adoption of AI, and that Washington is working to steer them away from mistakes it made along the way.
“They don’t have the resources that we do, they don’t have the experience that we do, they don’t have the scale that we do,” Cameron Stanley, chief digital and artificial intelligence officer at the Department of War, said at an event at the Billington Cybersecurity summit. Of Nato and the Five Eyes, an intelligence-sharing partnership of the US, UK, Canada, Australia and New Zealand, Stanley said Washington was “actively working with a number of our partners” so “they don’t make the same mistakes that we make”.
The comments come less than a year into Stanley’s tenure, during which the Pentagon’s AI office has rolled out several new tools while losing a number of senior staff. Since January, Stanley has overseen the launch of GenAI.mil, an internal chatbot platform he says has reached 1.7 million users, and Agent Network, a system designed to shorten the time between intelligence-gathering and a commander’s decision. Pentagon secretary Pete Hegseth has directed Stanley’s office to report AI deployment speed as a monthly metric, part of a wider push to expand military computing power.
Much of Stanley’s appearance focused on speed. He described watching a commander halt a scheduled briefing to take a 30-second phone call and issue an order on the spot, without a formal decision brief or a review of the room’s security clearance level. He called the moment “revolutionary”.
“I know it sounds simplistic,” Stanley explained. “It’s only simplistic because we’re good at it now.”
It’s a term he has used before. Project Maven, the Pentagon’s original AI targeting program launched in 2017, became the Palantir-built Maven Smart System, which the US leaned on heavily during its 2026 air campaign against Iran, helping strike more than 13,000 targets over the first 38 days, according to Stanley at conference in May. Speaking at Palantir’s AIPCon 9 conference in March, Stanley called Maven “revolutionary” too, saying it let commanders go from identifying a target to launching a strike within a single platform.
But the campaign has drawn scrutiny. More than 120 members of the US Congress signed a letter demanding answers from the Pentagon regarding civilian casualties and the use of artificial intelligence, following a 28 February strike on an elementary school in Minab, which Iranian officials say killed at least 168 people, many of them children.
Stanley ended by telling the audience that the department’s old habits were now its biggest liability.
“The way we’ve always done it is the most risky course of action,” he said, adding that the department needs to “think differently” if it wants AI tools in the hands of warfighters faster.

Poland has signed an agreement for a further $4 billion (14.8 billion zloty) from the United States Foreign Military Financing (FMF) programme, which provides grants and loans to fund the purchase of American military equipment.
Defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz called the development a “great honour”, because FMF is “granted only to the best allies”. The agreement is not only “another important step in the modernisation of the Polish armed forces” but also “strengthens the strategic partnership between Poland and the US”.
The US embassy in Warsaw likewise hailed the agreement as “reaffirming the strength of the US-Poland partnership as we work together to strengthen NATO, deter aggression, and support peace and security in Europe”.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has embarked on an unprecedented military procurement spree, with its defence budget rising to the highest relative level in NATO.
Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was also the largest importer of arms in NATO. Around 44% of those purchases came from the US, including Abrams tanks, Patriot air defence batteries, and HIMARS rocket artillery.
The new agreement marks the sixth time Poland has received funds through FMF, for a total of almost $20 billion. Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the latest financing would be used to “accelerate the implementation of existing contracts, including for Apache helicopters”.
In 2024, Poland signed a $10 billion deal to buy 96 AH-64E Apache attack helicopters, along with a logistics and training package and a stockpile of ammunition and spare parts. It will make Poland the second-largest operator of Apaches in the world, after only the US itself.
Thomas DiNanno, the US under secretary of state for arms control and international security, said that the new agreement “signifies our commitment to assistance, but also Poland’s commitment to ensuring security, building defence capabilities, and ensuring the security of NATO’s eastern flank”.
“Poland is not only a trusted partner; it is not only an ally on the front line; it is a model ally of the United States,” he added, repeating recent remarks by US defence secretary Pete Hegseth.
The terms of the financing have not been revealed, but Marta Postuła, vice president of Poland’s national development bank, BGK, through which the funds will be channelled, said it was “on more favourable terms than the last two [FMF] loan guarantee agreements”.
This, she added, was “due to the subsidisation of a portion of the financing costs through a grant awarded for this purpose by the US government”.

The issue of who Poland should buy military equipment from, and how such purchases should be funded, has become embroiled in domestic political disputes this year.
President Karol Nawrocki and the right-wing opposition with which he is aligned have criticised the government for signing Poland up to the EU’s SAFE programme, which is providing €43.7 billion (188.7 billion zloty) in loans for defence and security spending.
They argue that provisions requiring most of the money to be spent within Europe itself could damage Poland’s relations with the US and South Korea, who have in recent years been the main sources of military procurement.
However, speaking today, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the new loan agreement with the US shows that SAFE and FMF “do not compete with one another; they complement one another”.

While Nawrocki is a close ally of President Donald Trump, who endorsed him ahead of last year’s Polish presidential elections, the more liberal government, led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, has at times clashed with Washington.
In May this year, the sudden and unexpected cancellation of the rotational deployment of almost 4,000 US troops to Poland raised concern in Warsaw.
Shortly afterwards, Trump declared that he would deploy 5,000 additional troops to Poland. However, since then, no clear details of that plan have been announced, although Poland has formally submitted a request for the US to establish a new permanent US military base on its territory.
On Wednesday morning, Polish deputy defence minister Paweł Bejda told broadcaster TVP that an American delegation was in Poland this week to visit potential locations for the base and discuss the issue further.

articles.title: German foreign minister proposes sharing data on military-age Ukrainian men living in Germany with Kyiv
articles.body:
German foreign minister proposes sharing data on military-age Ukrainian men living in Germany with Kyiv
Ukrainian men of military age living in Germany should return to Ukraine, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said in an interview with a podcast published by the German newspaper Bild.
Wadephul said the German government could help Kyiv track them down. “We know who lives here, who receives welfare payments, for example, who is registered here, who has residency status,” he said.
Ukraine’s government could use that data to notify men of military age that they must report for service, he said. “I think this can be discussed, and that it needs to be discussed,” the German foreign minister added.
Berlin also wants Ukraine to place more defense orders with German defense companies.
“We are Ukraine’s biggest supporter in terms of financial and military assistance. And naturally, the German defense industry should benefit from that. […] At the moment we are not entirely satisfied with the volume of orders being placed in Germany. So we have now asked the Ukrainian government to look into this and ensure the situation improves,” Wadephul said.
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced a day earlier that Germany would send Ukraine part of its own stockpile of PAC-2 interceptor missiles for American-made Patriot air defense systems. “I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support for Ukraine. But please: if in doubt, decide in favor of Ukraine,” he said.

articles.title: Russian drone strike hits Ukrainian checkpoint on border with Moldova, killing two
articles.body:
Russian drone strike hits Ukrainian checkpoint on border with Moldova, killing two
Russian drones struck border infrastructure in Ukraine’s Odesa region, according to the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine. The strike hit the international vehicle checkpoint in Starokozache, on the border with Moldova.
According to preliminary data, the attack killed two people and injured three others, the Odesa regional military administration reported. Operations at the border crossing have been suspended.
The Russian Defense Ministry confirmed the strike, saying the checkpoint had been used “to deliver military cargo into Ukraine.”
The day before, Moldova’s Defense Ministry reported that a drone had entered the country’s airspace from Ukraine, prompting authorities to close it to flights. The drone later headed toward Romania, prompting local authorities to scramble two F-18 fighter jets.
The drone later returned to Moldovan airspace and came down in the country. No casualties were reported.

articles.title: Germany to Supply Ukraine With More AIM-9 and PAC-2 Missiles to Strengthen Air Defense
articles.body:

Germany to Supply Ukraine With More AIM-9 and PAC-2 Missiles to Strengthen Air Defense
Germany will provide Ukraine with additional missiles for its air defense systems as Kyiv seeks to strengthen protection against Russian attacks ahead of winter, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on September 8, according to Ukrinform correspondent.
Speaking at the opening of a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in the Ramstein format, Pistorius said Germany is expanding deliveries of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks alongside previously announced PAC-2 interceptors.

“In addition to PAC-2 interceptor missiles, Germany will further increase the continuous supply of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to provide Ukraine with more of them. These missiles are being delivered right now and will strengthen Ukraine’s air defense before winter arrives,” Pistorius said.
The German defense minister recalled his decision at the NATO summit to urgently supply Ukraine with PAC-2 interceptors from Bundeswehr stocks, while calling on other members of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group to review their own inventories and consider similar contributions.
“From NATO’s perspective, further substantial deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles by allies are acceptable,” Pistorius said.
Germany is also continuing regular deliveries of IRIS-T air defense systems and domestically produced guided missiles, Pistorius said, highlighting the effectiveness of the medium-range system in Ukraine.
Berlin’s support is expected to be complemented by additional Ukrainian orders for IRIS-T interceptors financed through the European Union’s defense loan for Ukraine.
“That is precisely why I am pleased that Ukraine intends to order several thousand additional IRIS-T guided missiles, which will be financed through the EU’s defense loan for Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
The additional German support comes as Ukraine works with its partners to expand its broader defenses against ballistic missile threats. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 8 that Kyiv is seeking US backing for its FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program while also working with European partners on the initiative.
“We are preparing our own FREYJA program. We very much hope that the Americans will support this program as well. But, nevertheless, with the Europeans we will definitely achieve the desired result,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: First Overseas-Bound F-15EX Departs Boeing, Heading to Oregon First
articles.body:
After months of delays from a factory strike, the first F-15EX fighter jet the U.S. Air Force will permanently base overseas left Boeing’s facilities in St. Louis on Aug. 28. Eventually, the aircraft will fly to Kadena Air Base in Japan and join the 18th Wing there, but for now it is going to Portland, Ore.
“This is an important next step toward bringing the F-15EX home to Kadena,” Brig. Gen. John Gallemore, 18th Wing commander, said in a release. “Our team is ready to welcome the F-15EX, and this is another milestone that brings us closer to putting this capability in the hands of the Airmen who will fly, maintain and employ it from Japan.”
The F-15EX is the first Eagle II jet to feature the 18th Wing’s historic, distinctive “ZZ” tail flash and will actually arrive at Kadena sometime in fiscal 2027, which begins Oct. 1.
Spokespeople for Headquartes Air Force, the 18th Wing, and the Air National Guard did not immediately respond to queries from Air & Space Forces Magazine on Sept. 8.
This new jet is the first of 36 F-15EXs to be stationed at Kadena. The fighter, often described as halfway between fourth- and fifth-generation aircraft, will help usher in a new era in U.S. airpower within the first island chain surrounding China
The transition to the EX has been a long time coming for Kadena—the Air Force started retiring the base’s legacy F-15C/Ds in 2022 and confirmed plans to replace them with the F-15EX in 2024. The first jet was supposed to arrive in spring 2026, but a lengthy strike at the Boeing plant in St. Louis late last year slowed production until this Aug. 28 delivery.
The new F-15EX’s stopover in Oregon isn’t surprising—the Oregon Air National Guard was the first Air Force location with combat-coded F-15EXs at its Portland ANG Base. The base will conduct the final systems integration, add software updates, and other technical preparations before the aircraft can go to Okinawa.
In the interim, the Air Force has rotated F-16, F-15, F-22, and F-35 squadrons through Kadena to keep the tactical fighter presence steady at a key strategic base fewer than 400 miles from Taiwan.
Those rotational forces haven’t always matched the capabilities the F-15EX will bring. Air & Space Forces Magazine recently reported on the extended tour of aging F-16Cs out of the Colorado Air National Guard’s 120th Fighter Squadron, which ran from January through June. They brought a dozen fighters.
Both the squadron commander and the head of its parent wing, the 140th Wing, said in a call with the media on Sept. 3 that while the platform could keep up with fifth-gen fighters in the region, the pilots and maintenance crews were pushing the limits of the more than 30-year-old airframe
The permanent stationing of the F-15EX will “enhance Kadena’s ability to generate ready combat airpower while providing opportunities to train and integrate alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force and other allies and partners,” according to the release.
The 18th Wing trains alongside the Japan Air Self-Defense Force F-15s at Naha Air Base in bilateral exercises and other training, according to the release.
Pacific Air Forces has been slowly phasing out its oldest fighters and introducing more modern jets in recent years. In addition to Kadena’s F-15s, the Air Force has also recently withdrawn the A-10s at Osan Air Base, South Korea.
The 35th Fighter Wing at Misawa Air Base, Japan, meanwhile, is slated to get 48 fifth-gen F-35 Lightning IIs, but only a trickle had arrived as of April. The wing transferred its F-16s to Osan last year.
The Air Force publicly confirmed delays in getting the F-15EX to Kadena in February.
The Eagle II is the first of its kind to include digital fly-by-wire flight controls, a large-area display glass cockpit with a touchscreen interface, an APG-82 Active Electronically Scanned Array radar, a Joint Helmet Mounted Cueing System, and an Eagle Passive/Active Warning Survivability System.
The jet flies faster and farther, carries a heavier payload than its F-15 predecessors, and has two additional weapons stations.

articles.title: How Qatar hopes to break the deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
How Qatar hopes to break the deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz
Qatar says "new ideas" are being discussed to end the US-Iran war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as Doha intensifies diplomacy with China and other regional and international partners.
The details have not been made public, and Qatar has not announced a formal new initiative.
But its latest diplomatic push comes as several proposals are already circulating over how to restore shipping through Hormuz without waiting for a comprehensive settlement to the wider US-Iran conflict.
Qatar's position is clear - the strait should be reopened immediately and without conditions, and should not be used as leverage in negotiations.
"It’s not acceptable at all to have this state of no war and no peace," Ibrahim Al Hashmi, director of the media department at Qatar's Foreign Ministry, said on Tuesday.
"Qatar is working hard with its partners, including China. Diplomatic efforts are being exerted and new ideas are being discussed," he added.
Al Hashmi said the most important requirement was "political will" from both Iran and the United States, while stressing that reopening Hormuz was a top priority for Qatar and other countries in the region.
Why is Qatar looking for a new approach?
The latest push follows the failure of an earlier agreement to produce a lasting settlement.
Washington and Tehran reached a memorandum of understanding in June with Qatari and Pakistani mediation, providing for a halt in military operations and arrangements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The agreement was meant to create space for further negotiations, including over Iran's nuclear programme and US sanctions, but implementation stalled and hostilities resumed.
The Hormuz dispute has since become one of the central obstacles to reviving negotiations.
Qatar has increasingly argued that the crisis cannot be allowed to settle into an indefinite state between war and peace, particularly because disruption to the strait has consequences far beyond Iran and the US.
Shipping through Hormuz has again slowed sharply amid the latest escalation, with only seven commodity vessels recorded passing through on Monday, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters.
Could Hormuz be dealt with separately?
One possibility emerging from the wider diplomatic activity is to find an interim solution for Hormuz before attempting to solve every dispute between Washington and Tehran.
Iran and Oman have been negotiating a temporary safe shipping route through the strait.
Iranian officials said this week that those talks had made "significant progress", with Tehran and Muscat working towards a temporary transit route while negotiations continue over a longer-term arrangement.
An earlier proposal envisaged inbound traffic passing through Iranian waters and outbound traffic using both Iranian and Omani territorial waters, followed by 30 to 60 days of talks on a more permanent route.
That plan is separate from Qatar's efforts, but it illustrates the type of narrower arrangement that could help break the deadlock.
Doha has previously argued that reaching an agreement on Hormuz could make it easier to restart wider US-Iran negotiations.
Where does China fit in?
China has now emerged more clearly in Qatar's diplomatic push.
Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on Tuesday, with Hormuz, regional security and possible solutions to the closure of the strait among the issues discussed.
Beijing has an obvious interest in restoring stable shipping through the Gulf because of its heavy reliance on energy imports from the region.
Its involvement also broadens the mediation effort beyond the countries that negotiated the June agreement.
Doha appears to be trying to assemble a wider diplomatic effort capable of addressing both the immediate shipping crisis and the larger political confrontation.
What might Qatar's "new ideas" involve?
Qatar has not disclosed them, so anything beyond its public statements remains interpretation.
But Ibrahim Freihat, professor of international conflict at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, has argued that an innovative approach could involve separating the different disputes instead of trying to resolve them through one comprehensive agreement.
"First, separating the issues instead of having all the files intertwined and interconnected. That makes a solution more difficult,” Freihat told Al Jazeera.
He argued that Hormuz itself could be treated as a separate negotiating track.
“Even the Hormuz issue itself could be addressed through a single track without requiring a comprehensive solution to the entire Hormuz question," he said.
Freihat also suggested replacing intermittent negotiating rounds with more permanent dialogue.
"Instead of negotiations taking place in separate rounds, they should become permanent negotiations,” he said. “In conflict terminology, they should become dialogue," he added.
He said a third element would be moving beyond purely bilateral US-Iran talks and giving Gulf countries a greater role in shaping a wider regional security arrangement.
Is there a new Qatari initiative?
Not formally, at least not yet. What Qatar has confirmed is that it is discussing new ideas with its partners, including China, and wants an unconditional reopening of Hormuz while wider diplomatic efforts continue.
The emerging approach therefore appears less like a single dramatic peace plan and more like an effort to break the crisis into manageable parts - reopen shipping, prevent further escalation and create enough political space for US-Iran negotiations to resume.
